definitions.definition: An 'accredited laboratory' is a laboratory that has been accredited by a recognised accreditation body and to which a Food Safety Officer may send one part of a food sample for independent analysis, at the request of the food business operator, as an alternative to the Food Analyst's analysis under Section 47 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
definitions.plain_english: An accredited laboratory is a testing facility that has been officially certified or approved by a recognised authority as competent to carry out food analysis. When a Food Safety Officer collects a food sample, the food business operator can request that one portion of that sample be sent to such a laboratory for independent testing. This provides the business operator a check against the government Food Analyst's findings.
real_world_examples: A biscuit manufacturer in Pune whose sample is collected by a Food Safety Officer requests that one of the four divided parts be sent to an NABL-accredited private food testing laboratory in Mumbai for independent chemical analysis, rather than relying solely on the government Food Analyst's report.

A spice exporter in Kerala, after a Food Safety Officer collects a sample of chilli powder suspected of containing Sudan dye, invokes their right under Section 47 to have one sample part sent to an accredited laboratory to generate an independent test report for comparison.

A Delhi-based dairy company, upon receiving notice that a sample of its packaged milk has been collected for analysis, requests despatch of a sample portion to an FSSAI-recognised accredited laboratory to verify whether fat and SNF content meet prescribed standards.

A packaged drinking water company in Hyderabad, whose product sample was seized during a market inspection, exercises its right to have the sample analysed at an accredited laboratory to contest the findings of the designated Food Analyst if the results differ.

A restaurant chain in Bengaluru operating as a food business operator requests the Food Safety Officer to send one sample portion of its cooking oil to an accredited laboratory after a routine inspection, to independently verify whether trans-fat levels comply with FSSAI regulations.
what_it_covers: A laboratory accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) or any other body recognised under FSSAI regulations, empanelled to analyse food samples collected by Food Safety Officers.

Any private or public food testing facility that holds valid accreditation from a competent authority and is notified or recognised by the Food Authority for the purpose of conducting independent food sample analysis under Section 47.

A laboratory to which the food business operator's requested sample portion is sent, in addition to the government Food Analyst, for the purpose of providing an alternate test report that may be compared against the official findings.
Facilities equipped to conduct chemical, microbiological, or physical analysis of food articles and adulterants in accordance with standards prescribed under the Food Safety and Standards Act.
what_it_excludes: An unaccredited or uncertified private laboratory that has not been approved or recognised by a competent accreditation body, even if it possesses sophisticated testing equipment.

The referral food laboratory designated under the Act for resolving disputes between the Food Analyst's report and the accredited laboratory's report — referral laboratories are a separate, higher-tier institution.
In-house quality control laboratories operated by food manufacturers themselves, which do not have independent accreditation status for the purposes of Section 47 analysis.
Laboratories approved solely for purposes other than food testing (e.g., pharmaceutical or environmental testing laboratories not accredited for food analysis under FSSAI framework).
Government Food Analyst laboratories, which are separately designated under the Act and not classified as 'accredited laboratories' for the purpose of this provision.
definitions.why_it_matters: The use of an accredited laboratory is critical because its test report, when at variance with the Food Analyst's report, triggers the mandatory referral of a sample to the referral laboratory under Section 47, whose decision is final and binding — thereby directly influencing whether a food business operator faces prosecution, penalties, or licence cancellation. The right to invoke an accredited laboratory acts as a statutory safeguard ensuring that enforcement action is not based solely on a single government analysis.

definitions.definition: An officer not below the rank of Additional District Magistrate of the district where the alleged offence is committed, notified by the State Government for the purposes of adjudication under Chapter X of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, who is empowered to inquire into contraventions of the Act, rules, or regulations, and impose penalties after giving the accused a reasonable opportunity of representation.
definitions.plain_english: An Adjudicating Officer is a senior government official (at least at the level of an Additional District Magistrate) appointed by the State Government to hear and decide cases involving violations of food safety laws. This officer can investigate complaints, hold hearings, and impose fines or other penalties on food businesses or individuals who break the rules. They function like a quasi-judicial authority, meaning they have many of the same powers as a civil court.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based snack manufacturer is found selling chips with misleading nutritional labels. The Additional District Magistrate notified as the Adjudicating Officer for that district hears the case, examines evidence from the Food Safety Officer, and imposes a financial penalty of up to three lakh rupees for misbranding.

A dairy company in Lucknow distributes adulterated milk that causes food poisoning and the death of a consumer. The Adjudicating Officer, after inquiry, orders the company to pay compensation of not less than five lakh rupees to the victim's legal heir and directs cancellation of the company's licence.

A street food vendor in Chennai repeatedly sells food under unsanitary conditions in violation of FSSAI regulations. The Adjudicating Officer, noting the repetitive nature of the contravention as required under Section 49, levies a higher penalty and issues a prohibition order against the vendor.

A Kolkata-based importer brings in a consignment of food products that are found to be sub-standard upon testing. The Adjudicating Officer for the district where the import was held conducts adjudication proceedings, considers the extent of loss caused to consumers, and imposes an appropriate penalty while directing recall of the food from the market.

A small packaged water company in Hyderabad is found to be manufacturing water without a valid licence. The Adjudicating Officer, after providing the company a reasonable opportunity to be heard, imposes a penalty and orders forfeiture of the manufacturing premises in view of the grievous public health risk posed.
what_it_covers: An officer of the rank of Additional District Magistrate or above, notified by the State Government for the district where the alleged food safety offence occurred.
Authority to adjudicate contraventions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, its rules and regulations, and to impose penalties as prescribed under Chapter X.
Power to award compensation to victims or their legal representatives in cases of injury or death caused by unsafe food.
Power to order corrective actions such as recall of food from the market, cancellation of licence, forfeiture of establishment, and publication of the offender's name at the offender's expense.
All proceedings before the Adjudicating Officer, which are deemed judicial proceedings under Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code.
what_it_excludes: Judicial officers of a regular criminal or civil court who may independently try food safety offences; the Adjudicating Officer is a distinct quasi-judicial authority.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (Food Authority) or its CEO, who perform regulatory and standard-setting functions rather than adjudicatory functions under Chapter X.
The Tribunal (Food Safety Appellate Tribunal), which is a separate appellate body and not the same as the Adjudicating Officer, even though both may adjudge penalties under certain provisions.
Food Safety Officers or Designated Officers, who are empowered to inspect, sample, and enforce but do not have the adjudicatory or penalty-imposing powers vested in the Adjudicating Officer.
Officers below the rank of Additional District Magistrate, who cannot be notified as Adjudicating Officers regardless of their food safety-related duties.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of a person as an Adjudicating Officer determines which authority has the legal power to conduct inquiries, impose financial penalties, award victim compensation, and issue orders such as licence cancellations or market recalls under Chapter X of the Act; without a validly notified Adjudicating Officer, penalty proceedings against food business operators for civil contraventions cannot be lawfully initiated or concluded. This definition also triggers the application of civil court procedural protections, making all proceedings before the officer deemed judicial proceedings with attendant legal consequences for perjury and contempt.

Their proceedings carry the same legal weight as court proceedings.
real_world_examples: A food manufacturer in Pune is found selling adulterated milk products. The State Government notifies the Additional District Magistrate of Pune as the Adjudicating Officer, who conducts an inquiry, gives the manufacturer a chance to present their case, and imposes a monetary penalty under the Act.

A consumer in Chennai dies after consuming a contaminated packaged snack. The Adjudicating Officer of the relevant district is approached to direct the manufacturer to pay compensation of not less than five lakh rupees to the legal representative of the deceased as provided under Section 65.

A Delhi-based food distributor is repeatedly found selling misbranded spices. The Adjudicating Officer, noting the repetitive nature of the contravention as required by Section 49 guidelines, imposes an enhanced penalty of up to three lakh rupees and orders corrective action or destruction of the misbranded stock.

In a Kolkata suburb, a street food vendor causes grievous injury to multiple consumers due to unsafe food preparation. The Adjudicating Officer orders cancellation of the vendor's licence, recalls the food from the market, and directs the publication of the offender's name and details in local newspapers at the offender's expense.

A food importer in Mumbai is found importing food articles without proper labelling. The Adjudicating Officer summoned witnesses and examined documents using civil court powers under Section 68, ensuring a fair inquiry before imposing the prescribed penalty.
what_it_covers: An officer holding the rank of Additional District Magistrate or above, notified by the State Government for the specific district where the alleged food safety offence occurred.
Adjudication proceedings involving imposition of civil penalties for contraventions such as selling misbranded, sub-standard, or unsafe food under Chapter X of the Act.
Powers to award monetary compensation to injured consumers or legal representatives of deceased consumers, order recall of food products, cancel licences, and issue prohibition orders.
Authority to summon persons, receive evidence, and conduct proceedings that are deemed judicial proceedings under Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code.
Directions to publish the name and details of guilty food business operators in newspapers at the offender's expense in cases of grievous injury or death.
what_it_excludes: Judicial magistrates or sessions court judges who try criminal offences under the Act — those are handled by the Special Court or designated criminal courts, not the Adjudicating Officer.
Food Safety Officers or Designated Officers who perform inspections, sampling, and licensing functions — their roles are distinct and do not include adjudicatory powers under Chapter X.
Officers below the rank of Additional District Magistrate, who cannot be notified as Adjudicating Officers regardless of their administrative seniority within other departments.
The Food Safety Appellate Tribunal, which hears appeals against orders of the Adjudicating Officer and is a separate authority with distinct jurisdiction.
Central Government officials acting in that capacity — the Adjudicating Officer is specifically a State Government-notified officer with jurisdiction confined to the district of the alleged offence.

definitions.definition: "adulterant" means any material which is or could be employed for making the food unsafe or sub-standard or mis-branded or containing extraneous matter.
definitions.plain_english: An adulterant is any substance or material that is used — or could be used — to make food harmful, below standard, falsely labelled, or contaminated with foreign matter. It does not have to actually be mixed into food yet; even a material that has the potential to be used for this purpose qualifies. This definition is broad and covers both intentional and potential misuse of substances in food.
real_world_examples: A vendor in a Delhi spice market mixes brick powder or red chalk into chilli powder to increase weight and mimic colour — the brick powder is an adulterant because it makes the food sub-standard and unsafe.
A dairy supplier in Uttar Pradesh adds water and urea to buffalo milk to increase volume and protein readings — urea here is an adulterant as it makes the milk unsafe for human consumption.

A Kolkata-based trader stores industrial-grade colour dyes (such as metanil yellow) alongside food intended for use in sweets — even before mixing, these dyes qualify as adulterants due to their potential employment to make food unsafe.

A rice mill operator in Punjab mixes discoloured, pest-damaged grains with premium basmati rice to inflate quantity — the inferior grains constitute an adulterant as they render the food sub-standard.
A street food operator in Mumbai uses non-food-grade starch to thicken gravies, which, when detected by a Food Safety Officer, is identified as an adulterant because it could make the food unsafe.

A ghee manufacturer in Rajasthan blends vegetable fat or vanaspati with pure ghee without declaring it on the label — the undisclosed vegetable fat is an adulterant as it causes the product to be mis-branded.
what_it_covers: Non-food substances intentionally mixed into food to increase weight or volume, such as chalk in flour or sand in spices.
Toxic or harmful chemicals added to food to enhance appearance, such as industrial dyes used in sweets or vegetables.
Inferior or substandard ingredients substituted for genuine ones, such as vanaspati blended into pure ghee without disclosure.
Materials not yet added to food but kept available and intended for use in adulteration, given the definition covers materials that 'could be employed'.
Substances that cause food to be mis-branded, such as artificial flavours or non-permitted colours used to pass off an inferior product as a premium one.
what_it_excludes: Contaminants that are unintentionally present in food as a result of environmental pollution, manufacturing processes, or packaging — these are separately defined as 'contaminant' under Section 3.

Extraneous matter that does not render food unsafe, such as incidental carry-over from raw materials or packaging materials, which falls under the distinct definition of 'extraneous matter' in Section 3.
Permitted food additives added within prescribed regulatory limits for legitimate technological purposes, as these are authorised under the Act and its regulations and do not qualify as adulterants.
Naturally occurring variations in food composition or quality degradation due to normal storage, which do not involve deliberate employment of any material.
Approved processing aids or preservatives used within permissible limits as specified by the Food Authority under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a substance as an adulterant directly triggers serious penal liability under Sections 38, 39, 41, 47, and 57 of the Act, including imprisonment and heavy fines for manufacture, storage, sale, or distribution of adulterated food. Whether a material qualifies as an adulterant determines whether a food business operator faces criminal prosecution, licence cancellation, or product seizure by a Food Safety Officer or Designated Officer.

definitions.definition: "advertisement" means any audio or visual publicity, representation or pronouncement made by means of any light, sound, smoke, gas, print, electronic media, internet or website and includes through any notice, circular, label, wrapper, invoice or other documents.
definitions.plain_english: An advertisement is any form of promotion or communication about food — whether seen, heard, or read — that is put out through any medium including TV, radio, internet, print, or even a label or invoice. It covers anything that promotes or represents a food product to the public. This broad definition ensures that no form of food promotion can escape regulatory scrutiny.
real_world_examples: A television commercial aired on Doordarshan or Star Plus promoting Maggi noodles as 'healthy' and 'nutritious' constitutes an advertisement under the Act, making any misleading health claims actionable.

A WhatsApp forward or Instagram sponsored post by a food delivery app like Zomato claiming that a particular packaged snack is 'zero sugar' qualifies as an advertisement through electronic media or internet.
A product wrapper on a packet of Haldiram's namkeen bearing the text 'No Artificial Colours' is considered an advertisement, as the definition explicitly includes wrappers and labels.

A circular distributed by a local dairy in Mumbai announcing that its milk is 'certified A2 and free from adulterants' is covered under the definition as it constitutes a visual representation through a notice or circular.
A roadside hoarding in Delhi bearing a food brand logo and nutritional claims for a health drink falls within 'print' and 'visual publicity' covered by the definition.

An invoice issued by a wholesale distributor that describes a consignment of edible oil as 'cold-pressed and chemical-free' constitutes an advertisement as invoices are explicitly included in the definition.
what_it_covers: Television and radio commercials promoting food products, including jingles and video spots broadcast on mainstream or digital channels.
Online content including social media posts, banner ads, influencer promotions, website landing pages, and email newsletters promoting food items.
Physical wrappers, labels, invoices, circulars, and notices that carry representations about the nature, quality, or composition of a food product.
Outdoor hoardings, banners, and pamphlets that visually publicise food products with claims about their benefits or characteristics.
Audio announcements or sound-based promotions at retail outlets, exhibitions, or food fairs that describe or promote food products.
what_it_excludes: Internal company documents or communications that are not intended for public dissemination and make no representation to consumers about a food product.
Scientific or technical research papers and academic publications that describe food compositions without any intent to promote or sell a product.
Regulatory or government-issued notices and communications about food safety recalls or warnings, which are official communications and not promotional in nature.
Private conversations or word-of-mouth recommendations between individuals that do not constitute a formal or organised publicity campaign.
Stock records or inventory management documents that merely list food items without making any quality, health, or nature-related representation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a communication qualifies as an 'advertisement' under the Act determines whether it is subject to the restrictions and prohibitions under Sections 24 and 53, which prohibit misleading advertisements about food products and prescribe penalties of up to ten lakh rupees for violations. A broad coverage of this definition ensures that food business operators cannot evade liability by using unconventional media channels — digital, documentary, or otherwise — to make false or misleading representations about their products.

definitions.definition: "article of food" is not separately defined in the Act but is used synonymously with "food" as defined in section 3(j): any substance, whether processed, partially processed or unprocessed, which is intended for human consumption and includes primary food, genetically modified or engineered food, infant food, packaged drinking water, alcoholic drink, chewing gum, and any substance including water used in the food during its manufacture, preparation or treatment.
definitions.plain_english: An 'article of food' refers to any item that a person eats or drinks, or that goes into making something to be eaten or drunk. This includes everything from raw vegetables and grains to packaged snacks, bottled water, and alcoholic beverages. Essentially, if it is meant to be consumed by a human being, it counts as an article of food under this law.
real_world_examples: A packet of Maggi instant noodles sold at a kirana store in Mumbai is an article of food subject to labelling and safety standards under the Act.
A bottle of packaged drinking water sold by a local manufacturer in Delhi under a private label is treated as an article of food, requiring licensing and compliance with quality standards.
Homemade ghee prepared by a dairy farmer in Anand, Gujarat and sold in local markets qualifies as an article of food and must meet the prescribed standards for milk fat products.
A mithai shop in Kolkata selling freshly prepared rasgullas is dealing in articles of food, making the shop owner a food business operator liable to inspections by Food Safety Officers.
Imported olive oil arriving at Chennai Port is an article of food subject to import regulations, sampling, and testing before it can be cleared for sale in India.
A cold drink manufacturer in Hyderabad producing carbonated beverages is manufacturing articles of food and must obtain a valid licence under the Act.
what_it_covers: Packaged and processed food products such as biscuits, chips, and ready-to-eat meals sold across India.
Packaged drinking water and non-alcoholic and alcoholic beverages including fruit juices, beer, and spirits.
Raw agricultural produce such as rice, wheat, and pulses when sold for human consumption.
Infant food and infant milk substitutes as defined under the Infant Milk Substitutes Act.
Genetically modified or engineered food products and food containing GM ingredients.
Chewing gum and any substance including water used during the manufacture or preparation of food.
what_it_excludes: Animal feed and fodder not intended for human consumption, such as cattle feed or poultry feed.
Live animals unless they have been prepared or processed for placing on the market for human consumption.
Plants prior to harvesting, such as standing crops in a field.
Drugs and medicinal products regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.
Cosmetics, narcotic substances, and psychotropic substances.
Substances that, although ingested, are classified as medicines and do not fall within the food category under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of something as an 'article of food' is the foundational trigger for the entire regulatory machinery under the Act — including licensing obligations, safety and quality standards, labelling requirements, sampling and analysis powers of Food Safety Officers, and penal provisions under sections 51 to 67 for offences such as selling sub-standard, misbranded, or unsafe food. If an item does not qualify as an article of food, none of these obligations or penalties apply.

definitions.definition: An 'authorised officer' under the Food Safety and Standards Act means an officer of the Food Authority who is duly empowered to take samples of imported articles of food and to perform related functions as assigned under the Act, particularly in respect of food imported into India, and who is required to follow such procedure as may be specified by regulations.
definitions.plain_english: An authorised officer is an official working under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) who has been given the legal power to collect food samples — especially from imported food products — and send them to approved laboratories for testing. Think of them as the FSSAI's frontline inspector at ports, airports, or border checkpoints. They ensure that food entering India meets safety standards before it reaches consumers.
real_world_examples: An authorised officer of FSSAI posted at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT), Mumbai, draws samples from a consignment of imported Chinese instant noodles and sends them to a notified laboratory to check for unsafe additives or contaminants.

At Indira Gandhi International Airport in Delhi, an authorised officer intercepts a shipment of imported Australian dairy products, takes samples, and dispatches them to an FSSAI-notified food laboratory for analysis within the prescribed timeline.

During a routine check at Chennai Port, an authorised officer finds a consignment of imported palm oil from Malaysia, collects samples as per the prescribed procedure under Section 47, and forwards the report to the Food Authority within five days.

An authorised officer at the Petrapole land border crossing in West Bengal samples imported Bangladeshi biscuits to verify compliance with Indian food safety standards before permitting their clearance into the domestic market.

An FSSAI authorised officer at an inland container depot in Tughlakabad, Delhi, inspects and samples a batch of imported energy drinks from Thailand suspected of containing prohibited substances, initiating enforcement action based on the laboratory report received within five days.
what_it_covers: An officer of the Food Authority (FSSAI) specifically empowered to collect samples from imported articles of food at ports, airports, land borders, or inland container depots.
The act of sending collected samples from imported food to a notified food laboratory and receiving the analysis report within five days, as mandated under Section 47(5).
Following procedural regulations prescribed by FSSAI regarding sampling, sealing, documentation, and dispatch of imported food samples for analysis.
Officers authorised to take regulatory action on imported food consignments based on laboratory findings, including initiating proceedings for non-compliant imports.
what_it_excludes: A Food Safety Officer appointed under State or UT governments, who deals with domestic food businesses and is separately defined and empowered under the Act.

A Designated Officer, who is a State-level official responsible for receiving and safe-keeping samples and adjudicating complaints under the Act, distinct from the authorised officer's import-focused role.
Private food safety auditors or third-party inspectors engaged by food business operators, who have no statutory power to collect official samples or send them to notified laboratories.
Customs officers or personnel from other regulatory bodies such as the Plant Quarantine Authority or Drug Inspectors, who may inspect imports but are not 'authorised officers' under this Act.
A Food Analyst, whose role is confined to laboratory testing and reporting, not to sampling or field enforcement activities.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of 'authorised officer' is critical because it exclusively confers the legal power to sample imported food and trigger the mandatory five-day laboratory analysis process under Section 47(5); any sampling done by an unauthorised person would be procedurally invalid, potentially rendering enforcement actions and import rejections legally untenable. It also determines accountability in the regulatory chain, as the authorised officer is bound by FSSAI regulations and is the recipient of the Food Analyst's report, which forms the basis for further regulatory or penal action against non-compliant importers.

definitions.definition: A 'batch' refers to a definite quantity of food of the same class or description produced under essentially the same conditions and within a defined period, such that where any food in that batch fails to comply with food safety requirements, it shall be presumed until the contrary is proved that all food in that batch also fails to comply with those requirements.
definitions.plain_english: A batch is a specific group or quantity of food items that were made together, at the same time, under the same conditions, and are considered to be of the same type and quality. If one item in a batch is found to be unsafe or defective, the law presumes that all other items in that same batch are also unsafe or defective. This presumption can be challenged by proving otherwise, but the default assumption favors consumer protection.
real_world_examples: A biscuit manufacturer in Pune produces 10,000 packets of cream biscuits in a single production run on a given date using the same raw materials and machinery. If FSSAI inspectors test one packet and find it contains a harmful contaminant, all 10,000 packets from that same production run are presumed unsafe under the batch presumption rule.

A dairy cooperative in Amul, Gujarat, processes and packages 5,000 litres of pasteurised milk into 500ml pouches on a particular morning shift. If one pouch from that shift tests positive for antibiotic residues exceeding permitted limits, the entire morning-shift batch of pouches is presumed non-compliant until the cooperative proves otherwise.

A Mumbai-based importer brings in a shipment of canned fish from Thailand, all produced in the same facility on the same production date with the same batch code. Customs food safety testing finds one can to have elevated heavy metal levels, triggering the presumption that all cans in that batch are unsafe, potentially leading to rejection of the entire consignment.

A small-scale pickle manufacturer in Rajasthan bottles 2,000 jars of mango pickle in a single production session. A food safety officer collects a sample from the market and the food analyst finds the acidity level non-compliant. The entire batch of 2,000 jars is presumed sub-standard, allowing authorities to recall or seize all jars bearing the same batch code.

A bakery chain in Bengaluru bakes and packages 500 units of whole-wheat bread loaves in one morning bake. A consumer complaint leads to testing which reveals mould contamination in a sampled loaf. The batch presumption applies, and all 500 loaves from that bake are treated as unsafe pending contrary evidence from the operator.
what_it_covers: All food units produced together in a single production run under the same conditions, bearing the same batch identification code or marker.
Packaged food items of the same class or description manufactured within a defined time period by the same food business operator at the same facility.
Imported food consignments where products of the same type share a common production date, facility, and batch identifier, subject to group-level compliance scrutiny.
Processed food items such as beverages, dairy products, snacks, or canned goods grouped together as a definite quantity from a continuous or single-session manufacturing process.
what_it_excludes: Food items of the same type but produced in separate, distinct production runs on different dates or under materially different conditions, which would constitute separate batches.
Fresh, unpackaged primary agricultural produce sold directly by farmers or fishermen, as Section 18(3) explicitly exempts farming operations and farm-level produce from the Act's provisions.
Food from different lots or consignments that happen to be of the same class or description but do not share a common production batch identity, origin, or production date.
Individual food items that are custom-prepared or made-to-order for specific consumers and are not part of any grouped or standardized production run.
definitions.why_it_matters: The legal consequence of the batch definition is critical: once a sample from a batch is found non-compliant with food safety requirements, a statutory presumption under Section 18(1)(g) arises that the entire batch is non-compliant, shifting the burden of proof to the food business operator to disprove it. This triggers obligations and potential liabilities under Sections 26 and related penal provisions, enabling authorities to recall, seize, or destroy all food in the batch and impose penalties on the operator without needing to test every individual unit.

definitions.definition: The Central Advisory Committee is a Committee established by the Food Authority under Section 11 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, consisting of representatives of food industry, agriculture, consumers, relevant research bodies, food laboratories, all Commissioners of Food Safety, and the Chairperson of the Scientific Committee as ex officio member, with the Chief Executive Officer serving as its ex officio Chairperson, whose primary function is to ensure close cooperation between the Food Authority and enforcement agencies and to advise the Food Authority on its work programmes, prioritisation, risk identification, and pooling of knowledge.
definitions.plain_english: The Central Advisory Committee is an official advisory body set up under India's food safety law to bring together representatives from various sectors — including food industry, farming, consumer groups, research bodies, and food labs — along with state-level food safety commissioners. It acts as a bridge between the Food Authority (FSSAI) and the people who actually enforce food safety rules on the ground. The committee advises FSSAI on its plans, priorities, and potential food safety risks, and also plays a role in recommending fees to be charged to food businesses and auditors.
real_world_examples: When FSSAI drafts its annual work programme, the Chief Executive Officer consults the Central Advisory Committee to incorporate inputs from food industry players like dairy cooperatives, consumer advocacy groups such as Consumer VOICE, and state food commissioners from Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu before finalising priorities.

During the outbreak of a food adulteration incident involving edible oils in Rajasthan, the Central Advisory Committee is convened at the request of one-third of its members to identify the risk, pool knowledge from accredited laboratories, and advise FSSAI on prioritising inspections and regulatory action.

When FSSAI considers recommending a graded fee structure for licensed food business operators such as large packaged food manufacturers versus small petty retailers, the Food Authority acts on the formal recommendation of the Central Advisory Committee before specifying fees to be charged by Commissioners of Food Safety under Section 82.

A representative of the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, attending as an invitee to a Central Advisory Committee meeting, provides inputs on relaxing certain labelling requirements for small-scale pickle manufacturers, which the committee then incorporates into its advisory recommendations to the Food Authority.

The Central Advisory Committee meets at least three times a year, and during one such meeting, it reviews feedback from food laboratories across India about recurring contaminants in spices, leading it to recommend that FSSAI prioritise a nationwide sampling drive for spice adulteration.

A consumer representative on the Central Advisory Committee raises concerns about misleading health claims on packaged nutraceuticals sold online, prompting the committee to advise FSSAI to add this issue to its work programme and engage the relevant Scientific Panel for a risk assessment.
what_it_covers: Representatives from the food industry, agriculture sector, consumer groups, relevant research bodies, and food laboratories appointed as members of the committee.
All Commissioners of Food Safety from various states as members, and the Chairperson of the Scientific Committee as an ex officio member.
The advisory function of recommending graded fees for licensed food business operators, accredited laboratories, and food safety auditors under Section 82.
The function of advising FSSAI on its work programme, prioritisation of tasks, identification of potential food safety risks, and pooling of scientific and technical knowledge.

Representatives of Central Government Ministries (Agriculture, Health, Consumer Affairs, Food Processing Industries, etc.) and government-recognised farmers' organisations attending as invitees to committee deliberations.
what_it_excludes: Private individuals or members of the general public who are not formally appointed representatives of the specified sectors or Ministries.
State-level advisory committees or bodies constituted by State Food Safety Authorities, which are separate from the Central Advisory Committee.

The Scientific Committee and Scientific Panels, which are distinct technical bodies under the Food Authority responsible for scientific risk assessments and not part of the Central Advisory Committee.
Adjudicating Officers and Designated Officers, who are enforcement and adjudicatory functionaries and do not form part of the Central Advisory Committee's composition.
Foreign government representatives or international food safety bodies, which have no formal role in the Central Advisory Committee's structure or deliberations.
definitions.why_it_matters: The Central Advisory Committee's advisory role is legally significant because the Food Authority's work programme and fee specifications under Section 82 require its recommendation or consultation, meaning any fee imposed on food business operators or accredited laboratories without such recommendation could be challenged as procedurally invalid. Its function of ensuring cooperation between FSSAI and enforcement agencies also directly influences the prioritisation of inspections, sampling drives, and regulatory actions that determine compliance obligations and penalties for food business operators across India.

definitions.definition: "Chairperson" means the Chairperson of the Food Authority.
definitions.plain_english: The Chairperson is the head of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI). This person leads the governing body of the FSSAI and plays a central role in its decision-making and administration. The position is the highest individual authority within the Food Authority.
real_world_examples: When the FSSAI needs to convene a meeting of its full board to approve new food safety regulations for packaged snacks, the Chairperson presides over and directs that meeting.

If a dispute arises among Members of the Food Authority regarding permissible limits of a food additive, the Chairperson exercises a casting vote or decisive authority to resolve the deadlock as provided under the Act.

During a national food safety emergency such as contaminated cooking oil affecting multiple states, the Chairperson coordinates with the Central Government and state authorities to initiate urgent regulatory action.

When the Food Authority is required to submit its annual report or recommendations to the Central Government regarding adulteration in spices, the Chairperson signs and forwards the official communication on behalf of the Authority.

In proceedings under Section 17 where the Food Authority exercises its powers, the Chairperson's office is the reference point for issuing directions to food business operators and state food safety authorities across India.

Any person acting in the capacity of Chairperson when the substantive appointee is absent or during a vacancy, to the extent permitted under the Act.

what_it_excludes: The Chief Executive Officer of the Food Authority, who is a separate statutory functionary with distinct administrative responsibilities.
Members of the Food Authority, whether ex officio or otherwise, who participate in the Food Authority's proceedings but do not hold the office of Chairperson.

State-level food safety officials such as the Commissioner of Food Safety or State Authority heads, who operate under parallel state-level structures and are not the Chairperson of the central Food Authority.
Any member of a Scientific Committee or Scientific Panel, whose roles are advisory and technical in nature rather than executive or presiding.

definitions.definition: The Chief Executive Officer is an officer of the Food Authority, not below the rank of Additional Secretary to the Government of India, appointed by the Central Government, who serves as the Member-Secretary of the Food Authority and is its legal representative, responsible for day-to-day administration, implementation of work programmes, financial oversight, and exercising the powers of the Commissioner of Food Safety in matters relating to food safety of articles of food.
definitions.plain_english: The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) is the top full-time executive who runs the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on a day-to-day basis. Appointed by the Central Government, this person must be a senior Indian Administrative Service or equivalent officer of at least Additional Secretary rank. The CEO acts as the legal face of the Authority, manages its staff and budget, chairs the Central Advisory Committee, and also holds the powers of a Commissioner of Food Safety when dealing with food safety matters.
real_world_examples: When FSSAI issues a nationwide recall order for adulterated spices found to contain excessive pesticide residues, the CEO signs off on the enforcement decision and communicates it to State Governments as the legal representative of the Food Authority.

The CEO of FSSAI chairs a Central Advisory Committee meeting in New Delhi where representatives from the food industry, consumer groups, and agricultural bodies deliberate on new labelling regulations for packaged snack foods sold across India.

After the close of a financial year, the CEO submits the annual accounts, a general activity report, and the proposed budget for the coming year to the Food Authority Board for approval, and then forwards these to the Central Government and all State Governments.

During a sudden outbreak of food poisoning linked to a popular ready-to-eat brand in Maharashtra, the CEO exercises the powers of the Commissioner of Food Safety to direct inspections, order product seizures, and coordinate with state authorities without waiting for state-level action.

The CEO approves expenditure for setting up a new FSSAI-accredited referral food laboratory in Hyderabad to strengthen testing capacity in southern India, exercising financial approval authority over all Authority expenditure.

When a foreign government raises concerns about Indian food exports not meeting their standards, the CEO engages directly with the Ministry of Commerce and the relevant embassy as part of maintaining regular dialogue between the Food Authority and the Central Government.

definitions.definition: "claim" means any representation which states, suggests, or implies that a food has particular qualities relating to its origin, nutritional properties, nature, processing, composition or otherwise.
definitions.plain_english: A 'claim' is any statement, suggestion, or implication made about a food product that tells consumers something special about it — such as where it came from, what nutrients it contains, how it was made, or what it is made of. This includes both direct statements and indirect hints. For example, saying a biscuit is 'high in fibre' or 'made with real fruit' is a claim.
real_world_examples: A popular Indian packaged atta (wheat flour) brand printing '100% whole wheat' on its packaging — this is a compositional claim that must be accurate and verifiable under FSSAI regulations.

A fruit juice brand advertising on television that its product contains 'no added sugar' — this is a nutritional claim implying the product is healthier, triggering FSSAI labelling and advertising compliance requirements.
An organic dal brand labelling its product as 'certified organic, sourced from Madhya Pradesh farms' — this is both an origin claim and a processing/quality claim that must be substantiated.

A probiotic yoghurt brand like Yakult or Epigamia stating 'contains live cultures that support gut health' on its packaging — this is a health/nutritional properties claim subject to FSSAI approval and scientific substantiation.
A bottled water company printing 'Himalayan mineral water — naturally alkaline' on its label — this is an origin and compositional claim that must meet FSSAI standards for packaged drinking water.
An energy drink advertised on social media as 'boosts stamina and athletic performance' — this implied health benefit constitutes a claim under the Act, requiring regulatory compliance.
what_it_covers: Explicit statements on packaging such as 'rich in Vitamin C' or 'high protein' that assert nutritional properties of the food.
Implied representations through imagery or language suggesting a food is natural, organic, or traditionally processed (e.g., 'grandma's recipe' implying traditional preparation).
Origin-based claims such as 'Darjeeling tea' or 'Alphonso mangoes from Ratnagiri' that link the food to a specific geographic source.
Processing claims like 'cold-pressed', 'stone-ground', or 'minimally processed' that suggest a particular method of manufacture.
Compositional claims such as 'contains zero trans fat', 'gluten-free', or 'made with real honey' that describe what the food is or is not made of.
Audio-visual representations in advertisements that suggest a food has superior health, quality, or safety attributes compared to others.
what_it_excludes: Mandatory statutory information required on labels such as net weight, batch number, or expiry date, which are regulatory disclosures rather than quality or property claims.
Generic product names or category descriptions (e.g., 'milk', 'bread', 'rice') that do not assert any particular quality, origin, or nutritional property.
Pricing or quantity-related representations (e.g., 'buy one get one free' or '500g pack') that relate to commercial terms rather than food qualities.
Hazard warnings or allergen declarations mandated by law, which are safety disclosures and not claims about positive qualities of the food.
Statements of identity such as 'vegetarian' or 'non-vegetarian' symbols mandated by FSSAI regulations, which are classification markers rather than quality claims.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a representation qualifies as a 'claim' determines whether FSSAI's regulations on labelling, advertising standards, and food safety audits apply — false or unsubstantiated claims can constitute misbranding or unfair trade practice under the Act, exposing food business operators to penalties, licence cancellation, and prosecution. It also governs what must be verified during a food safety audit, as the audit scope explicitly includes examining whether claims made by manufacturers are met.

definitions.definition: Cognizance, as used in the Food Safety and Standards Act, refers to the formal act of a court or Special Court taking notice of and assuming jurisdiction over an alleged offence under the Act, thereby initiating legal proceedings against the accused. A court takes cognizance when it applies its judicial mind to the facts of the case for the purpose of proceeding with the trial. No court shall take cognizance of an offence under this Act after the expiry of one year from the date of commission of the offence, subject to extension up to three years with written approval of the Commissioner of Food Safety.
definitions.plain_english: Cognizance means the moment when a court officially recognises and takes up a case for trial. Think of it as the court formally 'accepting' a complaint or case and deciding to proceed with it. Under food safety law, there is a strict time limit — usually one year from the date of the offence — within which a court must take up the case, or it loses the right to do so. This time limit is meant to ensure that legal action is taken promptly after a food safety violation occurs.
real_world_examples: A food inspector in Mumbai collects a sample of adulterated spices from a manufacturer in January 2023. If the Commissioner of Food Safety does not initiate prosecution and no court takes cognizance of the offence by January 2024, the case is time-barred and the manufacturer cannot be prosecuted unless the Commissioner approves an extension in writing.

A Special Court in Delhi takes cognizance of a case involving a large food company accused of selling misbranded packaged food. Mid-trial, the court realises the offence falls outside its special jurisdiction and transfers the case to the appropriate Chief Judicial Magistrate court under the CrPC, which then proceeds as if it had originally taken cognizance.

After the commencement of the FSS Act, a court in Chennai is approached to try an offence under the repealed Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. Since more than three years have passed since the FSS Act commenced, the court declines to take cognizance, as the window under Section 97 has closed.

A food safety officer in Hyderabad files a complaint against a restaurant for serving unsafe food containing pesticide residues above tolerance limits. The magistrate studies the complaint, applies judicial mind, and takes cognizance, issuing summons to the restaurant owner — formally beginning the prosecution process.

In a case involving a petty manufacturer in Kolkata who sold sub-standard food in March 2022, the Commissioner of Food Safety records written reasons and approves an extended prosecution period. A court takes cognizance in February 2025, which is within the extended three-year limit, validating the proceedings.
what_it_covers: A Special Court formally assuming jurisdiction over a food safety offence and beginning trial proceedings against a food business operator or manufacturer.
A regular criminal court taking cognizance of a food safety case transferred from a Special Court that found the offence outside its triable jurisdiction.
A Magistrate taking cognizance of a complaint filed by a food safety officer within the one-year limitation period, thereby issuing summons or warrants to the accused.
Courts taking cognizance of offences under repealed food safety enactments within three years of the FSS Act's commencement, as preserved under Section 97.
Extended cognizance proceedings where the Commissioner of Food Safety has approved prosecution beyond one year but within three years, with written reasons on record.
what_it_excludes: Administrative or departmental actions such as issuing improvement notices, penalty orders, or licence cancellations by food safety authorities, which do not involve a court taking cognizance.
Any attempt by a court to take cognizance of an offence after the one-year limitation period has expired without written approval from the Commissioner of Food Safety for extension.
Proceedings before the Adjudicating Officer or the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal, which are not courts taking cognizance in the criminal law sense.
Preliminary investigative steps by food safety officers such as inspection, sampling, or issuing notices, which precede and do not constitute cognizance.
Cognizance of offences under laws entirely unrelated to food safety, even if the accused is also a food business operator.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether and when a court takes cognizance determines whether a criminal prosecution under the FSS Act can validly proceed — failure to take cognizance within the prescribed limitation period permanently bars prosecution of the offender, regardless of the severity of the food safety violation. It also governs jurisdictional boundaries between Special Courts and regular criminal courts, directly affecting the accused's right to a properly constituted trial.

definitions.definition: In relation to Section 66 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, 'company' means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals. Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a company, every person who at the time the offence was committed was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence.
definitions.plain_english: A 'company' in the context of the Food Safety and Standards Act refers to any registered corporate body, partnership firm, or group of people acting together as a business entity in the food sector. When such a company breaks the rules under this Act, not just the company itself but also the individuals who were running it and responsible for its day-to-day operations can be held personally guilty. This ensures that the people actually making decisions cannot hide behind the company's legal identity to escape punishment.
real_world_examples: A large packaged snacks manufacturer like a private limited company registered in Mumbai sells chips found to contain unsafe levels of trans fats; both the company and its Managing Director can be prosecuted under Section 66.

A partnership firm running a chain of restaurant outlets in Delhi is found using adulterated cooking oil; all partners who were in charge of business operations at the time of the offence are personally liable alongside the firm.

A cooperative society engaged in dairy processing in Gujarat is found selling milk that does not meet the prescribed standards; the directors or persons in charge of the cooperative can be held guilty along with the cooperative body.

A public limited company operating a nationwide distribution network for packaged drinking water is found to be selling sub-standard water; the CEO and executive directors responsible for operations can be prosecuted personally in addition to the company.

A limited liability partnership (LLP) involved in importing food ingredients from abroad is found to have imported consignments with prohibited pesticide residues; the designated partners managing imports are personally liable under Section 66.

A sole proprietorship registered as a 'company' or trading concern running a bakery chain in Chennai is caught misbranding products with false nutritional claims; the proprietor as the person in charge is deemed guilty.
what_it_covers: Registered private and public limited companies incorporated under the Companies Act engaged in any food business activity.
Partnership firms and limited liability partnerships (LLPs) operating in the food manufacturing, processing, distribution, or sale sector.
Any association of individuals, cooperative societies, or unincorporated bodies carrying out food business operations collectively.
Every director, manager, secretary, or other officer of the company who was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the company's food business at the time of the offence.
A company that has committed an offence through negligence or lack of oversight by the persons managing it.
what_it_excludes: Individual sole proprietors acting in their personal capacity who are not part of any association or body corporate.
A director or officer who proves that the offence was committed without their knowledge or that they exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence.
Government departments or statutory bodies acting in a purely regulatory or administrative capacity rather than as a food business operator.
Employees of the company who are neither in charge of nor responsible for the conduct of the business and had no role in the commission of the offence.
Individual consumers or end-users who are not engaged in any food business activity.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'company' under Section 66 is critical because it extends criminal liability beyond the corporate entity itself to the individual officers and persons in charge, ensuring that directors and managers cannot use the corporate veil as a shield against prosecution for food safety offences. It determines who can be charged, convicted, fined, or imprisoned when a corporate food business operator violates standards related to unsafe food, adulteration, misbranding, or sub-standard products under the Act.

definitions.definition: "Competent authority" means the authority designated or recognised under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 or the Customs Act, 1962, or any other applicable Act, having the power to permit or order the disposal, destruction, or return of imported articles of food found to be in contravention of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006; and in the context of food recall procedures, it refers to the food safety authorities empowered under this Act to receive notifications from food business operators and co-operate in preventing risks to consumers.
definitions.plain_english: A 'competent authority' is the official government body or regulatory agency that has legal power to take action in a given situation. In food import matters, it is the authority under customs or foreign trade laws who can decide what happens to unsafe imported food. In food recall situations, it is the food safety authority that food businesses must immediately inform and work with when they suspect their food is unsafe.
real_world_examples: A consignment of imported Chinese noodles is found to contain banned additives at Chennai port; the Commissioner of Customs, acting as the competent authority under the Customs Act, 1962, orders the consignment to be returned to the importer rather than destroyed.

A Mumbai-based food business operator discovers that a batch of packaged biscuits it distributed across Maharashtra may be contaminated with salmonella; it immediately contacts the Commissioner of Food Safety of Maharashtra as the competent authority to initiate a food recall.

The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), acting as the competent authority under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992, issues an order permitting an importer to re-export a shipment of substandard edible oil seized at Delhi's Inland Container Depot.

An FSSAI-designated Food Safety Officer in Bengaluru is informed by a local juice manufacturer that its cold-pressed juice products may pose a microbial health risk; the officer, acting as the competent authority, co-operates with the operator to withdraw the product from retail shelves across Karnataka.

At Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (NHAVA Sheva), a shipment of imported honey from Germany fails pesticide residue tests; the competent authority under the Customs Act directs its destruction at the port of entry after the importer fails to arrange re-export within the stipulated period.
what_it_covers: The Commissioner of Customs acting under the Customs Act, 1962 to permit or order disposal of non-compliant imported food articles at Indian ports.
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) acting under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 to permit re-export or destruction of non-compliant imported food.
The Commissioner of Food Safety or designated food safety officers under the FSSAI framework who must be informed and co-operated with during food recall procedures under Section 28.
Any other statutory authority recognised under any other applicable Act that has jurisdiction over the import, disposal, or safety management of food articles.
what_it_excludes: Private certification bodies or third-party food safety auditors, who have no statutory enforcement powers under this Act.
Internal compliance officers or quality managers employed by food business operators, as they do not constitute a public statutory authority.
State-level municipal health officers acting in their local sanitation capacity, unless specifically designated under a relevant Act as a competent authority for food import or recall purposes.
Consumer courts or civil courts, which adjudicate disputes but do not exercise regulatory enforcement powers over food imports or recall procedures.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a body qualifies as a 'competent authority' directly determines which agency a food business operator must notify during a food recall under Section 28, and which authority can lawfully permit or order the destruction or return of non-compliant imported food under Section 67. Failure to notify the correct competent authority or non-co-operation with it may expose a food business operator to penalties under this Act in addition to liabilities under the Customs Act, 1962 and the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992.

definitions.definition: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India is the constitutional authority established under Article 148 of the Constitution of India, who is empowered under Section 83 of the Food Safety and Standards Act to audit the accounts of the Food Authority, and any person appointed by him in connection with such audit shall have the same rights and privileges as the Comptroller and Auditor-General generally has in connection with the audit of Government accounts.
definitions.plain_english: The Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) is India's top government auditor, appointed under the Constitution, who independently checks and verifies the financial accounts of government bodies and institutions. In the context of food safety law, the CAG is responsible for auditing the accounts of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to ensure public money is being spent properly. The CAG's audit report on FSSAI's accounts must be placed before Parliament every year.
real_world_examples: The CAG's office conducts an annual audit of FSSAI's expenditure, including funds spent on food testing laboratories and regulatory campaigns, and submits a report to the Central Government, which is then tabled in both Houses of Parliament.
A CAG-appointed auditor visits FSSAI's regional offices in Mumbai and Chennai to inspect financial records, vouchers, and expenditure documents related to food safety enforcement operations.

The Central Government consults the CAG when prescribing the format and form in which FSSAI must prepare and present its annual statement of accounts, ensuring standardisation with government accounting norms.

A CAG audit report reveals irregularities in FSSAI's procurement of food testing equipment, prompting Parliament to raise questions during budget sessions and calling FSSAI leadership for accountability.

The CAG appoints a deputy auditor-general to examine FSSAI's grant utilisation certificates from state food safety authorities, exercising the same rights as the CAG to demand production of books and documents.

Following an audit, the CAG certifies FSSAI's accounts for the financial year 2022-23, and the certified accounts along with the audit report are forwarded by FSSAI to the Central Government for laying before Parliament.
what_it_covers: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India as a constitutional functionary auditing FSSAI's annual accounts and financial records.
Any person duly appointed by the CAG to conduct audit of FSSAI's accounts, who carries the same rights and authority as the CAG in relation to such audit.
The CAG's right to demand production of books, accounts, connected vouchers, other documents and papers, and to inspect any office of the Food Authority.
The CAG's role in consulting with the Central Government on the prescribed form for FSSAI's annual statement of accounts.
The certification of FSSAI's accounts by the CAG or his appointee, and forwarding of the audit report to the Central Government for tabling before each House of Parliament.
what_it_excludes: Private auditors or chartered accountants not appointed by the CAG, who have no authority under Section 83 to audit FSSAI's accounts.
State government auditors or state accountant generals acting independently of the CAG in relation to FSSAI's central accounts.
Internal audit committees or finance officers of FSSAI itself, who do not possess the constitutional audit authority granted to the CAG.
Audit functions relating to private food business operators, manufacturers, or licensees, whose accounts are not subject to CAG oversight under this Act.
Regulatory or enforcement inspections of food premises or food safety standards, which are outside the financial audit mandate of the CAG under Section 83.
definitions.why_it_matters: The involvement of the Comptroller and Auditor-General is critical because it ensures independent constitutional oversight of FSSAI's financial management, and the mandatory tabling of the CAG's audit report before Parliament creates a mechanism of public accountability. Non-compliance by FSSAI with CAG's demands for documents or inspection rights would constitute a breach of statutory duty, potentially triggering parliamentary scrutiny and administrative consequences.

definitions.definition: A consignment, as used in the Food Safety and Standards Act, refers to a quantity of food of the same class or description dispatched, transported, or supplied together as a single unit, such that where any food in that consignment fails to comply with food safety requirements, it shall be presumed until the contrary is proved that all of the food in that consignment fails to comply with those requirements.
definitions.plain_english: A consignment is a specific quantity or shipment of food items of the same type that are sent or delivered together as one group. If one item in the group is found to be unsafe or non-compliant with food safety rules, the law assumes that all items in that entire shipment are also unsafe. This rule helps authorities act quickly to protect public health without having to test every single item individually.
real_world_examples: A truck carrying 500 boxes of packaged biscuits from a manufacturer in Pune to a distributor in Mumbai is a single consignment; if food safety officers find that samples from a few boxes fail safety standards, the entire truckload is presumed non-compliant.

A shipment of 10,000 kg of basmati rice imported through the Nhava Sheva port in Mumbai from Pakistan constitutes a consignment; if any portion is found to contain pesticide residues beyond permissible limits, the whole shipment is presumed to be contaminated.

A cold-chain delivery of 200 cartons of packaged paneer sent by a dairy in Haryana to supermarkets across Delhi-NCR forms a consignment; discovery of one carton with microbial contamination triggers a presumption that all cartons in that delivery are unsafe.

A supply of 1,000 bottles of cooking oil dispatched by a refinery in Gujarat to a wholesale dealer in Rajasthan constitutes a consignment; if any sample drawn by the Food Safety Officer fails the adulteration test, the entire lot is presumed adulterated.

An e-commerce food delivery platform dispatching a batch of 300 ready-to-eat meal kits of the same product type from a central fulfilment centre in Bengaluru to customers across Karnataka forms a consignment under the Act.
what_it_covers: A truck or vehicle load of food products of the same type dispatched together from a manufacturer to a distributor or retailer.
An imported shipment of food items declared under a single bill of lading or customs entry at a port of entry in India.
A batch of packaged food items of the same description sent together by a food business operator through a logistics or cold-chain network.
A delivery of raw food materials of the same class supplied by a primary producer or aggregator to a food processing unit.
what_it_excludes: Individual or isolated food articles that are not part of any grouped shipment or supply, such as a single packet purchased by a retail consumer.
Mixed consignments containing food items of entirely different classes or descriptions that are not covered under the same lot or batch identification.
Agricultural produce at the farm level, as Section 18(3) explicitly excludes farmers, farming operations, crops, and products of crops at the farm level from the Act's provisions.
Food prepared and served immediately at a point of consumption, such as a restaurant meal or street food sold on the spot, which does not form part of a dispatched consignment.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of consignment activates a statutory presumption under Section 18(g) that if any food item in a batch, lot, or consignment fails food safety requirements, the entire consignment is presumed non-compliant until the contrary is proved, enabling authorities to seize or recall the full shipment. This shifts the burden of proof to the food business operator and can trigger liabilities under Sections 26 and related penalty provisions for distribution or sale of unsafe or sub-standard food.

definitions.definition: "consumer" means persons and families purchasing and receiving food in order to meet their personal needs.
definitions.plain_english: A consumer is any individual person or family that buys or receives food for their own personal use and eating needs, not for resale or commercial purposes. This includes anyone who goes to a shop, market, restaurant, or other food outlet to get food for themselves or their household. The key idea is that the food is for personal consumption, not for business or trade.
real_world_examples: A family in Mumbai purchasing packaged biscuits, cooking oil, and milk from a local Kirana store for their daily household meals.
A college student in Delhi buying a meal from a roadside dhaba or a Quick Service Restaurant (QSR) like a McDonald's outlet for personal consumption.
A working professional in Bengaluru receiving a home-delivered meal ordered through a food delivery app like Zomato or Swiggy for their own lunch.
A housewife in Chennai purchasing fresh vegetables, packaged atta, and bottled drinking water from a supermarket such as Reliance Fresh for cooking at home.
A pilgrim in Varanasi receiving prasad or langar food distributed free of charge at a religious institution, receiving it to satisfy their personal dietary needs.
A school child receiving a mid-day meal provided under a government nutrition scheme at a government school in rural Rajasthan.
what_it_covers: An individual person buying packaged or unpackaged food from a retail outlet for personal or household eating purposes.
A family unit collectively purchasing food items such as groceries, dairy, or cooked meals to satisfy their domestic nutritional needs.
A person receiving food free of charge — such as through a government food scheme, charitable distribution, or religious institution — for personal consumption.
A single individual ordering food through an online platform or a restaurant for personal dining without any intent of resale.
Persons receiving food samples distributed at supermarkets or exhibitions for personal tasting and evaluation.
what_it_excludes: A food business operator or trader purchasing food in bulk for the purpose of resale, further processing, or commercial distribution, as their acquisition is not for personal needs.
A manufacturer or food business that procures food ingredients or raw materials as inputs for commercial food production.
A hawker, retailer, wholesaler, or distributor who buys food products as part of a commercial supply chain activity rather than for personal consumption.
A restaurant owner or caterer purchasing food stocks from a wholesaler for use in preparing and selling meals to paying customers.
An importer who brings food articles into India for trade or commercial purposes rather than for their own personal dietary needs.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'consumer' is critical because it identifies the class of persons whom the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 is primarily designed to protect; complaints, grievances, and enforcement actions under Section 65 can be initiated by or on behalf of consumers to seek redressal for unsafe, sub-standard, or misbranded food. Rights of compensation, adjudication of disputes, and the obligations imposed on food business operators, manufacturers, and sellers are all calibrated to safeguard this group, meaning whether a person qualifies as a 'consumer' determines their standing to invoke protective provisions of the Act.

definitions.definition: "Contaminant" means any substance, whether or not added to food, but which is present in such food as a result of the production (including operations carried out in crop husbandry, animal husbandry or veterinary medicine), manufacture, processing, preparation, treatment, packing, packaging, transport or holding of such food or as a result of environmental contamination and does not include insect fragments, rodent hairs and other extraneous matter.
definitions.plain_english: A contaminant is any unwanted substance that ends up in food — not because it was intentionally added as an ingredient, but because it crept in during farming, manufacturing, packaging, transport, or due to pollution in the environment. It covers harmful chemicals, heavy metals, pesticide residues, and similar substances that were never meant to be part of the food. Importantly, physical debris like insect parts or rodent hairs does not count as a contaminant under this law — those fall under a separate category called 'extraneous matter'.
real_world_examples: Excess pesticide residues (such as chlorpyrifos) found in rice or wheat grown in Punjab fields, which remain in the grain due to agricultural spraying practices, constituting a contaminant arising from crop husbandry.

Lead or cadmium heavy metal contamination detected in turmeric powder sold in local Indian markets, originating from industrial pollution of soil or water used in cultivation — a classic case of environmental contamination.
Aflatoxins produced by mould (Aspergillus flavus) in improperly stored groundnuts or maize in Maharashtra warehouses, introduced during the holding/storage stage of the food chain.

Residues of veterinary antibiotics such as oxytetracycline found in chicken meat sold in Delhi markets, entering the food as a result of animal husbandry practices where animals were treated before slaughter.
Mineral oil contamination in edible oils packaged in India due to migration from recycled cardboard packaging or lubricants used in processing machinery during the packaging stage.
Mercury contamination in fish caught from industrially polluted rivers or coastal waters near chemical plants in Gujarat, representing environmental contamination entering the food supply.
what_it_covers: Pesticide residues present in fruits, vegetables, or grains as a result of crop husbandry operations such as spraying during cultivation.
Heavy metals like lead, arsenic, cadmium, or mercury that enter food through contaminated soil, water, or air as a result of environmental contamination.
Residues of veterinary drugs or hormones found in meat, poultry, eggs, or dairy products arising from animal husbandry or veterinary medicine practices.
Mycotoxins such as aflatoxins that develop in food during improper storage or holding conditions.
Chemicals migrating from packaging materials into food during packing or transport, such as plasticisers or mineral oils.
Industrial pollutants such as dioxins or PCBs present in food as a result of environmental contamination of raw agricultural produce.
what_it_excludes: Insect fragments found in food, which are explicitly excluded from the definition of contaminant and fall under 'extraneous matter'.
Rodent hairs present in food, also explicitly excluded and classified separately as extraneous matter rather than a contaminant.
Food additives intentionally added to food for a technological purpose, which are governed by the separate definition of 'food additive' under the Act.
Adulterants deliberately added to food to make it unsafe, sub-standard, or mis-branded, which are covered under the distinct definition of 'adulterant'.
Substances added to food to maintain or improve its nutritional qualities, which are excluded from the 'food additive' definition and similarly outside the contaminant concept.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a contaminant determines the applicable regulatory standards, tolerance limits, and testing obligations under the Food Safety and Standards Act — food business operators can face penalties, product recalls, or prosecution under Section 20 if contaminant levels exceed prescribed limits. The distinction between a contaminant, an adulterant, and extraneous matter is legally critical because it determines which specific offence provision applies and the severity of punishment that follows.
