definitions.definition: A 'continuing offence' under the Food Safety and Standards Act refers to an offence of the same nature that persists or is repeated on a day-to-day basis after the initial commission and conviction, thereby attracting an additional daily fine which may extend up to one lakh rupees for each day the violation continues, as provided under Section 64(b) in the context of subsequent offences.
definitions.plain_english: A continuing offence is a violation that does not stop after it first occurs but keeps happening every day until the offender corrects the problem. For example, if a food business operator is caught and convicted for selling unsafe food and then continues doing the same thing again, each day that violation goes on counts as a continuing offence. This allows the court to impose an extra daily fine on top of the doubled punishment for a repeat conviction.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai snack manufacturer previously convicted for using banned artificial colours continues manufacturing and selling such adulterated products even after conviction, attracting a daily fine of up to one lakh rupees for each day the unlawful production persists.

A Delhi street food vendor, after being convicted for operating without a valid food safety licence, is found once again running the same unlicensed food stall day after day, making the ongoing daily operation a continuing offence subject to cumulative daily penalties.

A Kolkata dairy operator previously convicted for selling sub-standard milk continues to supply milk that fails to meet prescribed standards to local retailers on a daily basis, resulting in each day of continued supply being treated as a fresh instance of the continuing offence.

A Chennai food packaging company convicted for misbranding its products — by displaying false nutritional claims — keeps distributing the same mislabelled packages in the market for several weeks after conviction, with the court imposing a fine of up to one lakh rupees per day for the duration of the ongoing violation.

A Pune restaurant chain operator, previously penalised for maintaining unhygienic premises in violation of food safety standards, is re-convicted and found to be continuing the same unsanitary conditions on subsequent inspections, attracting daily fines for every day the unhygienic conditions remain unaddressed.
what_it_covers: An offence that continues unabated on a daily basis after a prior conviction for the same offence under the Act, such as ongoing sale of adulterated food.
Repeated non-compliance with food safety standards by a licensed or unlicensed food business operator who persists in the same violating conduct after being convicted.

Day-to-day continuation of prohibited activities — such as using banned food additives, selling misbranded food, or operating in unsanitary conditions — following a prior conviction for identical conduct.
Scenarios where the unlawful state or conduct (e.g., storing sub-standard food, maintaining contaminated premises) persists over a period of time rather than being a one-time isolated act.
what_it_excludes: A single isolated one-time offence that is fully completed at the moment of commission and does not persist over subsequent days, such as a one-off fraudulent sale that does not continue.
A first-time offender who has not been previously convicted under the Act, since Section 64 applies only to subsequent offences following a prior conviction.

Offences of a different nature or category from the original conviction — the continuing offence provision applies only where the subsequent offence is the same offence as the one previously convicted under.

Civil or regulatory defaults that do not amount to criminal offences under the Act, such as mere administrative non-compliance with licensing paperwork not reaching the threshold of a punishable offence.

It also reinforces the mandatory cancellation of the offender's food business licence, making the classification critical to both the quantum of punishment and the offender's ability to continue operating.

definitions.definition: The term 'contravention' is not formally defined in Section 3 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. As used throughout the Act, it means any act or omission that violates, breaches, or fails to comply with any provision of this Act, or any rule, regulation, standard, or order made or issued thereunder, including failure to obtain a licence, selling unsafe or sub-standard food, or disobeying directions of a competent authority.
definitions.plain_english: A 'contravention' simply means breaking or not following any rule, requirement, or order set out in the Food Safety and Standards Act or its associated regulations. This can include doing something the law prohibits, such as selling unsafe food, or failing to do something the law requires, such as obtaining a food business licence. When a contravention occurs, the person responsible can face penalties, prosecution, or other legal action.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai street food vendor sells chaat made with oil that contains harmful adulterants exceeding permissible limits, directly violating the food safety standards prescribed under the Act — this constitutes a contravention attracting penalty under Section 49.

A Delhi-based dairy company continues operating its milk processing unit without obtaining or renewing the mandatory licence under the Act, thereby contravening the licensing requirement under Section 31, making it liable for prosecution under Section 63.

A Bengaluru packaged food manufacturer labels its product as '100% organic' without meeting the prescribed standards for organic food, contravening the labelling and misbranding provisions, attracting adjudication under Section 67.

A Kolkata restaurant owner ignores an improvement notice issued by the Food Safety Officer directing rectification of unhygienic kitchen conditions within a specified time, and the failure to comply constitutes a contravention under Section 42, enabling the authority to escalate action.

A food importer in Chennai imports a consignment of edible oils that do not meet the quality and safety standards notified under the Act, constituting a contravention that triggers seizure, penalty, and possible prohibition under Sections 68 and 49.
what_it_covers: Selling, storing, or distributing food that does not meet the safety and quality standards prescribed under the Act or its regulations.
Operating a food business without obtaining the required licence or registration, or continuing operations after a licence has been suspended or cancelled.
Failing to comply with an improvement notice, prohibition order, or emergency prohibition order issued by a Designated Officer or Food Safety Officer.
Misbranding or mislabelling of food products in a manner inconsistent with the prescribed labelling standards.
Manufacturing or importing food articles containing contaminants, adulterants, or pesticide residues above the prescribed tolerance limits.
what_it_excludes: Acts or omissions that are expressly permitted or exempted under the Act, such as food sold by a petty manufacturer within the conditions of a valid exemption notified by the Central Government.
Procedural or administrative irregularities that do not amount to a substantive breach of any duty, standard, or prohibition imposed by the Act or its regulations.
Conduct that occurred before the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 came into force, which may have been governed by earlier repealed laws such as the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
Acts done in good faith and with due diligence in compliance with all applicable standards, where the food business operator can establish a valid due diligence defence under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The determination of whether a 'contravention' has occurred is the foundational trigger for all enforcement action under the Act — including the imposition of penalties under Sections 49 and 67, adjudication proceedings under Section 68, and criminal prosecution under Section 42; without a contravention, no liability, penalty, or prosecution can be initiated against a food business operator or any other person under the Act.

definitions.definition: A 'dealer' under the Food Safety and Standards Act refers to any person engaged in the trade or commerce of any article of food, including the buying, selling, or distribution of such articles, whether as a principal or agent, and includes any person in whose possession any article of food is found for the purpose of sale. The term is used in conjunction with manufacturers, importers, and distributors to denote persons in the food supply chain who handle or transact in food articles.
definitions.plain_english: A dealer is any person or business that buys and sells food products as part of a trade or commercial activity. This includes shopkeepers, traders, wholesalers, and retail outlets that deal in food items. They are part of the food supply chain between the manufacturer and the final consumer. The law treats dealers as responsible parties who can be held accountable if unsafe or adulterated food is found in their possession or sold through them.
real_world_examples: A wholesale grain trader in Azadpur Mandi, Delhi who buys rice and wheat in bulk from farmers and sells them to retailers across the city — classifiable as a dealer under the Act.
A kirana store owner in Mumbai who stocks and sells packaged food products such as biscuits, namkeen, and cooking oil to local customers is a dealer under this Act.
A distributor-cum-dealer in Chennai who receives consignments of packaged drinking water and soft drinks from manufacturers and supplies them to restaurants and hotels.
A dry fruit trader at Crawford Market, Mumbai who purchases imported nuts and spices and sells them retail or in bulk to other businesses, operating as a dealer in articles of food.
A trader in Ludhiana who stocks and sells adulterated edible oil — the Food Safety Officer may seize the stock and the court may implead him as a dealer during trial under Section 78.
A cold storage operator in Kolkata who also trades in frozen meat and fish products by buying from suppliers and selling to restaurants qualifies as a dealer in food articles.

what_it_covers: A retail shopkeeper or kirana store owner who stocks and sells packaged or loose food items to end consumers.
A wholesale food trader who purchases articles of food in large quantities from manufacturers or importers and resells them to retailers or other businesses.
Any person found in possession of an article of food intended for sale, including agents or commission traders operating in food markets.
A distributor who operates as both a logistics handler and a commercial seller of food articles, buying and selling in their own name.
A trader or merchant who deals in food additives, spices, or processed food products through a shop, warehouse, or market stall.
what_it_excludes: A consumer who purchases food solely for personal or household consumption and does not engage in any resale or commercial transaction.
A transporter or logistics provider who merely carries food articles from one point to another without any ownership, buying, or selling of the food.
A manufacturer who only produces food articles but does not independently engage in trading or selling them in the market — though they may separately qualify as a manufacturer.
A food safety officer or government inspector who seizes or holds food articles as part of enforcement duties, not for commercial sale.
An employee or staff member of a food business who handles food on behalf of their employer but does not personally trade in food articles.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'dealer' is legally significant because under Section 78, a court may implead a dealer as an accused during trial even if they were not originally prosecuted, making them criminally liable for offences under the Act. Additionally, under Section 38, Food Safety Officers have explicit powers to inspect premises, seize adulterated food, and demand accounts from dealers, placing compliance and enforcement obligations directly on them.

definitions.definition: 'Designated Officer' means the officer appointed under section 36.
definitions.plain_english: A Designated Officer is a government official specifically appointed under the Food Safety and Standards Act to oversee food safety enforcement within a particular area or district. This officer acts as a supervisory authority between the Commissioner of Food Safety and the Food Safety Officers who carry out on-ground inspections. They are responsible for issuing or cancelling licences, handling improvement notices, and taking action against food businesses that violate safety standards.
real_world_examples: In Mumbai, a Designated Officer receives a complaint about a local mithai shop using substandard ingredients and directs the Food Safety Officer to inspect the premises and collect samples for testing.

A Designated Officer in Chennai issues an improvement notice to a restaurant chain after reports of unhygienic food preparation practices, setting a deadline for the business to rectify violations before a licence cancellation proceeding is initiated.

After a Food Analyst's report confirms that a packaged spice brand in Delhi contains pesticide residues beyond permissible limits, the Designated Officer initiates action to suspend the food business operator's licence and refer the matter for adjudication.

During a state-wide food safety drive in Punjab, a Designated Officer coordinates multiple Food Safety Officers to conduct simultaneous raids on unlicensed food processing units and oversees seizure of adulterated edible oil stocks.

In Hyderabad, a Designated Officer reviews an emergency prohibition notice issued against a street food vendor whose products were linked to a food poisoning outbreak and decides whether to confirm or revoke the notice after investigation.
what_it_covers: An officer appointed by the State Government or Commissioner of Food Safety specifically under Section 36 of the Food Safety and Standards Act to perform designated enforcement functions.
Authority to grant, suspend, cancel, or modify licences issued to food business operators within their assigned jurisdiction.
Power to receive and act upon reports from Food Safety Officers, issue improvement notices, and initiate adjudication proceedings against non-compliant food businesses.
Responsibility to confirm or revoke emergency prohibition notices and prohibition orders related to unsafe or sub-standard food within their territorial jurisdiction.
Oversight of Food Safety Officers operating under their jurisdiction, including directing inspections and reviewing sampling and analytical reports.
what_it_excludes: Food Safety Officers appointed under Section 37, who are subordinate field-level officers responsible for inspections and sample collection, not the same as a Designated Officer.
The Commissioner of Food Safety appointed under Section 30, who is a higher state-level authority and holds separate, broader powers than the Designated Officer.
Food Analysts appointed under Section 45, who perform laboratory testing of food samples and are not vested with the enforcement and licensing functions of the Designated Officer.
Central Government officers or Food Authority members, who operate at the national level and are not appointed under Section 36 as Designated Officers.

Adjudicating Officers, who are appointed for the specific purpose of adjudicating penalties and compensations and perform a quasi-judicial function distinct from the Designated Officer's administrative enforcement role.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of an officer as a Designated Officer is critical because it determines who has the legal authority to grant, suspend, or cancel food business licences, issue improvement notices under Section 32, and take enforcement actions under Sections 29, 31, 33, 40, and 46; actions taken by any person not so appointed would lack statutory validity. Failure to comply with directions of a Designated Officer can expose food business operators to penalties, licence cancellation, and prosecution under the Act.

definitions.definition: "Director", in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm. In relation to a company, the term refers to any director of the body corporate who, with consent or connivance or by neglect, is attributable to the commission of an offence under the Food Safety and Standards Act.
definitions.plain_english: In the context of the Food Safety and Standards Act, a 'director' means a partner when the business is a firm (partnership), and a board-level director when the business is a company. This definition matters because if a food safety offence is committed by a business, the director can be held personally responsible if they consented to, ignored, or neglected to prevent the wrongdoing. Essentially, it pins personal criminal liability on the key decision-makers of a food business.
real_world_examples: A partnership firm in Mumbai selling adulterated ghee is found guilty of food safety violations. Each partner of the firm qualifies as a 'director' under Section 66 and can be prosecuted personally alongside the firm.

A large FMCG company in Bengaluru is found selling misbranded packaged food. The managing director and other board directors who knowingly approved misleading labelling can be individually charged under the Act.

A private limited company operating a chain of restaurants in Delhi is found serving unsafe food. A director who was aware of the unhygienic kitchen conditions but took no corrective action can be held liable as a 'director' under Section 66(2).

A partnership-based food processing unit in Ludhiana repeatedly violates contaminant limits. One of the partners (treated as 'director') who managed day-to-day operations and neglected compliance is personally prosecuted alongside the firm.

A food import company registered as a body corporate in Chennai is found importing substandard food articles. Its board-level directors who authorised the import despite known non-compliance are deemed guilty under the Act's definition of 'director'.
what_it_covers: A partner in a partnership firm that is engaged in a food business, who is deemed a 'director' for purposes of criminal liability under Section 66.
A board-level director of a body corporate (private or public limited company) involved in a food business, where the offence is attributable to their consent, connivance, or neglect.
A director of a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) engaged in food manufacturing or distribution, who can be personally held responsible for offences committed by the LLP.
what_it_excludes: A mere employee or salaried manager of a company who holds no directorial or partnership position and does not exercise control over food safety decisions.
A nominee or sleeping director who has no active role in the food business and can prove absence of knowledge and exercise of due diligence to prevent the offence.
A shareholder of a company who holds shares but is not on the board and has no managerial or operational responsibility over food safety matters.
A government-nominated independent director who played no role in the decision-making that led to the food safety offence.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'director' is critical because it determines who, beyond the company itself, bears personal criminal liability for food safety offences under Section 66(2); if a person qualifies as a 'director,' they can be prosecuted, convicted, and punished individually for offences committed with their consent, connivance, or due to their neglect, making it a powerful tool to deter senior decision-makers from ignoring food safety compliance.

definitions.definition: The term 'distributes' is not formally defined in the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, but is used consistently to mean the act of delivering, circulating, or spreading any article of food for human consumption to one or more persons, whether by the person himself or by any other person on his behalf, as part of or incidental to a food business. It encompasses any act by which food moves from one party to another in the supply or distribution chain, short of a direct retail sale to the ultimate consumer.
definitions.plain_english: Distributing food means passing it along to others — such as delivering it to shops, sending it to wholesalers, or spreading it through a supply chain — so it can eventually reach the people who eat it. It is different from actually selling food directly to a customer; it covers the movement of food between businesses or intermediaries. If you hand out, transport, or circulate food products as part of your trade or business, you are 'distributing' under this law.
real_world_examples: A food distributor in Mumbai picks up packaged biscuits from a manufacturer in Pune and delivers them to grocery stores across Maharashtra — this act of delivering to retailers constitutes 'distributes' under the Act.

A cold chain logistics company in Delhi transports dairy products from a dairy plant in Haryana to modern retail outlets such as Big Bazaar and DMart — the act of moving these products through the supply chain amounts to distribution.

A regional wholesale agent in Chennai receives consignments of spices from a manufacturer and redistributes smaller lots to local kirana stores and restaurants — this redistribution activity is covered under 'distributes'.

During a community festival in Kolkata, a catering contractor dispatches pre-packed food items from a central kitchen to multiple event venues across the city — delivering food to multiple locations in this manner constitutes distribution.

A pharma-linked nutraceutical company in Hyderabad appoints carrying-and-forwarding agents to move health supplement food products from their warehouse to chemists and health stores in different states — the agents' act of circulating these food products is distribution under the Act.

An online food aggregator platform in Bengaluru arranges for third-party logistics partners to deliver packaged meals from cloud kitchens to end consumers — the logistics partner's role in moving the food constitutes distribution.
what_it_covers: A wholesale distributor who receives bulk food consignments from a manufacturer and delivers them to multiple retailers across a region.
A carrying-and-forwarding agent or logistics operator who physically transports food articles from a factory or warehouse to retail outlets or other businesses on behalf of a food business operator.

An employer or principal who directs another person (agent, employee, contractor) to distribute food on their behalf — the principal remains liable as the Act explicitly covers acts done 'by any other person on his behalf'.
Free distribution or sampling of food articles (e.g., promotional food samples distributed at trade fairs or exhibitions) where no direct monetary sale occurs but food moves from one party to others.
A redistribution agent who breaks bulk consignments and circulates smaller quantities to sub-distributors or local dealers in a tiered supply chain.
what_it_excludes: The act of manufacturing food for sale, which is separately enumerated in the same sections and governed by the specific obligations and penalties applicable to manufacturers.
The final retail sale of food directly to the ultimate consumer, which is separately covered by the term 'sells' and the corresponding obligations of a seller or retailer under the Act.
Storage of food articles that does not involve any movement or transfer to another party, which is separately addressed by the term 'stores' in the same penal provisions.
Importation of food articles into India, which is a distinct and separately enumerated activity covered by the term 'imports' under the Act.
Purely personal or domestic transfer of food (e.g., sharing home-cooked food with family members) that is entirely outside the scope of any food business or commercial activity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person's conduct qualifies as 'distributes' directly determines their criminal and civil liability under sections such as 51, 52, 54, and 59 of the Act — if they distribute sub-standard, misbranded, unsafe, or extraneous-matter-containing food, they become liable to penalties ranging from one lakh rupees to imprisonment for life. Establishing that a party was distributing food (rather than merely storing or transporting it without commercial purpose) is therefore pivotal to whether penal provisions can be invoked against distributors and logistics intermediaries in the food supply chain.

definitions.definition: A distributor is a person engaged in the business of distributing or supplying articles of food between manufacturers, wholesalers, and sellers, and is liable under this Act for any article of food which is supplied after the date of its expiry, stored or supplied in violation of the safety instructions of the manufacturer, unsafe or misbranded, unidentifiable as to the manufacturer from whom it was received, stored or handled in violation of the provisions of this Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder, or received with knowledge of being unsafe.
definitions.plain_english: A distributor is a business or person who receives food products from manufacturers or wholesalers and supplies them further down the supply chain to retailers or sellers. They act as a middleman in the food supply chain. They are legally responsible for ensuring that the food they handle, store, and supply is safe, properly labelled, within its expiry date, and stored as per the manufacturer's instructions.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based company that purchases packaged biscuits from Parle or Britannia factories and supplies them to thousands of kirana stores and supermarkets across North India, maintaining a cold chain or dry warehouse for storage.
A regional distributor in Maharashtra who receives bottled drinking water from a manufacturer and supplies it to hotels, restaurants, and retail outlets across Pune and Nashik districts.

A pharmaceutical-food distributor in Chennai who supplies nutritional supplements and health food products received from a Chennai-based manufacturer to pharmacies and health stores across Tamil Nadu.

A frozen food distributor in Bengaluru who imports frozen meat products from a certified manufacturer and distributes them to restaurant chains and retail supermarkets across Karnataka, maintaining cold storage at their warehouse.

A spices and condiments distributor in Kolkata who receives bulk stock from a West Bengal manufacturer and repackages and supplies them to local grocery wholesalers and retailers across eastern India.
A beverage distributor in Hyderabad who receives soft drinks and packaged juices from a large FMCG manufacturer and supplies them to vending outlets, canteens, and retail chains in Telangana.
what_it_covers: A regional food distribution company that receives packaged food from manufacturers and supplies it to wholesalers, retailers, or institutional buyers across a defined territory.
A cold chain logistics operator who stores and distributes perishable food products such as dairy, meat, or frozen goods on behalf of manufacturers.
A dealer who acts as an authorised distributor for a specific food brand, holding inventory and supplying to sub-dealers or retailers within a licensed area.
A person or entity that distributes food articles even if they are also engaged in limited repackaging or labelling as part of their distribution activity.
An entity found in possession of adulterants in their distribution premises, as explicitly recognised under Section 38 of the Act.
what_it_excludes: A manufacturer who sells directly to consumers or retailers without any intervening distribution activity, as the manufacturer bears a separate and distinct liability under Section 27.
A seller or petty retailer who only sells food at the final point of sale to consumers and does not engage in bulk supply or intermediate distribution in the supply chain.
A transporter or logistics carrier who merely physically moves food products between parties without taking ownership, possession, or control over the food articles for distribution purposes.
A food safety officer or government authority that handles or seizes food articles in the exercise of statutory duties — such handling is not distribution in a commercial sense.
A consumer who purchases food for personal use and shares it informally, with no commercial intent to distribute or supply the food article.
definitions.why_it_matters: A distributor's classification under the Act directly determines their liability under Section 27 for offences such as supplying expired, unsafe, or misbranded food, and under Section 78 they may be impleaded as a party in criminal trials even where the original accused is someone else in the supply chain. Failure to comply with a distributor's obligations can result in penalties, prosecution, seizure of food stock, and cancellation of food business licences under the Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'document' is not formally defined in Section 3 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006; however, as used in Section 61, it encompasses any written, printed, electronic, or recorded material relevant to food safety inspections, investigations, or proceedings, including records, registers, certificates, licences, labels, invoices, reports, and any other instrument required to be maintained, produced, or examined under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'document' under this law refers to any written, printed, or electronic record or paper that is connected to food safety activities — such as licences, inspection reports, lab results, invoices, or registers. It is any material that authorities may ask a food business to produce or that officers may examine during inspections or legal proceedings. Essentially, it covers any recorded information relevant to checking whether food safety rules are being followed.
real_world_examples: A Food Safety Officer visits a Mumbai food processing unit and demands the production of its FSSAI licence certificate, batch production records, and raw material purchase invoices — all of these are 'documents' under Section 61.

During an investigation into a food poisoning outbreak in Delhi, health authorities require a restaurant to produce its food safety management records, temperature logs, and supplier agreements as 'documents' for scrutiny.

A Designated Officer in Chennai inspects a packaged food manufacturer and examines printed labels, test reports from accredited laboratories, and import permits for food additives, all of which qualify as 'documents' under the Act.

An FSSAI audit of a cold storage facility in Pune involves review of electronic delivery logs, refrigeration maintenance records, and pest control service certificates — each constituting a 'document' that must be made available to officers.

During court proceedings before a Special Court in Hyderabad involving misbranded food, the prosecution submits packaging wrappers, advertisement printouts, and analyst certificates as 'documents' to establish the offence.
what_it_covers: FSSAI licences, permits, and registration certificates maintained by food business operators
Laboratory test reports, analyst certificates, and food safety audit records
Purchase invoices, supplier agreements, batch production registers, and dispatch records
Printed labels, packaging materials, and advertisement copies associated with food products
Electronic records, digital logs, and computer-generated data relevant to food safety compliance
Inspection reports, improvement notices, and prohibition orders issued by authorities
what_it_excludes: Oral or verbal communications that have not been reduced to any written or recorded form
Physical food samples or specimens collected for laboratory analysis, which are governed separately under sampling provisions
Live animals or primary food articles in their unprocessed natural state, which are not 'recorded' instruments
Internal mental notes or unrecorded personal observations of officers not reduced to writing
Personal identification documents of individuals (such as Aadhaar or PAN cards) that are unrelated to food business operations
definitions.why_it_matters: The scope of 'document' under Section 61 directly determines the extent of powers exercisable by Food Safety Officers and authorised officers to inspect, seize, and rely upon records during enforcement actions, and failure to produce such documents or forgery thereof can attract penalties and prosecution under the Act. Whether a particular record qualifies as a 'document' decides whether its non-production constitutes obstruction of an officer's duty or whether it is admissible as evidence before a Special Court or Adjudicating Officer.

definitions.definition: Due diligence, as used in the Food Safety and Standards Act, means the taking of all reasonable precautions and the exercise of all reasonable care to prevent the commission of an offence under the Act, whether by the person themselves or by another person under their control. A person may establish due diligence by proving reliance on information or acts of an independent third party (not an employee or agent), conducting all reasonable checks on food, not importing the food from another country, selling food in the same or compliant condition as purchased, and having no knowledge or reasonable suspicion that their act or omission would constitute an offence.
definitions.plain_english: Due diligence means that a person took every reasonable step to make sure they did not break the food safety law. It is a legal defence — if you can prove you were careful, followed proper procedures, and did everything reasonably possible to prevent a violation, you may avoid being punished even if an offence technically occurred. For example, if you relied on a trustworthy supplier's checks and had no reason to suspect anything was wrong, you may successfully use this defence.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based packaged food distributor purchases biscuits from a licensed manufacturer with all FSSAI certifications and valid test reports. If those biscuits later turn out to be sub-standard, the distributor can claim due diligence by showing they verified the supplier's credentials, checked the labels, and had no reason to suspect non-compliance.

A Delhi restaurant owner sources fresh paneer from a reputed local dairy that provides quality assurance certificates. If the paneer is found to be adulterated during an inspection, the owner may invoke due diligence by demonstrating they relied on the supplier's certifications and conducted visual and freshness checks before use.

A Bengaluru supermarket chain with a documented food safety management system and a quality assurance programme aligned with FSSAI regulations sells imported olive oil. If the oil is later found to have a labelling contravention caused by the foreign exporter, the chain can argue due diligence by showing compliance with its internal food safety programme and that it did not import the product directly.

A Chennai food manufacturer who follows a HACCP-based food safety programme and regularly audits raw material suppliers is found to have trace pesticide residues in a product due to a farm-level default unknown to the manufacturer. The manufacturer invokes due diligence, proving all prescribed checks were carried out and the default originated with an independent third-party farmer, not an employee or agent.

A Kolkata petty retailer sells pre-packaged spices purchased from a wholesale dealer in the same sealed condition as received, with no tampering. If the spices are found to be misbranded, the retailer can claim due diligence by demonstrating the food was sold in the identical condition as purchased and that there was no reason to suspect any violation at the time of sale.
what_it_covers: A food business operator who followed all FSSAI-prescribed checks, maintained a documented food safety programme, and had no knowledge that an offence was being committed.
A company director or manager who proves the offence was committed without their knowledge and that they exercised all reasonable precautions to prevent it, under Section 66.
A retailer or distributor who sold food in the same condition as purchased, relied on checks carried out by an independent supplier, and did not import the food from another country.
A person who complied with a recognised quality assurance programme or industry code of practice based on national or international standards to manage food safety hazards.
A food business operator whose offence resulted solely from an act or default of an independent third party (not their employee or agent) on whose information they reasonably relied.
what_it_excludes: An employee or agent of the accused person whose act or default caused the offence — such persons cannot be treated as independent 'another person' to support the due diligence defence.
A director, employee, or agent of a defendant company — their default cannot be attributed to a third party for the purposes of the due diligence defence.

A person who directly imported food into India from another country and claims due diligence on the basis of third-party reliance, as the Act explicitly disallows this element of the defence for importers.
A defendant who had a mistaken but reasonable belief as to the facts constituting the offence — Section 80(C) expressly bars this as a valid defence under the Act.
A food business operator who sold food in a different condition from that in which it was purchased, where that difference itself resulted in a contravention of the Act or its rules.
definitions.why_it_matters: Due diligence is a complete statutory defence that, if successfully proved, can absolve an accused food business operator, company officer, or individual from criminal liability and punishment under the Act for food safety offences. Its application is decisive in proceedings under Sections 66 and 80 — without establishing due diligence, persons in charge of a company or those whose food caused harm face punishment including fines and imprisonment.

definitions.definition: An 'emergency prohibition notice' is a notice served by the Designated Officer on a food business operator, prior to applying to the Commissioner of Food Safety for imposition of a prohibition, where the Designated Officer is satisfied that the health risk condition exists with respect to any food business. Such notice must be served at least one day before the date of the application for an emergency prohibition order.
definitions.plain_english: An emergency prohibition notice is a formal written warning given by a senior food safety official to a food business owner, informing them that the official believes their business poses a serious health risk and intends to apply to the Commissioner to shut it down or restrict it. It is a mandatory step that must be taken at least one day before the official can formally apply for a legally binding prohibition order. Think of it as an urgent advance notice that legal action to close or restrict the business is imminent.
real_world_examples: A Designated Officer in Mumbai inspects a popular street food stall and finds severe rodent infestation and contaminated cooking oil posing an immediate health risk; he serves an emergency prohibition notice on the stall owner one day before applying to the Commissioner of Food Safety to shut down the stall.

During a surprise inspection of a dairy processing unit in Pune, the Designated Officer discovers that milk is being adulterated with harmful chemicals causing food poisoning in the local area; he issues an emergency prohibition notice to the dairy operator before seeking an emergency prohibition order from the Commissioner.

A restaurant in Delhi is found to be storing raw meat alongside ready-to-eat food under severely unhygienic conditions leading to multiple reported illness cases; the Designated Officer serves an emergency prohibition notice on the restaurant owner, signalling imminent application for a formal prohibition order.

A packaged snacks manufacturer in Chennai is found using banned pesticide-laced ingredients in its production line during a routine audit; the Designated Officer issues an emergency prohibition notice to the company's food business operator before approaching the Commissioner of Food Safety to impose a prohibition on the manufacturing premises.

A school canteen operator in Hyderabad is discovered serving food prepared under grossly unsanitary conditions after several students fall ill; the Designated Officer serves an emergency prohibition notice on the canteen operator at least a day before filing for an emergency prohibition order to prevent further harm.
what_it_covers: A written notice served by the Designated Officer on any food business operator when a health risk condition is found to exist at their food business premises.
The mandatory procedural step that must precede an application by the Designated Officer to the Commissioner of Food Safety for an emergency prohibition order.
Notices issued in respect of any type of food business — whether a manufacturer, distributor, retailer, restaurant, or any other operator — where an immediate health risk is identified.
Situations involving contaminated food, unsanitary processing conditions, use of harmful adulterants, or any circumstance meeting the 'health risk condition' threshold under the Act.
what_it_excludes: An 'emergency prohibition order' itself, which is the subsequent legally binding directive issued by the Commissioner of Food Safety imposing the actual prohibition — the notice merely precedes the application for such an order.

An 'improvement notice' issued under a different provision of the Act, which addresses non-compliance with food safety standards without the immediacy of a health risk condition warranting emergency action.
Any informal verbal warning or advisory communication given by a Food Safety Officer during routine inspections that does not constitute the formal statutory notice under Section 34.

Notices or actions taken by the Commissioner of Food Safety directly — the emergency prohibition notice is exclusively within the authority of the Designated Officer, not the Commissioner or a Food Safety Officer.
definitions.why_it_matters: Serving an emergency prohibition notice is a mandatory legal prerequisite before the Designated Officer can apply for an emergency prohibition order; failure to serve it invalidates the subsequent application and any resulting prohibition order. It also gives the food business operator at least one day's advance notice, triggering their right to respond or take remedial measures, while non-compliance with the subsequent prohibition order can result in imprisonment of up to two years and a fine of up to two lakh rupees.

definitions.definition: An emergency prohibition order is an order imposed by the Commissioner of Food Safety, upon application by the Designated Officer, when the Commissioner is satisfied that a health risk condition exists with respect to any food business, imposing a prohibition on that food business; such an order ceases to have effect only upon the issue of a certificate by the Designated Officer confirming that sufficient measures have been taken by the food business operator to justify its lifting.
definitions.plain_english: An emergency prohibition order is an official command issued by the Commissioner of Food Safety that immediately shuts down or restricts a food business that poses a serious health risk to the public. It is triggered after the Designated Officer applies for it, having already warned the food business operator at least one day in advance. The order remains in force until the Designated Officer is satisfied that the business has fixed the problem and issues a clearance certificate.
real_world_examples: A restaurant in Mumbai is found to be storing raw meat at unsafe temperatures alongside ready-to-eat food, causing multiple cases of food poisoning among customers; the Designated Officer serves an emergency prohibition notice and applies to the Commissioner of Food Safety, who issues an emergency prohibition order shutting down the restaurant immediately.

A dairy processing unit in Punjab is discovered to be adulterating milk with harmful chemicals and operating under grossly unhygienic conditions; the Commissioner of Food Safety issues an emergency prohibition order halting all production and sale activities until corrective measures are verified.

A street food vendor hub in Delhi is found using non-potable water contaminated with sewage for food preparation, posing a severe public health hazard; after the Designated Officer serves notice and applies, an emergency prohibition order is imposed on the entire operation.

A spice manufacturing plant in Gujarat is detected using banned pesticide-laden raw materials that render the final product unsafe for human consumption; the Commissioner of Food Safety issues an emergency prohibition order against the plant after the Designated Officer's application and one-day prior notice to the operator.

A school canteen in Chennai is found serving food prepared in premises infested with rodents and cockroaches, endangering the health of children; an emergency prohibition order is issued by the Commissioner of Food Safety, and a copy is affixed conspicuously at the canteen entrance by the Food Safety Officer.
what_it_covers: Any food business found to have a health risk condition, including restaurants, processing units, canteens, or manufacturing plants, against which the Commissioner of Food Safety imposes a prohibition after the Designated Officer's application.

Situations where both the Designated Officer and the Commissioner of Food Safety are independently satisfied that a health risk condition exists, warranting immediate prohibition of the food business operations.
Criminal liability of any person who knowingly contravenes an emergency prohibition order, making them punishable with imprisonment up to two years and a fine up to two lakh rupees.
The procedural requirement that a copy of the order be served on the food business operator or affixed at a conspicuous place on the business premises by the Food Safety Officer.
what_it_excludes: An emergency prohibition notice, which is only a precursor notice served on the food business operator by the Designated Officer and does not itself impose a prohibition — only the order issued by the Commissioner of Food Safety constitutes an emergency prohibition order.

A standard improvement notice or regular prohibition order issued under normal enforcement procedures, which do not require the same urgency and are not governed by the emergency provisions of Section 34.

Situations where the Designated Officer has not yet served at least one day's prior notice of intention to apply for the order, as such an application without prior notice does not validly lead to an emergency prohibition order.

Cases where the Commissioner of Food Safety is not satisfied that a health risk condition exists, in which circumstance no emergency prohibition order can be lawfully issued even if the Designated Officer applies.
definitions.why_it_matters: An emergency prohibition order immediately and legally restricts or halts all operations of a food business, and any knowing contravention constitutes a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment up to two years and a fine up to two lakh rupees. The order also triggers mandatory procedural obligations on the Designated Officer and the Food Safety Officer, including service of the order and issuance of a compliance certificate within prescribed timelines, determining when the prohibition lifts.

definitions.definition: Ex officio Members of the Food Authority are those Members who hold membership by virtue of their office or official position, as distinguished from the Chairperson and other Members who are selected through the Selection Committee constituted under Section 6, appointed for fixed terms, and entitled to prescribed salaries and allowances under Section 7.
definitions.plain_english: Ex officio Members are people who automatically become members of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) because of the official government post or job they already hold — not because they were specially chosen or appointed for that role. They do not go through the formal selection process and do not receive a separate salary or service terms for being on the Authority. When they leave their original government post, they automatically stop being members of the Authority too.
real_world_examples: The Secretary of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, who sits on the Food Authority as an ex officio Member by virtue of holding that ministerial post, without requiring nomination by the Selection Committee.

A senior official from the Ministry of Commerce and Industry included in the Food Authority in an ex officio capacity to ensure trade-related food policy coordination, automatically ceasing to be a member upon transfer or retirement from that post.

The Director General of Health Services (DGHS) participating in FSSAI board meetings as an ex officio Member because their statutory role in public health administration qualifies them for automatic membership.

A representative of the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare serving on the Food Authority as an ex officio Member, contributing expertise on primary food production without undergoing the panel-based selection process under Section 6.

An official from the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) acting as an ex officio Member of the Food Authority due to their institutional mandate over food quality standards, with their membership linked entirely to their tenure in that institutional role.
what_it_covers: Members of the Food Authority who hold their position solely by virtue of a government office or post they occupy, without undergoing selection by the Selection Committee under Section 6.

Senior Central Government officials from ministries or departments whose institutional role in food safety, health, agriculture, or trade makes their membership on the Authority functionally necessary and automatic.
Members whose tenure on the Food Authority is co-terminus with their tenure in the underlying official position, ending automatically upon transfer, retirement, or removal from that post.

Representatives of statutory bodies or government departments who are designated by the Act or rules to sit on the Food Authority as part of the Authority's composition without a fixed three-year term under Section 7.
what_it_excludes: The Chairperson of the Food Authority, who must be selected through the Selection Committee and appointed under a fixed term with prescribed salary conditions.

Appointed Members of the Food Authority (other than the Chairperson) who are selected through the formal Selection Committee process under Section 6, hold a fixed three-year term under Section 7, and are entitled to prescribed salaries and allowances.

Independent food technologists, scientists, or technical experts nominated in their personal capacity to the Food Authority, as their appointment is governed by the selection and nomination process, not by virtue of holding a specific official post.
Members of the Central Advisory Committee or Scientific Committees constituted under the Act, who are separate bodies and not part of the Food Authority membership structure.
definitions.why_it_matters: The distinction between ex officio Members and other Members is legally significant because ex officio Members are expressly excluded from the Selection Committee process under Section 6, the fixed tenure provisions under Section 7(1), and the salary and allowances framework under Section 7(2), meaning their rights, obligations, and removal conditions differ materially from appointed Members. This classification also determines whether a vacancy triggers the mandatory reference to the Selection Committee under Section 6(2) and whether post-cessation restrictions under Section 7(5) apply to them.

definitions.definition: "Extraneous matter" means any matter contained in an article of food which may be carried from the raw materials, packaging materials or process systems used for its manufacture or which is added to it, but such matter does not render such article of food unsafe.
definitions.plain_english: Extraneous matter refers to any foreign substance or material that ends up in food — either accidentally from the ingredients, packaging, or machinery used during production, or by being added in some way — but which does not make the food dangerous to eat. It is essentially unwanted material in food that affects quality or purity without posing a health hazard. Think of it as a contamination concern related to food standards rather than food safety.
real_world_examples: A packet of basmati rice sold in a Delhi supermarket is found to contain small pieces of husk and straw carried over from the milling and packaging process — these constitute extraneous matter since they originate from raw material handling but do not make the rice unsafe to consume.

A biscuit manufacturer in Pune finds that tiny plastic shavings from an aging conveyor belt have mixed into biscuit batches during production; these particles sourced from the process system qualify as extraneous matter unless proven to render the food unsafe.

A spice grinding unit in Chennai packs ground turmeric that is found to contain small fibrous plant stems and bark fragments from the raw turmeric root — material carried from the raw ingredient itself — classified as extraneous matter under FSS Act inspections.

A wheat flour brand distributed across Maharashtra is found during a Food Safety Officer inspection to contain small paper fibre fragments traceable to the paper lining of the storage bags used during packaging, constituting extraneous matter originating from packaging materials.

A jam manufacturer in Gujarat uses recycled glass jars, and minute glass dust residues are detected in a batch of mango jam — these traces from the packaging material are treated as extraneous matter provided they do not render the jam unsafe at the quantities found.
what_it_covers: Husk, straw, or plant fibres carried over from raw agricultural produce during processing of food articles such as rice, wheat, or spices.
Fragments of packaging materials such as paper fibres, plastic shavings, or metal particles that inadvertently enter food during manufacturing or packaging operations.

Residual matter from process systems such as machine lubricant traces, conveyor belt particles, or filter material fragments that mix into food during production, provided they do not make the food unsafe.
Insect fragments and rodent hairs found in food articles, which are explicitly excluded from the definition of 'contaminant' and thus fall under extraneous matter for enforcement purposes.
Dust, sand, or soil particles that are incidentally present in raw materials and carry through to the final packaged food product.
what_it_excludes: Any matter that renders the food article unsafe — once the extraneous matter causes the food to become dangerous to health, it crosses out of this definition and the food becomes 'unsafe food' under a more serious category.
Substances intentionally added to food for a technological purpose, such as food additives or processing aids, which are governed by separate definitions under the Act.

Contaminants as defined under the Act — substances present in food as a result of production, manufacture, environmental contamination, etc. — which are covered by a distinct definition, though insect fragments and rodent hairs are carved out of 'contaminant' and revert to this category.
Food additives and ingredients that are deliberately included in a food product's formulation, even if later found to be non-compliant with standards.
Adulterants — substances added to food to make it unsafe, sub-standard, or mis-branded — which fall under the separate definition of 'adulterant' and carry more serious legal consequences.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of extraneous matter in food can render it 'sub-standard' under Section 3 and trigger liability under Sections 26 and 54 of the FSS Act, potentially resulting in penalties for the food business operator; however, because extraneous matter by definition does not make food unsafe, it attracts lesser penalties than unsafe food offences under Section 48, making the precise classification critical to determining the severity of legal consequences for manufacturers, packers, and sellers.

definitions.definition: The term 'financial year' as used in the Food Safety and Standards Act refers to the twelve-month period for which the Food Authority prepares its budget showing estimated receipts and expenditure, as prescribed by the Central Government, and for which financial regulations governing the drawing up and implementation of the Authority's budget are adopted.
definitions.plain_english: A financial year is the official 12-month accounting and budgeting period used by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI). In India, this typically runs from April 1 of one year to March 31 of the following year. The FSSAI uses this period to plan its income and spending and to report its financial activities to the Central Government.
real_world_examples: FSSAI prepares its annual budget for the financial year 2024–25 (April 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025) and submits it to the Central Government as required under Section 81, detailing projected income from licensing fees and expenditure on food safety operations.

During the financial year 2023–24, the Central Government reviews and approves the financial regulations adopted by FSSAI that specify the procedure for implementing the Authority's budget, including procurement and expenditure controls.

FSSAI's Chief Executive Officer presents the authority's audited accounts for the concluded financial year 2022–23 to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India as part of the statutory accountability framework.

At the start of each financial year, FSSAI allocates funds to its regional offices across states such as Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal for food safety surveillance, laboratory testing, and officer training programs.

A parliamentary standing committee reviews FSSAI's performance and expenditure for the financial year 2021–22 to assess whether budgeted funds for food safety audits and consumer awareness campaigns were utilised effectively.
what_it_covers: The 12-month period (typically April 1 to March 31) for which FSSAI prepares and submits its budget to the Central Government.
The period during which FSSAI's financial regulations governing budget implementation are operative and applicable.
The accounting period referenced when FSSAI reports its estimated receipts (such as licence fees and grants) and expenditure (such as salaries, laboratory costs, and operational expenses).
The cycle within which the Central Government must give prior approval for FSSAI's financial regulations before they are adopted and implemented.
what_it_excludes: A calendar year (January 1 to December 31), which is not the standard financial year used for government budgeting in India under this Act.
Partial or interim accounting periods such as quarterly or half-yearly financial reviews, which do not constitute a 'financial year' for the purpose of budget preparation under Section 81.
The financial accounting periods of private food business operators or manufacturers regulated under the Act, which are governed by the Companies Act or Income Tax Act and not by this provision.
Budget periods of State Food Safety Authorities or State Governments, which operate under separate state financial regulations and appropriation processes.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'financial year' directly governs when FSSAI must prepare and submit its budget to the Central Government, making timely compliance with Section 81 a mandatory statutory obligation; failure to do so on schedule could constitute a procedural violation affecting the lawful operation and funding of the Authority. It also determines the period within which financial regulations must be adopted and implemented with Central Government approval, impacting the legality of FSSAI's expenditure decisions.

definitions.definition: A 'firm' is included within the meaning of 'company' under Section 66 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, and in relation to a firm, 'director' means a partner in the firm. A firm is thus an association of individuals carrying on business in partnership, and for the purposes of offences under this Act, it is treated as a body corporate with its partners bearing the same liability as directors of a company.
definitions.plain_english: A 'firm' refers to a partnership business — where two or more people jointly run a business together. Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, a firm is treated like a company when it comes to food safety offences. This means that the partners of the firm can be personally held responsible if the firm commits any food safety violation.
real_world_examples: A partnership firm 'Sharma & Sons' running a food processing unit in Kanpur is found selling adulterated spices. All partners actively involved in the business can be prosecuted under the Act, just as directors of a company would be.

A small partnership firm operating a chain of dhabas in Delhi is found using substandard cooking oil across its outlets. The managing partner nominated as responsible for food safety is held liable for the violations.

Two partners running a bakery firm in Pune are found to have misbranded their packaged bread. Both partners are deemed guilty unless one can prove the offence occurred without their knowledge and despite due diligence.

A trading firm in Mumbai importing food articles is found to be dealing in unsafe food items. The partner in charge of imports is proceeded against under the Act in the same manner as a company director would be.

A partnership firm operating a cold storage and distribution business in Amritsar is found storing food in unsanitary conditions. The partner heading operations is treated as a 'director' and held liable for the contravention.
what_it_covers: A registered partnership firm carrying on any food business operation such as manufacturing, processing, distribution or sale of food articles
An unregistered association of individuals jointly conducting a food business, treated as a firm for purposes of liability under the Act
A partner in the firm who is in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the firm's food business at the time an offence is committed
A partner specifically nominated by the firm as responsible for food safety at a particular establishment, branch, or unit
what_it_excludes: A sole proprietorship, where there is only one individual running the business and no partnership or association of individuals exists
A body corporate such as a private limited company or public limited company, which is separately and expressly covered as a 'company' under Section 66
A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) business entity, which is governed by its own distinct legal framework and is not an 'association of individuals' in the partnership sense
A co-operative society registered under applicable co-operative laws, which has its own distinct legal personality separate from a firm
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'firm' determines whether its partners can be personally prosecuted for food safety offences under Section 66, just as directors of a company would be; this directly triggers criminal liability, penalties, and prosecution of individual partners. If the entity is not recognised as a firm or company, the individual members may escape the vicarious liability imposed under Section 66.

definitions.definition: "Food" means any substance, whether processed, partially processed or unprocessed, which is intended for human consumption and includes primary food to the extent defined in clause (zk), genetically modified or engineered food or food containing such ingredients, infant food, packaged drinking water, alcoholic drink, chewing gum, and any substance, including water used into the food during its manufacture, preparation or treatment but does not include any animal feed, live animals unless they are prepared or processed for placing on the market for human consumption, plants, prior to harvesting, drugs and medicinal products, cosmetics, narcotic or psychotropic substances: Provided that the Central Government may declare, by notification in the Official Gazette, any other article as food for the purposes of this Act having regards to its use, nature, substance or quality.
definitions.plain_english: Food refers to anything a person eats or drinks — whether raw, partly cooked, or fully processed — that is meant for human consumption. This includes things like packaged snacks, bottled water, alcoholic beverages, chewing gum, and even water used during cooking or manufacturing. However, it does not cover items like animal feed, medicines, cosmetics, or plants still growing in fields before they are harvested.
real_world_examples: A packet of Haldiram's namkeen sold at a Delhi railway station kiosk is 'food' under the Act because it is a processed substance intended for human consumption, making it subject to FSSAI labelling and safety standards.

Packaged drinking water bottled by Bisleri or Kinley at a plant in Maharashtra is explicitly covered as 'food,' meaning the manufacturer must obtain an FSSAI licence and comply with prescribed quality standards.

A local toddy shop in Kerala serving alcoholic drinks derived from palm sap is dealing in 'food' under the Act, and the operator must ensure the product meets safety standards and holds a valid food business licence.
A street vendor in Mumbai selling freshly cut sugarcane juice is selling 'food,' and any adulteration or use of unsafe water in preparation can attract penalties under the Act.

A company in Pune manufacturing infant formula (baby food) is producing 'food' under the Act, and the product is subject to stringent composition, labelling, and safety regulations prescribed by FSSAI.
Chewing gum brands like Centre Fresh sold in Indian retail stores are classified as 'food,' requiring compliance with ingredient safety standards and FSSAI registration.
what_it_covers: Processed packaged foods such as biscuits, chips, and ready-to-eat meals sold in Indian supermarkets
Packaged drinking water, including mineral water and packaged natural water brands sold commercially
Alcoholic beverages such as beer, wine, and spirits intended for human consumption
Chewing gum and confectionery products available in Indian retail markets
Genetically modified or engineered food and food products containing GM ingredients
Infant food, including infant formula and complementary baby food products
Water used during the manufacture, preparation, or treatment of any food product
what_it_excludes: Animal feed and fodder intended solely for livestock or poultry consumption, not for humans
Live animals that have not been prepared or processed for placement on the market for human consumption
Plants prior to harvesting, such as standing crops in a field before they are reaped
Drugs and medicinal products regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940
Cosmetics such as lip balm or face cream, even if they contain edible-grade ingredients
Narcotic or psychotropic substances controlled under the NDPS Act, 1985
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an article qualifies as 'food' under the Act determines whether a business operator must obtain an FSSAI licence or registration, comply with safety and labelling standards, and remain subject to inspection, sampling, and penalties under Sections 50, 53, and 65; failure to comply once an article is classified as food can result in fines, product recall, or prosecution, while articles falling outside this definition are entirely outside the Act's enforcement reach.

definitions.definition: Any substance not normally consumed as a food by itself or used as a typical ingredient of the food, whether or not it has nutritive value, the intentional addition of which to food for a technological (including organoleptic) purpose in the manufacture, processing, preparation, treatment, packing, packaging, transport or holding of such food results, or may be reasonably expected to result (directly or indirectly), in it or its by-products becoming a component of or otherwise affecting the characteristics of such food but does not include 'contaminants' or substances added to food for maintaining or improving nutritional qualities.
definitions.plain_english: A food additive is a substance that is deliberately added to food during its making, processing, packaging, or storage to serve a specific technical purpose — such as preserving freshness, improving colour, enhancing flavour, or maintaining texture — but is not something people would normally eat on its own. It does not include accidental contaminants or vitamins and minerals added to improve nutrition. Only substances intentionally added for a technological function fall under this definition.
real_world_examples: A biscuit manufacturer in Pune adds sodium benzoate to extend the shelf life of cream-filled biscuits — sodium benzoate qualifies as a food additive because it is intentionally added for a preservation (technological) purpose and becomes part of the final product.

A soft drink company in Bengaluru uses tartrazine (Yellow 5) to give its lemon-flavoured drink a bright yellow colour — tartrazine is a food additive as it is intentionally added for an organoleptic (colour) purpose and affects the characteristics of the beverage.

A Delhi-based paneer producer adds calcium chloride during curdling to improve the texture and firmness of paneer — calcium chloride functions as a food additive (firming agent) intentionally used for a technological purpose in processing.

A Mumbai bakery uses potassium bromate as a flour treatment agent to improve dough elasticity and bread volume — this substance is intentionally added for a technological purpose during preparation and thus meets the definition of a food additive.

An ice cream manufacturer in Chennai uses carrageenan (a seaweed-derived stabiliser) to prevent separation and maintain a smooth texture during storage and transport — carrageenan is a food additive as it is intentionally added to affect the physical characteristics of the product.

A packaged juice company in Hyderabad adds ascorbic acid purely as an antioxidant to prevent browning and oxidation of the juice during packaging — when added for this technological purpose (not as a vitamin supplement), it qualifies as a food additive.
what_it_covers: Preservatives such as sodium benzoate or potassium sorbate intentionally added to packaged foods to extend shelf life.
Artificial or natural colours like tartrazine or beta-carotene added to food products for visual (organoleptic) appeal.
Emulsifiers, stabilisers, and thickeners such as lecithin or xanthan gum added to maintain texture and consistency during processing or storage.
Flavour enhancers like monosodium glutamate (MSG) deliberately added to snack foods or instant noodles to improve taste.
Antioxidants such as BHA (butylated hydroxyanisole) added to oils and fat-containing foods to prevent rancidity during transport and holding.
Firming agents, anti-caking agents, bleaching agents, and leavening agents intentionally used during food manufacture for a defined technological function.
what_it_excludes: Contaminants — substances that enter food accidentally through production, processing, packaging, or environmental contamination, which are explicitly excluded from the definition.
Vitamins, minerals, and other nutrients added to food solely for the purpose of maintaining or improving its nutritional quality (e.g., fortification of milk with Vitamin D).
Substances that are themselves normally consumed as food (e.g., salt, sugar, or spices used as typical ingredients in cooking or food preparation).
Typical ingredients of a food product that serve no distinct technological additive function beyond their standard culinary role (e.g., flour in bread, milk in yoghurt).
Processing aids that are used during manufacture but are removed from the final food product and do not become a component of or affect the characteristics of the finished food.
Pesticide residues or veterinary drug residues present in food as a result of agricultural or veterinary practices, which are governed separately under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a 'food additive' determines whether it must comply with the standards, permissions, and usage limits prescribed under Section 19 of the Food Safety and Standards Act and associated FSSAI regulations — use of an unpermitted or excess food additive can render the food 'unsafe' or 'sub-standard', exposing the food business operator to penalties, licence cancellation, and prosecution under the Act. Misclassifying a contaminant or nutritional supplement as a food additive (or vice versa) can also affect which regulatory pathway and liability provisions apply.

They are not the main ingredients of food but are added intentionally to achieve a desired effect. In India, the Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI) sets the rules for which additives are allowed and in what quantities.
real_world_examples: A biscuit manufacturer in Pune adds sodium benzoate as a preservative to extend the shelf life of its cream-filled biscuits — the permissible limit for this food additive is governed by FSSAI regulations under Section 16.

A soft drink company in Mumbai uses tartrazine (Yellow 5) as an artificial colouring agent in its lemon-flavoured beverage; the quantity used must comply with FSSAI-specified limits for food additives.
A bread-making unit in Delhi uses potassium bromate as a flour-treatment agent to improve dough elasticity; FSSAI has banned this substance, making its use a violation of food additive regulations.
A dairy plant in Gujarat adds carrageenan as a thickening and stabilising agent to flavoured milk products, subject to the maximum permissible limits set by the Food Authority under Section 16.

A packaged namkeen (snack) producer in Hyderabad uses monosodium glutamate (MSG) as a flavour enhancer; the product label must declare the additive and the quantity used must be within FSSAI-prescribed limits.
An ice cream manufacturer in Chennai uses annatto extract as a natural colouring additive; compliance with FSSAI's specified limits is mandatory to avoid misbranding and sub-standard classification.

Humectants, sweeteners, and acidity regulators added for specific technological functions during food manufacture or processing.
what_it_excludes: Contaminants or extraneous matter that are unintentionally present in food and are not added for any technological purpose.
