definitions.definition: 'Food Analyst' means an analyst appointed under section 45.
definitions.plain_english: A Food Analyst is a qualified scientist or technical expert officially appointed by the government under the Food Safety and Standards Act to test and analyse food samples collected by Food Safety Officers. They examine samples in recognised laboratories to determine whether food meets legal safety and quality standards. Their written report on the analysis is the primary technical evidence used in legal proceedings against food business operators.
real_world_examples: A Food Analyst at the State Public Health Laboratory in Mumbai receives a sealed sample of packaged milk collected by a Food Safety Officer from a Dharavi dairy outlet and tests it for adulteration with water, starch, and detergent, then issues an official analysis report.

A Food Analyst appointed by the Delhi government analyses a sample of street-vendor chaat masala seized from Chandni Chowk and finds it contains lead levels exceeding FSSAI-prescribed limits, triggering prosecution of the vendor.

A Food Analyst in Tamil Nadu tests a consignment of imported cashew nuts at Chennai port for aflatoxin contamination and certifies them unsafe, enabling the Designated Officer to order rejection or destruction of the consignment.

A Food Analyst at a NABL-accredited laboratory in Hyderabad examines a baby food sample collected from a supermarket and confirms it does not conform to the compositional standards prescribed under FSSAI regulations, providing the evidentiary basis for issuing an improvement notice.

A Food Analyst appointed under section 45 in Punjab tests samples of adulterated ghee collected during a festive season raid and submits a certificate of analysis that is used as primary evidence in adjudication proceedings before the Adjudicating Officer.
what_it_covers: A scientist or technical expert formally appointed by the State or Central Government under section 45 of the FSSAI Act to carry out chemical, microbiological, or other scientific analyses of food samples.

An analyst working at a recognised or accredited food laboratory who tests samples sent by Food Safety Officers or Designated Officers and issues official analysis reports admissible as evidence in legal proceedings.
An analyst whose certificate or report of analysis is used to determine whether a food article is unsafe, sub-standard, misbranded, or contains adulterants or contaminants beyond permissible limits.

A person empowered under sections 38, 40, 43, 45, 46, and 91 to receive food samples under prescribed procedures, analyse them, and submit findings that can trigger prosecution, penalty, or prohibition orders.
what_it_excludes: A Food Safety Officer, who collects and sends food samples but is not authorised to conduct the official analysis or issue the analysis report.

A private laboratory technician or analyst working in a non-recognised or non-accredited laboratory who has not been formally appointed under section 45 and whose findings carry no statutory evidentiary value.
A Designated Officer or Commissioner of Food Safety, who exercises administrative and enforcement powers but is not tasked with laboratory analysis of food samples.
A food business operator's in-house quality control analyst, who may test food internally but holds no statutory appointment and cannot issue legally recognised analysis reports under the Act.
A referral laboratory scientist who re-analyses a contested sample but does so in the capacity of the referral institution, not as an individually appointed Food Analyst under section 45.
definitions.why_it_matters: The official report of a Food Analyst is the primary admissible scientific evidence in prosecutions, adjudication proceedings, and penalty actions under the Act — without a validly appointed Food Analyst conducting the analysis, the entire evidentiary chain for establishing food adulteration, sub-standard quality, or unsafe conditions collapses, potentially defeating enforcement action. The appointment status under section 45 determines whether the analyst's certificate is legally binding or challengeable, directly affecting convictions, fines, licence cancellations, and prohibition orders against food business operators.

definitions.plain_english: A Food Analyst is a qualified government-appointed scientist or technical expert who is officially authorized to test and analyze food samples to check whether they meet the safety and quality standards laid down by law. They receive food samples collected by Food Safety Officers and issue official analysis reports that can be used as evidence in legal proceedings. Only their reports carry legal validity for enforcement actions under the Food Safety and Standards Act.
real_world_examples: A Food Analyst at the Public Health Laboratory in Mumbai receives a sample of adulterated turmeric powder seized from a spice market by a Food Safety Officer and tests it for artificial colour content, then issues an official certificate of analysis used to prosecute the seller.

A Food Analyst appointed by the Delhi government analyzes a sample of packaged milk collected from a Mother Dairy outlet to determine whether it meets the prescribed fat and SNF (solids-not-fat) standards under FSSAI regulations.

In Tamil Nadu, a Food Analyst examines a sample of mid-day meal food collected from a government school after students complained of illness, and the analyst's report confirming contamination triggers legal action against the caterer.

A Food Analyst in Uttar Pradesh tests a sample of loose sweets collected during Diwali raids on a halwai shop and certifies the presence of non-permitted synthetic dyes, enabling the Designated Officer to initiate prosecution under the Act.

A Food Analyst appointed at a State food laboratory in Hyderabad analyzes imported noodles samples for pesticide residues beyond permissible limits and submits a statutory analysis report that leads to a product recall order.

During a routine market surveillance drive in Kolkata, a Food Analyst receives sealed samples of bottled water and tests them for microbial contamination; a positive finding results in suspension of the manufacturer's licence.
what_it_covers: A scientist or technical officer formally appointed by the competent authority under section 45 of the FSSA, 2006 to conduct food analysis.
An analyst working at a recognized government or accredited food laboratory who is empowered to receive food samples from Food Safety Officers and issue legally valid certificates of analysis.

A Food Analyst who analyzes food samples sent under section 42 (analysis of food) and section 47 (purchaser's right to have food analyzed) and whose report can be produced as evidence in a court of law or before an Adjudicating Officer.
State government-employed food scientists posted at State Public Analyst laboratories who hold the requisite qualifications prescribed under FSSAI regulations and are duly notified as Food Analysts.
what_it_excludes: Private laboratory technicians or scientists working in non-recognized or non-accredited private labs who have not been formally appointed under section 45, even if they perform food testing commercially.
Food Safety Officers (appointed under section 37) who collect and send food samples but are not authorized to conduct or certify the analysis themselves.
Referral laboratory scientists or NABL-accredited lab personnel who analyze food samples but have not been specifically appointed as Food Analysts under section 45 of the Act.
General medical practitioners, nutritionists, or food technologists in private practice who assess food quality for advisory purposes but hold no statutory appointment under the Act.
Customs or import inspection officers who visually examine imported food consignments at ports of entry without conducting formal laboratory analysis under section 45.

definitions.definition: An 'article of food' refers to any article or substance intended for human consumption, including any ingredient, additive, or constituent thereof, as used in the context of Section 27 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, encompassing all food products across the supply chain from manufacture to retail sale, which must comply with the safety, labelling, and quality requirements prescribed under the Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: An 'article of food' is any product that is made, packed, stored, distributed, or sold for people to eat or drink. This includes everything from raw ingredients to fully processed packaged goods found in shops and markets. The term is used to determine who — the manufacturer, packer, distributor, or seller — is responsible if that product is unsafe, expired, or does not meet legal food standards.
real_world_examples: A packet of Amul butter sold at a grocery store in Mumbai that is found to be stored beyond its expiry date, making the seller liable under Section 27 for selling an expired article of food.

A batch of Maggi noodles manufactured by Nestlé India that is found to contain lead levels above the prescribed limit, making the manufacturer liable as the article of food does not meet safety requirements under the Act.

A consignment of adulterated mustard oil distributed by a wholesaler in Delhi to retail shops without any identifiable manufacturer details, triggering wholesaler liability under Section 27 for an unidentifiable-source article of food.
A local mithai shop in Kolkata selling sweets prepared and stored in unhygienic conditions, rendering the seller liable under Section 27 for handling the article of food in unsanitary circumstances.

A cold drink distributor in Chennai supplying carbonated beverages after the best-before date printed on the bottle, making the distributor liable for supplying an expired article of food in violation of the Act.

A packer of packaged spices in Rajasthan who uses non-permitted food coloring agents, resulting in the packer being held liable because the article of food does not conform to the regulations prescribed under the Food Safety and Standards Act.
what_it_covers: Packaged and processed food products such as biscuits, chips, dairy products, and beverages manufactured and sold in India.
Raw food ingredients and primary agricultural produce that have been processed, packed, or prepared for direct human consumption.
Food items distributed through the wholesale and retail chain, including items sold by street vendors, temporary stall holders, and petty retailers.
Imported food products brought into India for sale or distribution that must meet domestic food safety standards.
Homemade or locally prepared food articles sold commercially, such as sweets, snacks, or ready-to-eat meals offered in the market.
what_it_excludes: Medicines, drugs, and pharmaceutical products regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, even if ingested, as they are not intended as food for general human consumption.
Animal feed and pet food products not intended for human consumption, which fall outside the scope of food safety obligations under this Act.
Cosmetic or topical products such as lip balms or skin creams that may be ingested incidentally but are not manufactured or sold as food articles.
Water supplied through public utilities for general use unless it is packaged and sold as drinking water as an article of food under the Act.
Industrial raw materials or chemical substances that may enter the food supply as contaminants but are not themselves manufactured or intended as articles of food.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a product as an 'article of food' under Section 27 directly determines which party in the supply chain — manufacturer, packer, wholesaler, distributor, or seller — bears legal liability for safety violations, expiry breaches, misbranding, or unhygienic handling, and triggers penalties, prosecution, and compensation obligations under the Act. If a product does not qualify as an article of food, none of these liability provisions apply, shielding all parties from enforcement action under the Food Safety and Standards Act.

The Food Authority granted recognition to a private food testing laboratory in Pune after it was accredited by NABL, enabling it to conduct statutory food sample analysis for enforcement purposes.

The Food Authority constituted Scientific Panels to evaluate novel food ingredients proposed for use in health supplements, before permitting their sale in the Indian market.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Food Authority issued emergency guidelines to food business operators on hygiene and sanitation protocols to prevent food contamination at processing units.

definitions.definition: "food business" means any undertaking, whether for profit or not and whether public or private, carrying out any of the activities related to any stage of manufacture, processing, packaging, storage, transportation, distribution of food, import and includes food services, catering services, sale of food or food ingredients.
definitions.plain_english: A food business is any organisation or operation — big or small, government-run or private, profit-making or not — that is involved in any step of getting food to people. This includes making food, processing it, packing it, storing it, transporting it, distributing it, importing it, serving it in restaurants or canteens, catering for events, or simply selling food or food ingredients. Even a small roadside stall or a school cafeteria qualifies as a food business under this definition.
real_world_examples: A large FMCG company like Nestlé India manufacturing packaged noodles and distributing them across the country through retail chains constitutes a food business at the manufacturing, packaging, and distribution stages.
A dabba-wala service in Mumbai that collects home-cooked meals and delivers them to office workers constitutes a food business engaged in food services and transportation of food.
A state government-run mid-day meal scheme kitchen preparing and serving cooked food to schoolchildren is a food business, since the definition explicitly includes public and non-profit undertakings.
A local kirana store in Chennai selling packaged atta, rice, and cooking oil is engaged in the sale of food ingredients and therefore qualifies as a food business.
A wedding caterer in Delhi preparing and serving food at private events is a food business covered under catering services, regardless of whether it operates formally or informally.
An importer in Mumbai bringing in frozen seafood from South-East Asia through the Nhava Sheva port is carrying out an import-stage food business activity and falls squarely within this definition.
what_it_covers: Private food manufacturers processing and packaging food products for sale in the Indian market.
Government-run canteens, institutional kitchens, and welfare scheme kitchens providing food to beneficiaries.
Restaurants, dhabas, cloud kitchens, and catering companies serving prepared food to customers.
Importers bringing food articles or food ingredients into India through any mode of transport.
Wholesalers, distributors, and retailers involved in the storage, distribution, or sale of food or food ingredients.
Online food aggregators and delivery platforms that facilitate the transportation and sale of food to consumers.
what_it_excludes: Personal or household cooking and consumption where food is prepared solely for one's own family without any commercial or public dimension.

Farmers engaged purely in growing and harvesting crops who have not yet processed or offered the produce for sale, as primary agricultural activity prior to placing food on the market is outside the operational scope.
Manufacturers of animal feed, cosmetics, drugs, or narcotic substances, since these fall outside the definition of 'food' itself under the Act and therefore cannot constitute a food business.
Businesses dealing exclusively in live animals not prepared or processed for human consumption, as such animals are excluded from the definition of food.
Entities handling plants prior to harvesting, since unprocessed crops in the field are not considered food under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a food business determines whether it must obtain a licence or registration under Section 31 of the Act, comply with food safety standards, and submit to inspections and enforcement actions by Food Safety Officers; failure to operate as a licensed food business attracts significant penalties including fines and business closure under the Act.

definitions.definition: "food business operator" in relation to food business means a person by whom the business is carried on or owned and is responsible for ensuring the compliance of this Act, rules and regulations made thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: A food business operator is the person who runs or owns a food-related business and is legally responsible for making sure all food safety rules and standards are followed. This can be an individual, a company, or any entity involved in making, selling, storing, or distributing food. They are the primary accountable party whenever food safety laws are enforced.
real_world_examples: A restaurant owner in Mumbai who operates a chain of dine-in eateries is the food business operator responsible for obtaining FSSAI licences and ensuring hygienic food preparation standards are met at all outlets.

A proprietor of a packaged namkeen manufacturing unit in Indore who produces snacks for pan-India distribution is a food business operator and must comply with labelling regulations, obtain the appropriate central or state licence, and maintain quality standards.

An e-commerce platform like Swiggy or Zomato operating cloud kitchens in Bengaluru qualifies as a food business operator for those kitchen operations and is responsible for ensuring the food produced therein meets FSSAI standards.

A milk cooperative society such as Amul, which processes, packages, and distributes dairy products across India, is a food business operator and must register or obtain a licence and adhere to all food safety and standards regulations for dairy products.

A street food vendor running a permanent stall selling chaat in Delhi's Connaught Place is a food business operator (classified as a petty retailer or petty manufacturer) and must obtain a basic registration under the FSS Act.

An importer bringing in canned fish from Thailand through the Chennai port is a food business operator in respect of those imports and is legally responsible for ensuring the consignment meets Indian food safety standards before it is placed on the market.
what_it_covers: An individual proprietor who manufactures, processes, packages, or sells food articles, including small-scale or home-based food producers who are required to register under the FSS Act.
A private limited company or corporate entity that owns and operates food manufacturing plants, catering establishments, or food retail chains across India.
A food importer who brings food articles into India and places them on the domestic market, being the person responsible for ensuring imported food conforms to Indian food safety standards.
A catering service provider supplying meals to schools, hospitals, or corporate canteens, who is responsible for the hygiene and safety of food prepared and served.
A food storage or warehousing entity that holds food articles for distribution, where the person operating or owning the warehouse is accountable for maintaining safe storage conditions.
what_it_excludes: A mere employee or worker at a food establishment who does not own or carry on the business, and who does not bear management responsibility for regulatory compliance.
A consumer who purchases and uses food solely for personal or family consumption, with no commercial activity involved in the food supply chain.
A transporter who merely provides logistics or haulage services for food articles but does not own the food business, carry on the food business, or exercise control over food safety compliance.
Government regulatory officers such as Food Safety Officers or Designated Officers who inspect or enforce food safety laws but do not carry on a food business.
A landlord who rents out premises to a food business but has no role in operating or owning the food business itself.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identification of a food business operator determines who bears primary legal liability under the FSS Act for offences such as manufacturing or selling unsafe, sub-standard, or misbranded food, and who is subject to duties including obtaining licences or registration (Sections 31–32), maintaining food safety management systems, complying with improvement notices, and facing penalties, prosecution, or prohibition orders under Sections 47, 55, and 63. All enforcement actions, penalties, and compliance obligations under the Act are directed at and enforceable against the food business operator.

definitions.definition: Foods for special dietary uses means foods which are specially processed or formulated to satisfy particular dietary requirements which exist because of a particular physical or physiological condition or specific diseases and disorders, wherein the composition must differ significantly from ordinary comparable foods, and which may be formulated as powders, granules, tablets, capsules, liquids, jelly or other dosage forms for oral administration, but not parenterals; such products are not represented as conventional food, do not claim to cure or mitigate any specific disease or disorder except as permitted by regulations, and do not include drugs under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, narcotic or psychotropic substances, or substances listed in Schedules E and E1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945.
definitions.plain_english: Foods for special dietary uses are specially made food products designed to meet the nutritional needs of people who have specific health conditions, physical states, or diseases that require a different diet than the general population. These products — such as diabetic foods, gluten-free products for celiac patients, or protein supplements for people with metabolic disorders — have a composition that is significantly different from regular everyday foods. They can come in various forms like powders, capsules, or liquids but must be taken orally, and they cannot claim to treat or cure any disease.
real_world_examples: A company in Pune manufactures a low-glycaemic index, sugar-free biscuit range specifically formulated for Type 2 diabetes patients, labelled as 'Food for Special Dietary Use — Diabetics', sold through medical stores and pharmacies across Maharashtra.

A Mumbai-based firm imports and distributes gluten-free flour blends and pasta specially processed for individuals diagnosed with celiac disease or gluten intolerance, sold in specialty health stores.

A Chennai nutrition brand launches a high-calorie, protein-dense powder formulated for paediatric patients suffering from malnutrition or failure-to-thrive conditions, distributed through hospitals and dieticians.

A Delhi startup sells ready-to-drink liquid meal replacements designed for post-bariatric surgery patients who cannot digest solid food normally, marketed as special dietary use products under FSSAI regulations.

An Ahmedabad manufacturer produces phenylalanine-free food products specifically for infants and children diagnosed with Phenylketonuria (PKU), a rare metabolic genetic disorder requiring strict dietary management.
what_it_covers: Specially processed gluten-free foods formulated for persons with celiac disease or gluten intolerance whose dietary needs differ significantly from the general population.
Low-protein or amino-acid-modified food products designed for patients with inherited metabolic disorders such as Phenylketonuria (PKU) or maple syrup urine disease.
High-calorie or nutrient-dense liquid or powder formulations designed for post-surgical patients, cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, or individuals with severe malabsorption conditions.
Diabetic-specific foods formulated with low glycaemic ingredients that significantly differ in sugar and carbohydrate composition from comparable ordinary foods.
Infant or paediatric foods specially formulated to meet the physiological dietary requirements of premature infants or infants with specific metabolic or growth disorders.
what_it_excludes: Drugs as defined under clause (b) of section 3 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, including Ayurvedic, Siddha, and Unani drugs as defined in clauses (a) and (h) of that section.

Narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances as defined in the Schedule of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act 1985 and substances listed in Schedules E and E1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945.
Products administered parenterally (i.e., intravenously or by injection), even if they serve a dietary or nutritional purpose.
Conventional everyday food products marketed to the general healthy population without any special formulation for a specific physiological condition or disease.
Products that claim to cure, treat, or mitigate a specific disease or disorder in ways not permitted by regulations made under the Food Safety and Standards Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Any person who manufactures, distributes, sells, or imports foods for special dietary uses without complying with the standards and regulations prescribed under Section 22 commits an offence under the Food Safety and Standards Act, potentially attracting penalties, product seizure, and prosecution. The classification also determines whether a product is regulated as a food (under FSSAI) or a drug (under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act), which has significant consequences for licensing, labelling, permissible claims, and enforcement jurisdiction.

definitions.definition: "Food ingredients" is not separately defined in the Act; however, as used in Section 22 and read with Section 3(y) defining "ingredient," food ingredients means any substance, including food additives, used in the manufacture or preparation of food and present in the final product, possibly in a modified form, and includes genetically modified or engineered substances used as components of food.
definitions.plain_english: Food ingredients are the individual substances or components that are mixed or used together to make a food product. These include basic raw materials like flour, sugar, and spices, as well as food additives added during manufacturing. If a substance ends up in the final food product in any form, it qualifies as a food ingredient.
real_world_examples: A biscuit manufacturer in Mumbai uses refined wheat flour, sugar, hydrogenated vegetable fat, and salt — all of these are food ingredients used in making the final biscuit product sold across India.

A dairy company in Amul's supply chain uses cultures, stabilisers, and skimmed milk powder to produce flavoured yogurt; each of these substances is a food ingredient subject to FSSAI standards under Section 22.

A Maggi noodles factory uses tapioca starch, wheat flour, salt, and flavour enhancers; these are food ingredients, and any genetically modified version of these substances would attract the specific provisions of Section 22.

A fruit jam producer in Pune incorporates pectin, citric acid, and permitted synthetic colours along with fruit pulp; all these substances used in the manufacturing process and present in the final product are classified as food ingredients.

A Hyderabad-based baby food manufacturer uses fortified vitamins, minerals, and whey protein concentrate as ingredients — these are food ingredients that must comply with FSSAI safety and labelling standards.
what_it_covers: Primary raw materials such as wheat flour, rice, sugar, or milk used in manufacturing packaged food products.
Food additives like emulsifiers, preservatives, and stabilisers that are intentionally incorporated into a food product during processing and remain in the final product.
Genetically modified or engineered substances used as components in food manufacture, as specifically referenced in the definition of 'food' and the scope of Section 22.
Processing-derived substances that transform during manufacture but are still present in a modified form in the finished food product.
Substances such as vitamins, minerals, and protein concentrates added to fortified or specialised food products.
what_it_excludes: Contaminants, which are substances not intentionally added but present due to environmental or production contamination — these are separately defined and treated under the Act.
Processing aids that are used during manufacture but are not present in the final food product in any significant or functional quantity.
Substances used in packaging, labelling, or external coating that do not become part of the food itself and are not consumed along with the food.
Live animals, plants prior to harvesting, drugs and medicinal products, which are explicitly excluded from the definition of 'food' and therefore cannot qualify as food ingredients under this Act.
Animal feed and veterinary medicines, which are excluded from the scope of 'food' under Section 3 and thus fall outside the concept of food ingredients.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a food ingredient determines whether it falls under the regulatory approvals, safety standards, and labelling obligations prescribed under Section 22, particularly for novel or genetically modified food ingredients, triggering licensing conditions, prior approval requirements, and potential liability for unsafe or sub-standard food under Sections 50–59 of the Act.

definitions.definition: "food laboratory" means any food laboratory or institute established by the Central or a State Government or any other agency and accredited by National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories or an equivalent accreditation agency and recognised by the Food Authority under section 43.
definitions.plain_english: A food laboratory is a testing facility or institute — set up by the Central Government, a State Government, or any other organisation — that has been officially accredited by NABL (or a similar body) and recognised by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to analyse food samples. Only laboratories meeting these two conditions (accreditation and FSSAI recognition) qualify as 'food laboratories' under this law. These labs are authorised to test food products for safety, quality, and compliance with food standards.
real_world_examples: The Central Food Laboratory in Kolkata, established under the Central Government and accredited by NABL, is recognised by FSSAI under section 43 to test food samples sent by Food Safety Officers across India.

A State Government of Maharashtra sets up a food testing institute in Pune, obtains NABL accreditation, and gets it recognised by FSSAI — making it a valid 'food laboratory' where Food Analysts can officially analyse samples collected from local food businesses.

A private testing agency in Hyderabad obtains NABL accreditation and subsequently applies for and receives FSSAI recognition under section 43, thereby qualifying as a food laboratory permitted to conduct official food sample testing under the Act.

A Food Safety Officer in Delhi collects adulterated milk samples from a dairy and sends them to the Government of India's Central Food Technology Research Institute (CFTRI) lab, which is both NABL-accredited and FSSAI-recognised, for official analysis and generation of a Food Analyst's report.

During a food safety drive, Tamil Nadu's state-recognised food laboratory in Chennai analyses spice samples collected from local markets for pesticide residues and adulterants, and its report is used as legal evidence in proceedings against the food business operator.
what_it_covers: Central Government-established food testing laboratories that have obtained NABL accreditation and FSSAI recognition under section 43, such as the Central Food Laboratory.
State Government food testing institutes that are accredited by NABL or an equivalent body and formally recognised by the Food Authority under section 43.
Private or non-governmental food testing agencies or institutes that have secured NABL (or equivalent) accreditation and have been granted recognition by the Food Authority under section 43.

Food testing institutes accredited by an accreditation agency equivalent to NABL (such as a foreign or internationally recognised body) and recognised by FSSAI, provided both conditions are satisfied.
what_it_excludes: In-house quality control laboratories of food manufacturing companies, even if technically equipped, as they are not established for the purpose of official recognition under section 43 nor typically NABL-accredited for this purpose.
Any food testing facility or institute that is NABL-accredited but has not been formally recognised by the Food Authority under section 43 of this Act.
University or research institution laboratories that conduct food-related research but have not obtained NABL accreditation and FSSAI recognition specifically as a food laboratory under section 43.
Hospital or clinical laboratories that may test food-related contaminants for medical purposes but are not recognised by the Food Authority under section 43.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a facility as a 'food laboratory' determines whether its analytical reports and Food Analyst findings are legally admissible as evidence in prosecutions, adjudication, and appeals under the Act; only reports from recognised food laboratories carry statutory authority. If a laboratory does not meet this definition, samples analysed there cannot support enforcement actions such as penalties, prosecution, or prohibition orders against food business operators.

definitions.definition: Food poisoning refers to any illness or adverse health condition arising from the consumption of contaminated, adulterated, or unsafe food or drink, the occurrence of which registered medical practitioners are required to report to the designated officer as notified by the Food Authority under Section 35 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
definitions.plain_english: Food poisoning means getting sick after eating or drinking something that is contaminated, spoiled, or unsafe. It can be caused by harmful bacteria, viruses, chemicals, or toxins present in food. Under this law, doctors who come across such cases are required to report them to the relevant food safety authority so that appropriate action can be taken.
real_world_examples: A mass outbreak of vomiting and diarrhea among students in a Mumbai school after consuming mid-day meals prepared with stale rice and curry, reported by the school doctor to the local food safety officer.
Several guests at a wedding in Delhi falling ill after consuming paneer dishes that had been kept unrefrigerated for hours, leading the attending physician to notify the Commissioner of Food Safety.

A cluster of patients in a Kolkata hospital emergency ward suffering from jaundice and liver symptoms traced back to adulterated mustard oil sold by a local vendor, reported by the treating doctor under Section 35.

Travellers in a Rajasthan town developing severe gastroenteritis after consuming water mixed with contaminated street food, with the local registered medical practitioner filing a food poisoning report with the notified officer.

Factory workers in Pune hospitalized after consuming canteen food contaminated with pesticide residues, with the occupational health doctor reporting the food poisoning incident as mandated under the notification issued by the Food Authority.
what_it_covers: Illness caused by consumption of bacterially contaminated food, such as Salmonella or E. coli infected products sold in local markets.
Adverse health conditions arising from ingestion of food adulterated with toxic substances, such as synthetic colors, pesticides, or harmful preservatives.
Gastroenteritis, nausea, vomiting, or systemic illness occurring in individuals after consuming unsafe street food, packaged food, or food prepared in mass catering establishments.
Outbreaks of illness in schools, hospitals, or community gatherings where the common source is identified as contaminated food or beverages.
Chemical toxicity or allergic reactions caused by consumption of food containing prohibited food additives or contaminants beyond tolerance limits.
what_it_excludes: Illnesses or injuries caused by non-food sources, such as waterborne diseases unrelated to food consumption, even if presenting with similar symptoms.
Adverse reactions caused by prescribed medications, drugs, or medical treatments that are not food or food ingredients under the Act.
General nutritional deficiency conditions such as anaemia or vitamin deficiency that arise from poor diet but not from contaminated or unsafe food.
Allergic reactions to food that are pre-existing medical conditions of the individual unrelated to any contamination or adulteration of the food consumed.
Occupational illnesses of food handlers caused by chemical exposure during food processing that do not result from consumption of the food itself.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of this definition triggers the mandatory reporting obligation under Section 35, requiring registered medical practitioners to notify the designated officer of every food poisoning occurrence, thereby enabling the Food Authority to investigate the source, take enforcement action against responsible food business operators, and prevent further public health harm. Failure to report such occurrences by a notified practitioner may constitute non-compliance with the Food Authority's notification, and the reported data can trigger inspections, seizures, and prosecutions under the Act.

definitions.definition: "food safety" means assurance that food is acceptable for human consumption according to its intended use.
definitions.plain_english: Food safety is the guarantee that a food product is safe and suitable for people to eat, based on what that food is meant to be used for. For example, baby food must meet stricter safety standards than a general snack because its intended use is feeding infants. It is essentially a promise that what you eat will not harm you when consumed as expected.
real_world_examples: A packaged biscuit manufacturer in Pune ensuring that the biscuits are free from contaminants, adulterants, and harmful additives before they are sold in supermarkets, so consumers can safely consume them as a snack.
A street food vendor in Delhi preparing chaat using clean water, fresh ingredients, and hygienic utensils to ensure the food served does not cause illness to customers who consume it on the spot.

A dairy company in Gujarat conducting microbiological tests on pasteurised milk to confirm it is free from harmful pathogens like Salmonella or E. coli before distribution to consumers across the state.
A baby food producer in Mumbai verifying that their infant formula meets all FSSAI-prescribed nutritional and safety standards, ensuring it is safe for consumption by infants as per its intended use.

A restaurant chain in Bengaluru implementing a Food Safety Management System (FSMS) including regular kitchen audits, temperature monitoring of stored food, and staff hygiene training to maintain food safety across all outlets.
what_it_covers: Ensuring packaged drinking water is free from chemical and biological contaminants and is safe for drinking as intended.
Verifying that processed food products such as ready-to-eat meals do not contain adulterants or unsafe levels of food additives before they reach consumers.
Confirming that infant food products meet heightened safety standards appropriate to their intended use for vulnerable consumers such as newborns and young children.
Guaranteeing that food served in restaurants or catering establishments is prepared and stored under conditions that prevent contamination or spoilage.
Ensuring imported food articles comply with Indian food safety standards before being placed on the market for human consumption.
what_it_excludes: Animal feed, which is not intended for human consumption and therefore falls outside the scope of food safety as defined under this Act.
Live animals not yet prepared or processed for human consumption, as they are not considered food under the Act.

Drugs, medicinal products, cosmetics, and narcotic or psychotropic substances, even if ingested, as these are expressly excluded from the definition of food and hence from food safety assurance obligations.
Plants prior to harvesting, which are not yet in a form intended for direct human consumption.
Non-food substances used in industrial or agricultural processes that may come into contact with food but are not themselves food items placed on the market for consumption.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a product meets the definition of food safety determines whether a food business operator is in compliance with FSSAI regulations or is liable for offences such as selling unsafe food, sub-standard food, or misbranded food under the Act. Failure to ensure food safety can trigger penalties, licence cancellation, improvement notices, prohibition orders, and even criminal prosecution under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

definitions.definition: "food safety audit" means a systematic and functionally independent examination of food safety measures adopted by manufacturing units to determine whether such measures and related results meet with objectives of food safety and the claims made in that behalf.
definitions.plain_english: A food safety audit is a thorough, unbiased check-up of the food safety practices followed by a food manufacturing unit. It is carried out by an independent party to see whether the factory's methods and outcomes actually match the food safety goals and any claims the unit has made. Think of it as an official inspection that verifies a manufacturer is doing what it says it is doing to keep food safe.
real_world_examples: A third-party accredited agency visits a biscuit manufacturing plant in Pune and independently reviews its hygiene practices, raw material sourcing, pest control records, and HACCP documentation to verify compliance with FSSAI food safety standards.

FSSAI-empanelled food safety auditors conduct a systematic audit of a packaged dairy products company in Gujarat to determine whether its pasteurisation and cold-chain processes meet the prescribed food safety objectives under FSS regulations.

An independent auditor examines the food safety management system of a large restaurant chain in Delhi-NCR, checking kitchen sanitation, staff hygiene training records, and temperature logs to verify that the operator's claims of FSMS compliance are substantiated.

A food safety audit is conducted at a spice processing unit in Rajasthan after the unit applies for a higher licence category, with auditors verifying whether actual manufacturing controls align with the food safety measures declared in the licence application.

Under Section 44 of the FSS Act, the Food Authority directs a food safety audit of a multinational beverage company's bottling plant in Maharashtra following a consumer complaint, with an independent auditor assessing whether the plant's quality control measures meet statutory food safety objectives.
what_it_covers: Systematic on-site examination of a food manufacturing unit's HACCP plans, GMP records, and hygiene controls to verify alignment with food safety objectives.
Independent review of documented food safety measures, including testing protocols, sanitation procedures, and staff training records maintained by a food business operator.
Verification of whether the results achieved by a manufacturing unit's food safety programme match the claims made by the unit in its licence application or regulatory filings.
Audits conducted by FSSAI-empanelled food safety auditors under Section 44 to assess compliance of food businesses with food safety management systems prescribed by regulation.
what_it_excludes: Routine inspections carried out by Food Safety Officers under Section 38, which are regulatory surveillance activities rather than systematic independent examinations constituting a formal audit.
Analysis of food samples by a Food Analyst in a food laboratory, which is a testing function and not an examination of the food safety measures adopted by a manufacturing unit.
Internal quality checks performed by a food business operator's own staff, as the definition requires functional independence from the unit being examined.
Adjudication or penalty proceedings initiated under the Act, which are legal proceedings and not examinations of food safety measures.
Audits of non-manufacturing entities such as retailers, hawkers, or itinerant vendors, since the definition specifically refers to measures adopted by manufacturing units.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an activity qualifies as a 'food safety audit' determines whether it triggers the obligations and powers under Section 44, including the Food Authority's power to cause such audits to be conducted and the requirement for food business operators to comply with audit directions. A finding arising from a food safety audit can form the basis for regulatory action, improvement notices, or licence suspension, and auditors conducting such audits must be recognised food safety auditors as prescribed under the Act.

definitions.plain_english: A Food Safety Management System is a structured set of practices and procedures that a food business must follow to ensure the food it produces or handles is safe to eat. It includes maintaining cleanliness and hygiene in the facility, following proper manufacturing methods, and identifying and controlling points in the production process where safety hazards could arise. Think of it as a formal rulebook a food company must implement to prevent contamination and ensure food quality.
real_world_examples: A biscuit manufacturer in Pune implementing HACCP-certified processes to monitor critical control points such as baking temperature and packaging sealing, ensuring no microbial contamination reaches consumers.

A dairy plant in Anand, Gujarat adopting Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) by maintaining sterile processing equipment, trained hygiene personnel, and documented cleaning schedules as mandated under FSSAI regulations.

A restaurant chain operating across Delhi-NCR implementing Good Hygienic Practices (GHP) by ensuring regular handwashing protocols, proper storage temperatures for raw meat, and pest control measures in kitchens.

A spice processing unit in Rajasthan undergoing a food safety audit by an FSSAI-approved auditor to verify that its Food Safety Management System is compliant with HACCP principles, including traceability records and supplier verification.
A packaged drinking water company in Mumbai maintaining a documented FSMS that tracks each production batch from source water testing to final bottling, as required for renewal of its FSSAI licence.
what_it_covers: Adoption of Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) by any food business operator in India, including manufacturers, processors, and packagers.
Implementation of Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) methodology to identify, evaluate, and control food safety hazards at critical stages of production.
Good Hygienic Practices (GHP) including sanitation, personal hygiene of food handlers, and cleanliness of premises and equipment.

what_it_excludes: Informal or undocumented food handling practices that have not been formally adopted as part of a structured system, even if they incidentally result in safe food.
Quality management systems focused solely on product grading, taste, or sensory standards that do not address safety hazards or hygienic practices.

Animal feed production operations, which are excluded from the definition of 'food' under the Act and therefore not subject to FSMS requirements.
Cosmetics, drugs, and medicinal products, which fall outside the scope of 'food' under the Act and thus outside the ambit of Food Safety Management System obligations.

A packaged drinking water manufacturer in Tamil Nadu maintaining a documented system covering source water quality testing, UV treatment validation, bottle sanitation checks, and recall procedures, audited by an FSSAI-recognised certification body.

An e-commerce food aggregator platform ensuring that cloud kitchens listed on its platform adhere to documented food safety management systems covering ingredient sourcing, allergen management, and delivery temperature controls as required under FSSAI regulations.

definitions.definition: 'Food Safety Officer' means an officer appointed under section 37.
definitions.plain_english: A Food Safety Officer is a government-appointed official responsible for inspecting food businesses, collecting food samples, and enforcing food safety laws at the ground level. They are the frontline enforcement agents under the Food Safety and Standards Act, empowered to enter premises, check records, and take action against violations. Their appointments are made under section 37 of the Act by the Commissioner of Food Safety.
real_world_examples: A Food Safety Officer in Mumbai visits a popular street food stall at Juhu Beach, collects samples of pav bhaji, and sends them to a food laboratory to check for adulterants or unsafe ingredients.

A Food Safety Officer in Delhi enters a licensed dairy processing plant to inspect hygiene conditions, check storage temperatures, and review records to ensure compliance with food safety regulations.
A Food Safety Officer in Chennai detects that a local grocery store is selling packaged spices beyond their expiry date and initiates proceedings by issuing an improvement notice under the Act.

A Food Safety Officer in Kolkata receives a complaint about a school canteen serving contaminated mid-day meals, conducts an inspection, seizes the suspicious food items, and forwards the samples to an accredited laboratory for analysis.

A Food Safety Officer in Bengaluru conducts a surprise raid on a cold storage facility and finds that frozen meat products are being stored at improper temperatures, posing a health risk to consumers, and proceeds to take enforcement action.
what_it_covers: Officers formally appointed by the Commissioner of Food Safety under section 37 to enforce food safety standards at the ground level.
Officials empowered under sections 41 and 42 to enter, inspect, and search food business premises and seize non-compliant food articles.
Officers authorised to collect food samples from manufacturers, retailers, distributors, or any food business operator for testing at accredited laboratories.
Government officials who can issue improvement notices, prohibition orders, or initiate prosecution proceedings against food business operators violating the Act.
Officers assigned to specific local areas or jurisdictions within a State or Union Territory for systematic food safety surveillance and enforcement.
what_it_excludes: The Designated Officer appointed under section 36, who operates at a higher supervisory level than a Food Safety Officer and handles licensing decisions and adjudication.
The Commissioner of Food Safety appointed under section 30, who is a senior administrative authority and not a field-level enforcement officer.
Food Analysts appointed under section 45, who are laboratory scientists responsible for testing and analysing food samples but do not conduct field inspections or enforce compliance.
Private food safety auditors or third-party inspectors hired by food businesses, who have no statutory enforcement powers under the Act.
Police officers or general law enforcement personnel who may assist in raids but are not Food Safety Officers within the meaning of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The status of a person as a Food Safety Officer is the legal prerequisite for lawfully exercising inspection, search, seizure, and sampling powers under sections 41, 42, and 47 of the Act — any action taken by an unauthorised person would be void and expose evidence to challenge. Whether an officer holds this designation determines whether criminal proceedings initiated against a food business operator are legally valid and whether collected samples are admissible for prosecution.

A restaurant chain operating across Mumbai and Delhi develops and implements a documented food safety programme covering supplier checks, temperature monitoring, and staff hygiene training to comply with FSSAI licensing conditions and to protect itself against prosecution.

A packaged spices manufacturer in Rajasthan prepares a food safety programme that includes regular testing of raw materials for pesticide residues and aflatoxins, maintaining records to demonstrate due diligence if a sub-standard food allegation is made by a food safety officer.

A school mid-day meal caterer in Tamil Nadu is required under state-level FSSAI guidelines to maintain a food safety programme covering preparation, storage, and distribution of meals, enabling it to defend against any prosecution by showing systematic hazard management.

A seafood export unit in Kerala prepares a comprehensive food safety programme aligned with HACCP and ISO 22000 standards to satisfy both FSSAI requirements and international buyer audits, and uses documented compliance as evidence of due diligence during an FSSAI inspection.

definitions.definition: A food is deemed to fail 'food safety requirements' where it is unsafe, where it is unfit for human consumption, or where it is so contaminated, whether by extraneous matter or otherwise, that it would not be reasonable to expect it to be used for human consumption in that state. Under Section 18(1)(g) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, where any food fails to comply with food safety requirements and is part of a batch, lot or consignment of food of the same class or description, it shall be presumed until the contrary is proved that all of the food in that batch, lot or consignment fails to comply with those requirements.
definitions.plain_english: Food safety requirements are the set of legally prescribed standards and conditions that food must meet to be considered safe for human consumption. These include standards relating to contamination, hygiene, composition, labelling, and fitness for use. If a food product does not meet these requirements, it is treated as unsafe or non-compliant. Importantly, if one item in a batch fails, the entire batch is presumed to fail unless proven otherwise.
real_world_examples: A consignment of packaged spices imported from a foreign country is found to contain pesticide residues exceeding permissible limits set by FSSAI; the entire lot is presumed to fail food safety requirements and can be seized or rejected at the port of entry.

A batch of milk packets distributed by a dairy cooperative in Maharashtra is found to be adulterated with detergent; food safety officers invoke the batch presumption under Section 18 to quarantine all packets from that production run across the state.

A mid-day meal supplier in a Delhi government school uses cooking oil that tests positive for adulteration with non-edible oil; the Food Safety Officer deems the entire stock of that oil batch non-compliant with food safety requirements.

A snack manufacturer in Gujarat produces a consignment of namkeen in which one randomly tested packet contains extraneous matter (metal shavings); food safety authorities presume the entire consignment fails food safety requirements pending further investigation.

A food business operator selling packaged drinking water in Tamil Nadu is found to have coliform bacteria levels exceeding standards in one bottle from a lot; the designated officer treats the entire lot as failing food safety requirements and initiates recall procedures.
what_it_covers: Food that is unsafe or unfit for human consumption due to contamination by extraneous matter, biological, chemical, or physical hazards exceeding prescribed tolerance limits.

An entire batch, lot, or consignment of food of the same class or description where any single item from that batch has been found to be non-compliant, by operation of the statutory presumption under Section 18(1)(g).

Food that is sub-standard, misbranded, or fails to meet composition and labelling standards prescribed under FSSAI regulations, including packaged food, imported food, and food served in food service establishments.
Food processed under unsanitary or unhygienic conditions that renders it unfit or unsafe, even if the end product has not yet been individually tested.
Food containing residues of veterinary drugs, pesticide residues, or contaminants beyond permissible limits as specified by FSSAI regulations.
what_it_excludes: Raw agricultural produce, crops, livestock, aquaculture products, and farm-level supplies in the hands of a farmer or fisherman, as these are explicitly excluded from the Act's provisions under Section 18(3).

Food that meets all prescribed FSSAI standards for safety, composition, labelling, and hygiene — such food does not fail food safety requirements even if it may be commercially inferior or not preferred by consumers.
Non-food substances, packaging materials, or agricultural inputs such as fertilisers and pesticides in their pre-application form, which are not themselves 'food' under the Act.
Minor procedural or administrative non-compliances unrelated to safety, such as minor labelling errors that do not affect the safety or fitness of the food for human consumption.
Food safety audits, certifications, and food safety management system documentation failures that are administrative in nature and do not directly render the food product unsafe or unfit.
definitions.why_it_matters: Non-compliance with food safety requirements triggers serious legal consequences including seizure, recall, destruction of the entire batch or consignment, and criminal prosecution of the food business operator under the Act. The statutory presumption in Section 18(1)(g) means that a single non-compliant sample can render an entire production lot liable to regulatory action, making this term central to both enforcement powers and the liability of food business operators.

definitions.definition: A fumigant, for the purposes of Section 21 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, means any insecticide applied in gaseous or vapour form directly to an article of food for pest control purposes, provided it is registered and approved under the Insecticides Act, 1968 (46 of 1968). No insecticide may be used directly on any article of food except such approved fumigants.
definitions.plain_english: A fumigant is a chemical substance used in gas or vapour form to kill pests like insects or rodents in stored food or grain. Unlike general pesticides that are sprayed on crops, fumigants are applied directly to the food itself, which is why they are strictly regulated. Only fumigants that are officially registered and approved under India's Insecticides Act, 1968 are legally permitted to be used directly on food items.
real_world_examples: A Food Corporation of India (FCI) warehouse in Punjab uses aluminium phosphide (Celphos) tablets to fumigate stored wheat grain directly — this is a registered fumigant under the Insecticides Act, 1968 and is thus permitted under Section 21.

A rice mill in Andhra Pradesh applies methyl bromide gas to bags of paddy in a sealed chamber to eliminate weevils before export — since methyl bromide is registered under the Insecticides Act, 1968, this use qualifies as a lawful fumigant application.

A spice exporter in Kerala uses phosphine gas fumigation on cardamom lots destined for European markets to meet phytosanitary requirements — this constitutes lawful fumigant use as phosphine is registered under the Insecticides Act, 1968.

A cold storage facility in Maharashtra attempts to use an unregistered chemical compound directly on stored onions to prevent insect infestation — because this chemical is not registered under the Insecticides Act, 1968, its use violates Section 21 of the FSS Act and the operator is liable for prosecution.

A dal mill operator in Madhya Pradesh uses magnesium phosphide pellets directly inside storage bags of lentils to control pulse beetle — this is permissible as the product is registered and approved under the Insecticides Act, 1968.

An importer storing basmati rice in a bonded warehouse in Mumbai applies ethylene oxide fumigation to the consignment — while ethylene oxide is a registered fumigant, its residue levels must also comply with tolerance limits set under Section 21 regulations.
what_it_covers: Aluminium phosphide (phosphine-releasing) tablets or pellets registered under the Insecticides Act, 1968, used directly on stored grain such as wheat, rice, or pulses.
Methyl bromide gas applied in sealed fumigation chambers directly to food commodities for export phytosanitary treatment, where registered under the Insecticides Act, 1968.

Magnesium phosphide formulations used directly inside storage bags or silos containing food articles such as lentils, maize, or spices, provided they hold valid registration under the Insecticides Act, 1968.

Ethylene oxide used as a fumigant on spices or dried food products, where the substance is registered and approved under the Insecticides Act, 1968 and residues remain within prescribed tolerance limits.
what_it_excludes: Insecticides or pesticides that are sprayed on growing crops in the field before harvest — these are governed as general pesticide residues under Section 21, not as fumigants applied directly to food.

Any chemical substance used directly on food that is not registered and approved under the Insecticides Act, 1968, regardless of its fumigant-like properties — such use is outright prohibited under Section 21.

Veterinary drugs, antibiotic residues, and solvent residues that may enter food through animal products or processing — these are separately regulated as residues under Section 21 and do not fall under the fumigant category.

Disinfectants or sanitisers applied to food contact surfaces, storage equipment, or premises walls to control pests or microbes — these are not fumigants applied directly to the article of food itself.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a registered fumigant under the Insecticides Act, 1968 determines whether its direct application to an article of food is lawful or a punishable contravention under Section 21 of the FSS Act; using a non-registered insecticide directly on food can render the food unsafe or sub-standard and expose the food business operator to penalties, licence cancellation, and criminal prosecution.

definitions.definition: "Functional food" means food which is specially processed or formulated to satisfy particular dietary requirements which exist because of a particular physical or physiological condition or specific diseases and disorders, wherein the composition of these foodstuffs must differ significantly from the composition of ordinary foods of comparable nature, and may contain one or more of plants or botanicals or their parts, minerals, vitamins, proteins, metals, amino acids, enzymes, substances from animal origin, or a dietary substance to supplement the diet; such product is labelled as a functional food, not represented as a conventional food, may be formulated as powders, granules, tablets, capsules, liquids, jelly or other dosage forms (but not parenterals), and is meant for oral administration, provided it does not claim to cure or mitigate any specific disease, disorder or condition except as permitted by regulations.
definitions.plain_english: A functional food is a specially made food product designed to meet specific dietary needs due to a person's physical condition, health state, or disease, and it contains special ingredients like plant extracts, vitamins, minerals, or proteins that are not typically found in regular everyday foods. It can come in forms like powders, capsules, tablets, or liquids that you take by mouth. It cannot claim to cure or treat any disease, and it is not considered a regular food or a medicine.
real_world_examples: A probiotic fortified yogurt drink sold in Indian supermarkets under a brand like Yakult, specifically formulated for gut health and labelled as a functional food for digestive well-being.

Protein powder sachets marketed by companies like Horlicks or Ensure in India, formulated for elderly individuals with specific protein-deficiency conditions and sold with claims of supporting muscle strength.
Omega-3 fatty acid enriched edible oil products sold in Indian retail chains like Big Bazaar, formulated for consumers with cardiovascular dietary requirements and containing fish oil extracts.

Turmeric and ashwagandha extract capsules sold by brands like Himalaya or Dabur, processed from botanical sources and labelled as functional health supplements for immunity support, formulated in dosage form for oral administration.

Iron and folic acid fortified flour products specifically processed for anaemic women in India, marketed under government-supported nutrition programmes or commercial brands like Aashirvaad, differing significantly in composition from ordinary wheat flour.
what_it_covers: Foods specially formulated with plant extracts, vitamins, minerals, or animal-origin substances to meet specific physiological or dietary needs, such as protein supplements for muscle disorders.
Products in the form of powders, granules, tablets, capsules, or liquids that are labelled as functional foods, not represented as conventional food, and administered orally.

Foods containing ingredients like amino acids (within Recommended Daily Allowance for Indians), enzymes within permissible limits, or dietary substances intended to supplement total dietary intake for persons with specific health conditions.

Fortified or processed food products whose composition differs significantly from comparable ordinary foods, such as omega-3-enriched edible oils or probiotic dairy products targeting specific health conditions.
what_it_excludes: Drugs as defined under clause (b) of Section 3 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, including ayurvedic, siddha, and unani drugs as defined in clauses (a) and (h) of that section.

Narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances as defined in the Schedule of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, and substances listed in Schedules E and EI of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.
Products administered parenterally (i.e., injections or intravenous products), as functional foods are limited to oral administration only.

Conventional everyday food products that do not differ significantly in composition from ordinary foods of comparable nature and are not specially processed for any dietary or physiological requirement.
Products that make claims to cure, treat, or mitigate a specific disease or disorder beyond health benefit or health promotion claims permitted by regulations under this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Any person who manufactures, distributes, sells, or imports a product qualifying as a functional food without complying with the regulations framed under Section 22 of the Food Safety and Standards Act commits an offence subject to penalties under the Act. Conversely, if a product does not meet this definition, it cannot be regulated or restricted under the special regime applicable to functional foods, nutraceuticals, and health supplements, which determines licensing obligations, labelling requirements, and permissible health claims.

definitions.definition: The General Clauses Act refers to the General Clauses Act, 1897 (10 of 1897), a central legislation of India that provides general rules of interpretation and savings provisions applicable to central enactments and orders made thereunder. Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, it is specifically invoked in Section 97(2) to apply the savings provision under Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, when any State law corresponding to this Act stands repealed upon commencement of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The General Clauses Act, 1897 is a foundational Indian law that contains standard rules about how laws should be read and what happens when one law replaces another. When the Food Safety and Standards Act replaces a State food safety law, the General Clauses Act ensures that rights, penalties, proceedings, and other legal matters under the old State law are protected and continue to have effect. It acts like a legal safety net so that repealing an old law does not accidentally cancel ongoing cases or obligations.
real_world_examples: When the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 came into force, it effectively repealed State-level food adulteration laws such as the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act enforced by State governments. The General Clauses Act, 1897 (Section 6) ensured that any prosecution already initiated under the old State law could continue without interruption.

A food business operator in Maharashtra who had acquired a licence under a State food regulation that was repealed upon commencement of the FSS Act could still rely on rights accrued under that old law, because the General Clauses Act preserved those entitlements during the transition period.

A court in Tamil Nadu handling a pending appeal against a penalty imposed under a repealed State food safety order could continue those proceedings as if the State law had not been repealed, by virtue of the savings clause imported through the General Clauses Act.

A consumer complaint filed against an adulterated food product under a now-repealed State food law in Karnataka remained valid and enforceable because the General Clauses Act prevented the repeal from wiping out liabilities already incurred by the food manufacturer.

When the FSS Act repealed the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, any forfeiture of goods ordered under the old law was still executable against a Rajasthan-based spice manufacturer, as the General Clauses Act saved all penalties and forfeitures already imposed before the repeal.
what_it_covers: Savings of rights, privileges, obligations, and liabilities that arose under any State food safety law repealed upon commencement of the FSS Act, as protected by Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
Continuation and enforcement of legal proceedings, investigations, and remedies that were initiated under a State food law before it was repealed by the FSS Act.
Preservation of penalties, forfeitures, and punishments already incurred under a corresponding State food safety law that stood repealed when the FSS Act came into force.
what_it_excludes: New offences or violations that occur after the commencement of the FSS Act, which are governed solely by the FSS Act and its rules and regulations, not the General Clauses Act.

Repeal of central enactments and orders listed in the Second Schedule of the FSS Act, for which the FSS Act itself (Section 97(1)) provides its own specific savings clause without invoking the General Clauses Act.
Licences issued under repealed enactments or orders, whose continuation is separately governed by Section 97(3) of the FSS Act and not through the General Clauses Act mechanism.
Matters relating to cognizance of offences under repealed Acts after three years from commencement of the FSS Act, as Section 97(4) imposes its own bar independent of the General Clauses Act.

definitions.definition: "Genetically engineered or modified food" means food and food ingredients composed of or containing genetically modified or engineered organisms obtained through modern biotechnology, or food and food ingredients produced from but not containing genetically modified or engineered organisms obtained through modern biotechnology.
definitions.plain_english: Genetically modified food refers to any food or food ingredient that either contains organisms whose genetic material has been altered using modern biotechnology techniques, or has been produced using such altered organisms even if the final product no longer contains them. This includes crops, grains, oils, and processed foods derived from genetically engineered sources. In India, such foods cannot be manufactured, distributed, sold, or imported without compliance with the regulations under the Food Safety and Standards Act.
real_world_examples: Bt brinjal (Bt eggplant) developed by inserting a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis into the brinjal genome — any food product made from or containing Bt brinjal would qualify as genetically modified food under Section 22.

Soybean oil imported from the United States that is derived from genetically modified Roundup Ready soybean plants, even if the final oil does not contain the GM organism itself, would be classified as genetically modified food.

Golden Rice, which is biofortified with beta-carotene through genetic engineering, if manufactured or sold in India as a food ingredient or packaged rice product, would be subject to the restrictions under Section 22.

A snack food manufacturer in Mumbai using corn starch derived from genetically engineered maize varieties imported from the USA or Argentina would be required to comply with the GM food regulations before selling the product in Indian markets.

An Indian company importing canola oil derived from genetically modified canola crops grown in Canada must ensure that the product meets all applicable standards and approvals under Section 22 before distributing it through retail channels in India.

Packaged tofu or soy-based health drinks sold in Indian supermarkets that use genetically modified soybean as raw material must be labelled and regulated as genetically modified food under the FSSA framework.
what_it_covers: Food products that directly contain living genetically modified or engineered organisms, such as fresh GM vegetables or GM crop grains sold for consumption.
Processed food ingredients like oils, starches, or flours that are produced from genetically modified organisms even when the final product does not retain any live GM organism or its DNA.
Imported articles of food composed of or derived from genetically engineered organisms obtained through modern biotechnology, regardless of the country of origin.
Food and food ingredients where genetic modification was achieved through techniques such as recombinant DNA technology, gene editing, or other modern biotechnological methods.
Any combination food product where one or more ingredients are sourced from genetically modified crops or engineered organisms, such as multi-ingredient packaged snacks containing GM soy lecithin.
what_it_excludes: Foods developed through conventional plant breeding techniques such as hybridisation or selective breeding, as these do not involve modern biotechnology within the meaning of the definition.
Organic foods, which by definition under the same section must be produced in accordance with specified organic production standards that prohibit the use of genetically modified organisms.

Foods for special dietary uses, nutraceuticals, health supplements, and functional foods that are governed separately under Section 22 and do not fall within the GM food sub-category unless they independently meet the GM food definition.
Drugs, ayurvedic, siddha, and unani preparations regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which are excluded from the food category altogether under the Act.
Conventional foods in which no genetic modification of any ingredient or organism has occurred at any stage of production, processing, or manufacture.
definitions.why_it_matters: Any person who manufactures, distributes, sells, or imports genetically modified food without complying with the regulations prescribed under Section 22 commits an offence under the Food Safety and Standards Act, attracting penalties and possible prohibition orders. Whether a food article qualifies as genetically modified food determines which regulatory approvals, labelling requirements, and safety assessments are mandatory before the product can legally enter the Indian food supply chain.
