definitions.definition: An act or intended act done honestly and without any fraudulent intent or malice under this Act or the rules or regulations made thereunder, as contemplated under Section 88, which protects officers and members of the Central Government, State Government, Food Authority and other constituted bodies from legal proceedings for anything done or intended to be done in such honest discharge of their duties.
definitions.plain_english: Good faith means doing something honestly and sincerely, without any intention to deceive or cause harm. Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, if a government officer or food authority official takes an action genuinely believing it to be correct and lawful, they cannot be sued or prosecuted for it. This protection exists to allow officials to perform their duties without fear of personal legal liability.
real_world_examples: A Food Safety Officer in Maharashtra raids a food processing unit based on a credible complaint and seizes a consignment of allegedly adulterated spices; even if laboratory tests later clear the product, the officer is protected from a civil suit by the manufacturer because the seizure was made in good faith.

A Designated Officer in Tamil Nadu issues an improvement notice to a restaurant based on an inspection report indicating unsanitary conditions; if the notice turns out to contain a procedural error, the officer cannot be personally prosecuted as the action was taken in good faith under the Act.

The Commissioner of Food Safety in Delhi orders an emergency prohibition notice against a dairy unit suspected of supplying unsafe milk during a food poisoning outbreak; even if subsequent investigation does not conclusively prove contamination, the action taken in good faith is protected from legal challenge against the officer personally.

A Food Authority member in Karnataka approves a regulatory action against a food business operator based on risk assessment data later found to be incomplete; since the decision was made honestly and without malicious intent, no suit can be filed against that member personally.

An authorised officer at a port in Mumbai detains an imported consignment of food articles suspected of containing banned contaminants; if the consignment is later found to comply with standards, the officer faces no legal liability as the detention was carried out in good faith under the Act.
what_it_covers: Actions taken by Food Safety Officers during inspections, raids, or seizures that are later found to be based on incorrect information, provided the officer acted honestly at the time.
Decisions made by members or officers of the Food Authority in issuing notices, orders, or regulations that may be procedurally imperfect but were made without fraudulent intent.

Acts performed by officers of the Central or State Government while implementing provisions of the Act, even if such acts cause inconvenience or financial loss to food business operators, as long as they were done sincerely.
Intended acts — i.e., actions that were planned or initiated in honest pursuit of regulatory duties but not yet completed — are equally protected under this provision.
what_it_excludes: Actions taken with malicious intent, personal vendetta, or corrupt motive by an officer — such acts would fall outside the protection of good faith and could expose the officer to legal proceedings.
Acts that are entirely outside the scope of the Act, rules, or regulations — an officer acting ultra vires or in a personal capacity cannot claim the protection of good faith under Section 88.
Deliberate falsification of inspection records, laboratory reports, or official documents by a food safety officer, which would constitute mala fide conduct and strip away the immunity.
Actions taken by private individuals or food business operators — good faith protection under Section 88 applies exclusively to government officers and authority members, not to regulated entities.
definitions.why_it_matters: The concept of good faith under Section 88 is the threshold condition that determines whether a suit, prosecution, or other legal proceeding can be maintained against a government officer or Food Authority member; if good faith is established, the proceeding is barred entirely. This protects regulatory enforcement from being chilled by litigation threats while ensuring accountability where malicious or corrupt conduct is proven.

definitions.definition: Grievous injury, as used in the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, refers to a serious bodily harm or injury caused to a consumer as a result of consuming unsafe or adulterated food, being of a nature more severe than a non-grievous injury but falling short of causing death, and for which the Act prescribes enhanced criminal punishment of imprisonment up to six years and compensation up to three lakh rupees.
definitions.plain_english: A grievous injury is a serious physical harm caused to a person who consumes unsafe or adulterated food — more severe than a minor injury but not resulting in death. This could include serious illnesses, organ damage, or long-term health conditions caused by eating bad food. The law treats this as a more serious offence than causing a minor injury, and the person responsible can face heavier jail time, fines, and compensation orders.
real_world_examples: A consumer in Mumbai suffers acute liver failure after consuming adulterated cooking oil sold by a local vendor, requiring hospitalisation for several weeks — this would constitute grievous injury under the Act.
Several children in a Delhi school midday meal scheme develop severe kidney damage after eating food contaminated with toxic chemicals added by the supplier, resulting in long-term medical treatment.
A customer in Hyderabad purchases packaged milk adulterated with urea and melamine, subsequently suffering serious gastrointestinal damage requiring surgery — qualifying as grievous injury.

A consumer in Chennai buys readymade food from a restaurant that used expired and chemically preserved meat, causing the consumer to suffer permanent neurological damage from botulinum toxin poisoning.

A patient in a hospital in Kolkata receives a hospital-supplied diet contaminated with high levels of pesticide residue, leading to severe organ damage requiring intensive care treatment for over a month.
what_it_covers: Serious or permanent physical harm to a consumer caused by consuming unsafe, adulterated, or sub-standard food, such as organ failure or severe poisoning.
Long-term debilitating health conditions resulting from food-borne illness traced to a food business operator's product, requiring prolonged medical treatment.
Hospitalisation or surgical intervention necessitated by consumption of food that was manufactured, stored, distributed, sold, or imported in violation of the Act.
Bodily injuries that are more severe than a non-grievous injury but do not result in the death of the consumer, such as permanent disability or disfigurement caused by toxic food additives.
what_it_excludes: Non-grievous injury, which refers to minor or temporary physical harm caused by unsafe food, attracting lesser penalties under Section 59.
Death of the consumer, which is treated as a separate and more serious category under the Act with distinct minimum imprisonment and compensation provisions.
Financial or economic harm suffered by a consumer (such as monetary loss from purchasing substandard food without any physical health impact), which does not constitute grievous injury.
Situations where consumption of food causes no injury whatsoever, even if the food technically qualifies as unsafe or sub-standard under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an offence results in grievous injury determines the severity of criminal punishment — imprisonment up to six years and fine up to five lakh rupees under Section 59 — as opposed to lesser penalties for no injury or non-grievous injury. It also triggers mandatory compensation up to three lakh rupees under Section 65, enables licence cancellation and property forfeiture by the Adjudicating Officer, and activates the jurisdiction of Special Courts constituted under Section 74 for expedited trial.

definitions.definition: A hawker is a person who carries on a petty food business by selling articles of food while moving from place to place or at temporary locations, without a fixed establishment, and who is exempt from the requirement of obtaining a licence under Section 31 but is required to register with the designated authority. As used in Sections 31 and 69, a hawker falls within the class of small-scale food business operators alongside petty retailers, itinerant vendors, and temporary stall holders.
definitions.plain_english: A hawker is someone who sells food by moving around streets, markets, or public places rather than from a fixed shop or establishment. In India, this includes people who sell food from carts, baskets, or on foot. They do not need a formal food licence but must register with the food safety authority. They can still be held accountable for food safety violations and their offences can be settled by paying a fine.
real_world_examples: A person selling chaat, pani puri, or bhel puri from a pushcart moving through residential neighbourhoods in Mumbai, who is required to register with the local food safety authority but does not need a full food business licence.
A vendor in Delhi who walks through markets selling freshly cut fruit from a basket balanced on their head, moving from one area to another without a fixed stall or shop.
A person in Chennai who sells freshly prepared idlis and vadas from a mobile carrier, going door to door in an apartment complex every morning.
A tea seller in Kolkata who carries a kettle and cups, moving between offices and bus stops to sell chai, without any fixed premises or establishment.
A vendor at a local mela or weekly bazaar in a tier-2 city who sets up temporarily to sell packaged snacks or sweets and moves to the next bazaar the following week.
A person selling roasted peanuts or bhutta (roasted corn) from a mobile cart during evening hours near parks and public spaces in Pune, who has registered under the food safety registration scheme.
what_it_covers: A person selling cooked or raw food articles by moving from place to place without a fixed shop or permanent establishment.
A street food vendor operating from a mobile cart, handcart, cycle, or on foot in public spaces, markets, or residential areas.
A person who sells food temporarily at different locations and is required only to register (not obtain a licence) under Section 31(2).
A hawker against whom a reasonable belief exists that they have committed an offence under the Act, making them eligible for compounding of the offence under Section 69.
A person selling packaged or unpackaged food items in transit through streets, railway platforms, or bus stands without a fixed premises.
what_it_excludes: A petty manufacturer who manufactures food at a fixed location and sells it — this is a separate category under Section 31(2) distinct from a hawker.
A licensed food business operator running a fixed shop, restaurant, hotel, or food stall with a permanent establishment, who must obtain a licence rather than merely register.
A temporary stall holder who sets up at a defined event or location for a specific duration — treated as a separate class alongside hawkers under Section 31(2).
A wholesaler or distributor supplying food in bulk to retailers or businesses, who operates on a commercial scale beyond the scope of a hawker.

definitions.definition: ―hazard‖ means a biological, chemical or physical agent in, or condition of, food with the potential to cause an adverse health effect.
definitions.plain_english: A hazard is anything present in food — whether a germ, a harmful chemical, or a physical object — that has the potential to harm a person's health. It includes not just actual harmful agents but also conditions in the food itself that could lead to harm. The key point is that it is about potential risk, not just proven harm.
real_world_examples: Salmonella bacteria found in raw chicken sold at a market in Mumbai — a biological hazard that can cause severe food poisoning if the chicken is consumed undercooked.
Excessive pesticide residues such as chlorpyrifos detected in vegetables grown in Punjab, exceeding permissible limits and posing a chemical hazard to consumers.
Small bone fragments or metal shards from processing equipment found in packaged biscuits manufactured in a Hyderabad factory — a physical hazard that could injure a consumer.
Aflatoxins produced by mould in improperly stored groundnuts or maize in Maharashtra warehouses — a biological/chemical hazard arising from fungal contamination during storage.

Lead contamination in turmeric powder sold in local spice markets in Rajasthan due to the addition of lead chromate as an adulterant to enhance colour — a chemical hazard with serious long-term health effects.
Broken glass pieces found in bottled beverages due to a defective bottling line at a Karnataka soft drink plant — a physical hazard posing immediate injury risk to consumers.
what_it_covers: Biological agents such as pathogenic bacteria (e.g., E. coli, Salmonella), viruses, parasites, or moulds present in food that can cause illness.
Chemical agents including pesticide residues, heavy metals, food adulterants, mycotoxins, or unauthorised food additives present in food at harmful levels.
Physical agents such as metal fragments, glass shards, stones, or bone pieces that are present in food and can cause physical injury upon consumption.
Conditions of food such as improper pH levels, water activity, or temperature abuse that create an environment enabling growth of harmful microorganisms.
Naturally occurring toxins in food, such as cyanogenic glycosides in improperly processed cassava or alkaloids in certain plant-based foods.
what_it_excludes: Extraneous matter as separately defined under Section 3 of the Act, which does not render the food unsafe and is therefore not a hazard in the legal sense.
Mere quality deficiencies or sub-standard characteristics of food that do not carry the potential to cause an adverse health effect on the consumer.
Risks arising from food packaging or labelling errors that do not involve any agent or condition within the food itself with potential to cause health harm.
Substances or agents present in non-food items such as animal feed, cosmetics, or medicinal products, which fall outside the definition of food under this Act.
Conditions external to the food product, such as unhygienic handling environments or premises conditions, unless they have already introduced an agent into the food itself.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identification of a 'hazard' is foundational to triggering obligations under the Food Safety Management System, including Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) protocols, which food business operators must adopt under the Act. A finding that a hazard exists in food can lead to regulatory actions including improvement notices, prohibition orders, recall of unsafe food, and prosecution of the food business operator for placing unsafe food in the market.

definitions.definition: A 'health risk' exists with respect to a food business when, based on a conviction of the food business operator for an offence under the Act, the court is satisfied that the operations, processes, premises, equipment, or management of that food business pose a risk to the health of consumers or the public. It is a judicially determined condition, established upon conviction, that justifies the imposition of prohibition orders restricting or halting the food business's activities.
definitions.plain_english: A 'health risk' means that a court has found, after a food business owner has been convicted of breaking food safety rules, that the way the business is run — including its processes, equipment, or premises — is dangerous to people's health. It is not just a suspicion; it is a formal judicial finding that the business poses a real threat to consumers. Once this is established, the court can order the business to stop using certain equipment, premises, or processes, or can even ban the owner from managing any food business.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based packaged snacks manufacturer is convicted for repeatedly using adulterated edible oil. The court, after examining evidence of contaminated machinery and unhygienic storage, determines a health risk exists and issues a prohibition order banning use of the factory premises for any food business.

A Mumbai street food vendor operating a chain of outlets is convicted for using banned food colours. The court finds that the mixing process used across all outlets poses a health risk and prohibits the operator from using those specific processes in any of the outlets.

A Kolkata cold storage facility used by a fish distribution company is found to be operating at unsafe temperatures, leading to bacterial contamination. Following conviction, the court determines a health risk exists and bans the use of the cold storage equipment for any food business.

A Bengaluru-based restaurant owner is convicted for serving food prepared in premises infested with rodents and cockroaches. The court, satisfied that a health risk exists, issues an order prohibiting the use of the restaurant kitchen and dining area for any food business until sufficient measures are taken.

A Hyderabad dairy operator is convicted for adding urea and detergent to milk. The court finds a health risk exists with respect to the dairy's processing line and prohibits not only the use of the specific processing equipment but also bars the operator from managing any dairy food business.
what_it_covers: Use of contaminated, defective, or unsanitary equipment or premises in a food business that poses danger to consumer health, as determined by a court after conviction.
Processes or treatments applied during food preparation, manufacturing, or distribution that are found by the court to be unsafe or hazardous to consumers following a criminal conviction.
The conduct or management practices of a convicted food business operator whose continued participation in the food business is deemed by the court to endanger public health.

Any situation where the combination of convicted offence and operational conditions of the food business leads a court to conclude that ongoing operations will cause or are likely to cause harm to consumers.
what_it_excludes: A mere suspicion or administrative concern about a food business's practices that has not been established through a formal conviction before a court — such situations may trigger emergency provisions under Section 34 but do not constitute a 'health risk' under Section 33.

Food quality deficiencies or regulatory non-compliances that do not rise to the level of posing a risk to consumer health, such as minor labelling errors or documentation lapses, even if they result in penalties.
Risks to health arising from food consumed by the food business operator or their employees, as the health risk under Section 33 is directed at the risk posed to consumers or the general public.
Administrative or financial irregularities of a food business operator that do not relate to the safety or healthfulness of the food produced, processed, or sold by the business.
definitions.why_it_matters: The judicial determination that a 'health risk' exists is the direct legal precondition for a court to impose a prohibition order under Section 33, which can shut down premises, ban equipment use, or disqualify a food business operator from managing any food business — making it one of the most severe non-penal consequences under the Act. Without this finding, even a convicted food business operator cannot be subjected to these operational prohibitions, and the absence of a health risk finding means that prohibition orders cannot be issued or maintained.

definitions.definition: A 'health risk condition' exists with respect to a food business where the state of the food business, its premises, equipment, processes, or the food itself poses an imminent or serious risk of injury to health of the public or consumers. Though not formally defined in a standalone provision, it is the condition that must be satisfied before the Designated Officer may serve an emergency prohibition notice or apply for an emergency prohibition order under Section 34.
definitions.plain_english: A 'health risk condition' means a situation where a food business is operating in a way that poses a serious or immediate danger to people's health — for example, due to severely unsanitary premises, contaminated food, or dangerous processes. When such a condition is found to exist, government officials can immediately take steps to shut down or restrict that food business. It is essentially the threshold that must be crossed before emergency action can be taken against a food operator.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai street food stall is found using water from a sewage-contaminated source to prepare food, creating an imminent risk of cholera or typhoid — a health risk condition exists, prompting the Designated Officer to serve an emergency prohibition notice.

A licensed dairy plant in Punjab is found storing milk at temperatures that encourage rapid bacterial growth, with multiple batches already showing dangerous pathogen levels — the Designated Officer applies to the Commissioner of Food Safety for an emergency prohibition order on the grounds that a health risk condition exists.

A Chennai restaurant is discovered using a banned pesticide-laden vegetable supplier and already has two reported food poisoning cases among customers — the Designated Officer determines a health risk condition exists and initiates emergency prohibition proceedings.

A Delhi-based packaged food manufacturer is found operating with rodent infestation throughout the production facility, with rodent droppings detected in finished product batches — this constitutes a health risk condition justifying emergency prohibition action under Section 34.

A school canteen in Hyderabad is found serving mid-day meals cooked in utensils contaminated with heavy metals, posing a serious poisoning risk to children — the Designated Officer identifies a health risk condition and serves an emergency prohibition notice on the operator.
what_it_covers: Severely insanitary or contaminated food business premises where food is prepared or stored, posing an immediate risk of illness to consumers.
Food processes or equipment at a business that are defective or compromised in a manner likely to cause serious injury or disease to those consuming the food produced.
Situations where a food business is found handling, producing, or selling food that is unsafe, adulterated, or contaminated with pathogens, toxins, or harmful substances at dangerous levels.
Operating conditions at a food business — such as pest infestation, use of banned substances, or breakdown of refrigeration — that create a foreseeable and serious risk to consumer health.
Circumstances where food already distributed or being distributed from a business poses a risk of mass food poisoning or disease outbreak.
what_it_excludes: Minor or technical regulatory non-compliance that does not pose an immediate or serious risk to consumer health, such as minor labelling defects or administrative lapses.
Situations where a food business has already voluntarily ceased operations or recalled the offending product, eliminating the ongoing health risk.
Food quality issues that affect the standard or composition of food but do not pose any direct risk of injury to health, such as sub-standard nutrient content within safe limits.
Complaints or concerns about food that are speculative or unverified and lack sufficient evidence of an actual imminent health risk.
Improvement notice scenarios where deficiencies observed are capable of being rectified within a reasonable period without posing an immediate danger to public health.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence of a 'health risk condition' is the mandatory legal prerequisite that triggers the Designated Officer's power to serve an emergency prohibition notice and apply for an emergency prohibition order under Section 34; without its establishment, no emergency prohibition can be imposed. Any person who knowingly contravenes an emergency prohibition order issued on this basis is liable to imprisonment up to two years and a fine up to two lakh rupees.

definitions.definition: A 'health supplement' means a food which is specially processed or formulated to satisfy particular dietary requirements, which may contain plants or botanicals, minerals, vitamins, proteins, amino acids, enzymes, or substances of animal origin, and which is presented in the form of powders, granules, tablets, capsules, liquids, jelly or other dosage forms (but not parenterals) for oral administration; it is not represented as a conventional food, does not claim to cure or mitigate any specific disease or disorder, and does not include a drug under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 or any narcotic or psychotropic substance.
definitions.plain_english: A health supplement is a specially made food product meant to add to your daily diet and support general health and wellbeing. It can come in the form of tablets, capsules, powders, or liquids and may contain vitamins, minerals, herbal extracts, or proteins. Unlike medicines, it cannot claim to cure or treat any disease, and it is meant to be taken by mouth only. Common examples include vitamin C tablets, protein powders, and herbal energy capsules sold at pharmacies or health stores.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based company sells whey protein powder in sachets marketed as a dietary supplement for gym-goers to increase their daily protein intake — this qualifies as a health supplement under Section 22.

A Bengaluru startup sells tulsi and ashwagandha capsules labelled as 'immunity boosters' under the FSSAI health supplement category, making health promotion claims but not claiming to cure any disease.

A Patanjali product marketed as a chyawanprash-based dietary supplement in tablet form containing herbs, vitamins, and minerals, sold at retail outlets across India, regulated as a health supplement by FSSAI.

A Delhi importer brings in omega-3 fish oil softgel capsules from the US labelled as a health supplement; the importer must comply with Section 22 requirements and FSSAI regulations before distribution.
A Hyderabad company manufactures iron and folic acid supplement granules specifically formulated for pregnant women to address dietary deficiency, sold under FSSAI health supplement licence.

A Kolkata-based brand sells probiotic capsules containing live beneficial bacteria marketed as a gut health supplement, distinct from pharmaceutical probiotic drugs, regulated under health supplement norms.
what_it_covers: Vitamin, mineral, or protein supplements in tablet, capsule, powder, or liquid form intended to supplement daily dietary intake.
Plant or botanical extracts (e.g., ashwagandha, tulsi, ginseng) in concentrated powder or hydroalcoholic extract form sold for oral consumption as a food supplement.
Animal-origin substances such as fish oil, collagen peptides, or whey protein formulated into dosage forms like softgels or sachets for supplementing diet.
Amino acid or enzyme-based oral supplements within Recommended Daily Allowance limits for Indians, sold to bridge nutritional gaps.
Products making permissible health benefit or health promotion claims (but not disease cure claims) and labelled explicitly as 'health supplement' as per FSSAI regulations.
what_it_excludes: Drugs as defined under clause (b) of Section 3 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, including allopathic medicines prescribed for treating diseases.
Ayurvedic, Siddha, and Unani drugs as defined under clauses (a) and (h) of Section 3 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which are regulated separately.

Narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances listed in the Schedule of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 and substances in Schedules E and E1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.
Products administered parenterally (by injection or intravenous route), which are excluded regardless of their nutritional content.
Conventional foods such as regular packaged meals, beverages, or snacks that are not specially formulated to supplement dietary intake.
Any product that claims to cure, treat, or mitigate a specific disease or disorder, as such a claim would take it outside the health supplement category and into drug regulation territory.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a product qualifies as a 'health supplement' under Section 22 determines whether it must be manufactured, distributed, sold, or imported only in compliance with FSSAI's specific health supplement regulations, including labelling, permissible ingredients, and claim restrictions. Misclassifying a product — for instance, marketing a drug as a health supplement or vice versa — can attract penalties for misbranding, unlicensed manufacture, or sale of unsafe food under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

definitions.definition: 'import' means bringing into India any article of food by land, sea or air.
definitions.plain_english: Import means physically bringing any food item into India through any mode of transport — whether by road (land), through a port (sea), or via an airport (air). It does not matter whether the food is processed, unprocessed, or packaged; if it is brought across India's borders for human consumption, it qualifies as an import under this law. This triggers specific food safety obligations under the Food Safety and Standards Act.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based trading company ships a container of Swiss chocolates through Nhava Sheva Port — this constitutes 'import' under the Act, requiring the importer to hold a valid FSSAI central licence and comply with labelling and safety standards before the goods can be released.

An airline catering firm brings pre-packaged foreign meals via Indira Gandhi International Airport in Delhi for use on international flights operating within Indian airspace — this is treated as import, attracting FSSAI inspection and clearance requirements.

A retailer in Amritsar sources packaged spices and dry fruits from Pakistan through the Wagah-Attari land border crossing — this transaction qualifies as import of food by land under the Act, and the consignment must meet FSSAI standards before entering the domestic market.

An e-commerce company imports bottled exotic sauces and condiments from the United States through Chennai Seaport for sale on its Indian platform — this is an import, and the food business operator must ensure the products conform to FSSAI regulations on labelling, additives, and safety before listing them for sale.

A Kolkata-based importer brings dried fish and seafood from Bangladesh through the Petrapole-Benapole land border — this constitutes import by land, and the consignment is subject to inspection by the Designated Officer at the port of entry under Section 51 of the Act.
what_it_covers: Bringing packaged or unpackaged food items into India through any seaport such as Nhava Sheva, Chennai, or Kolkata.
Carrying food consignments into India via international airports such as Delhi, Mumbai, or Bengaluru, including through courier or cargo.
Transporting food items across India's land borders, such as through the Wagah-Attari border with Pakistan, Petrapole with Bangladesh, or Moreh with Myanmar.
Importing raw, processed, or partially processed food ingredients such as edible oils, food additives, or agricultural commodities intended for human consumption.
Bringing in packaged drinking water, alcoholic beverages, infant food, or genetically modified food products from foreign countries into Indian territory.
what_it_excludes: Domestic transportation of food within India between states or cities, even if it crosses multiple jurisdictions, as no international border is crossed.
Transit shipments passing through Indian ports or airports that are not cleared for entry into the Indian market and are re-exported without being brought into Indian commerce.
Live animals transported into India that are not prepared or processed for placing on the market for human consumption, as live animals are excluded from the definition of 'food' under the Act.

Drugs, medicinal products, cosmetics, narcotic or psychotropic substances, and animal feed brought into India, as these are excluded from the definition of 'food' and therefore fall outside the scope of 'import' under this Act.

Personal baggage containing small quantities of food carried by an individual traveller for purely personal consumption, which may be governed by Customs regulations rather than triggering full FSSAI import compliance obligations.

It also determines the jurisdiction of the Designated Officer to inspect, sample, and detain consignments at ports of entry, and triggers liability under the Act's penalty provisions for non-compliant imported food.

definitions.definition: An 'importer' is a person who imports any article of food into India, and who is subject to the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act including compliance with directions of Food Safety Officers, liability for penalties under this Act in addition to penalties under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 and the Customs Act, 1962, and may be impleaded in criminal proceedings for offences under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: An importer is any person or business that brings food products into India from a foreign country for the purpose of sale or distribution. They are responsible for ensuring that the food they bring in meets India's food safety standards and regulations. If their imported food is unsafe or violates the law, they can face penalties under multiple laws and the food can be seized, destroyed, or sent back.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based trading company imports canned fruits from Thailand and sells them in Indian supermarkets — the company is an 'importer' and must ensure the canned goods meet FSSAI standards before clearance at customs.

A Delhi firm imports olive oil from Italy and distributes it to retail stores across India — if the oil is found to be adulterated or mislabelled, the firm as importer is liable for penalties under both the FSSAI Act and the Customs Act, 1962.

An individual entrepreneur in Chennai imports organic honey from New Zealand for sale on an e-commerce platform — as the importer, they must comply with FSSAI import regulations and directions of Food Safety Officers during inspections.

A Hyderabad-based food company imports ready-to-eat noodles from China and fails to comply with a Food Safety Officer's direction to submit samples for testing — the company as importer is liable for a penalty up to two lakh rupees under Section 55.

A Kolkata importer brings in dairy products from Australia that are found to contain contaminants beyond permissible limits — the competent authority may order the food to be destroyed or returned to the importer under Section 67.

A Gujarat company imports energy drinks from the United States without proper labelling as required by FSSAI regulations — the company as importer is proceeded against under this Act in addition to facing action under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992.
what_it_covers: A company registered in India that imports packaged or processed food products from foreign countries for commercial sale or distribution.
An individual or entity that brings in raw agricultural or food ingredients from abroad for use in food manufacturing within India.
An e-commerce business or trader who sources and imports specialty or organic food items from overseas markets for retail sale to Indian consumers.
An entity that holds the import licence and is named as the consignee for food articles cleared through Indian customs ports.
A food business operator who imports food under their own brand name from contract manufacturers located outside India.
what_it_excludes: A domestic manufacturer or processor who sources and processes food entirely within India and does not bring any food article from outside the country.
A retailer or dealer who purchases already-imported food from an importer within India and resells it, without themselves being involved in the act of importation.
A customs broker or freight forwarder who facilitates paperwork or logistics for food imports but does not own or take title to the imported food articles.
A consumer who brings a small quantity of food for personal use while travelling internationally, not for commercial sale or distribution.
A distributor who receives imported food from an importer and only distributes it within the domestic market, having had no role in the act of importing.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an 'importer' determines their exposure to penalties under Section 55 for non-compliance with Food Safety Officer directions and to dual liability under Section 67 alongside the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 and the Customs Act, 1962; it also determines whether they can be impleaded in criminal proceedings under Section 78, making the classification critical for enforcement, prosecution, and disposal of non-compliant food articles.

definitions.definition: The term 'imports' as used in the Food Safety and Standards Act refers to the act of bringing or causing to be brought any article of food into India from outside the country, whether by a person acting on their own behalf or through any other person, for the purpose of sale, distribution, or human consumption, subject to all standards, prohibitions, and regulations prescribed under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: Imports means bringing food products into India from another country. Any person who brings food into India — whether they do it themselves or through a middleman — must follow all food safety rules set under this law. If the imported food is unsafe, substandard, or mislabelled, the importer can be penalised.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based trading company imports canned fruit juices from Thailand and sells them in Indian supermarkets; the juices must meet FSSAI standards or the importer faces penalties under Section 51.
A Delhi importer brings in cheese from France without obtaining the required licence under applicable food import regulations, violating Section 25 and attracting prosecution.

An e-commerce platform operating in India imports protein supplements from the United States that carry misleading health claims on their labels; the importer is liable under Section 52 for misbranded food.

A Kolkata-based food business operator imports dried spices from Vietnam that are found to contain pesticide residues above the permissible tolerance limit, making them sub-standard and subject to penalties.

A Chennai company imports packaged biscuits from Malaysia where the packaging contains extraneous matter such as plastic fragments, triggering liability under Section 54 for importing food containing extraneous matter.
what_it_covers: Bringing any article of food into India from a foreign country for the purpose of sale or distribution in the Indian market.
Importing food through an agent, broker, or any other third party acting on behalf of the principal importer.
Importing food articles that require a licence under applicable Acts, rules, or regulations, whether or not such licence has been obtained.
Bringing into India any food that is unsafe, misbranded, sub-standard, or contains extraneous matter, which triggers penal liability under the Act.
Importation of food in contravention of any standard prescribed by the Food Authority under this Act or rules/regulations made thereunder.
what_it_excludes: Domestic manufacture, storage, sale, or distribution of food articles that are produced and traded entirely within India without any cross-border movement.
Personal consumption quantities of food brought by travellers for their own private use that are not intended for sale or commercial distribution.
Re-export of food articles that enter India only in transit and are not meant to enter the Indian food supply or market.
Export of food articles from India to other countries, which is a distinct activity not covered by the import-related provisions of this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'imports' determines whether Sections 25, 51, 52, and 54 apply, directly triggering penalties of up to five lakh rupees for sub-standard food, three lakh rupees for misbranded food, and one lakh rupees for food containing extraneous matter; it also determines whether the Food Authority's standards and licensing requirements under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 are attracted.

definitions.definition: "improvement notice" means a notice issued under section 32 of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: An improvement notice is an official written notice issued by a food safety authority to a food business operator when they are found to be violating food safety laws or standards. It tells the business exactly what is wrong and what corrective steps must be taken within a specified time period. It is essentially a formal warning with legally binding instructions to fix problems before stricter action is taken.
real_world_examples: A Food Safety Officer inspects a dal mill in Rajasthan and finds that the premises lack proper pest control and sanitation facilities; an improvement notice is issued directing the owner to install pest-proof storage and clean the facility within 30 days.

A mid-sized packaged snack manufacturer in Pune is found using equipment with rusted surfaces that could contaminate food; an improvement notice is served requiring the operator to replace or repair the equipment within a stipulated deadline.

A street food vendor operating a permanent stall in Chennai is found to be storing raw meat and ready-to-eat foods in the same refrigerator without separation; an improvement notice is issued detailing the specific hygienic practices to be adopted immediately.

A bakery in Delhi is found labelling its products without listing allergens as required under FSS regulations; the Designated Officer issues an improvement notice directing the business to update its labelling within 15 days or face licence suspension.

A cold storage facility in Amritsar handling dairy products is found maintaining temperatures above prescribed limits; an improvement notice is issued requiring installation of appropriate refrigeration systems and temperature monitoring logs within a specified period.
what_it_covers: A notice issued by the Designated Officer or authorised food safety authority directing a food business operator to comply with specific provisions of the Act or regulations within a prescribed time frame.
Cases where a food business is found to be operating in contravention of food safety, hygiene, or labelling standards but the violation is considered remediable without immediate prohibition.
Specific written instructions detailing the nature of the violation, the legal provision being contravened, the corrective measures required, and the deadline by which compliance must be achieved.
Notices issued in relation to food premises, equipment, processes, labelling practices, or food safety management systems that fall short of prescribed standards under the FSS Act.
what_it_excludes: An emergency prohibition notice, which is issued for immediate serious health risks and does not allow time for corrective action unlike an improvement notice.
A prohibition order, which is a more severe enforcement measure issued after non-compliance or when the violation cannot be remedied by corrective steps alone.
Criminal prosecution or penalty orders initiated directly under the Act for grave offences such as selling unsafe or adulterated food, which bypass the improvement notice stage.
Informal verbal warnings or advisory communications given by food safety officers during inspections that have no statutory force under section 32.
Notices or communications issued by non-authorised persons or bodies not empowered under the FSS Act to issue improvement notices.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an improvement notice applies determines whether a food business operator has a legal opportunity to rectify violations before facing licence suspension, prohibition orders, or criminal prosecution; failure to comply with an improvement notice within the specified period can trigger escalated enforcement actions including prosecution and penalties under the Act.

definitions.definition: "ingredient" means any substance, including a food additive used in the manufacture or preparation of food and present in the final product, possibly in a modified form.
definitions.plain_english: An ingredient is any substance that goes into making or preparing a food product and is still present in the final product, even if its form has changed during cooking or processing. This includes food additives like preservatives or colours. For example, flour, sugar, salt, and artificial flavouring in a biscuit are all ingredients.
real_world_examples: Wheat flour, sugar, edible vegetable oil, and cocoa powder used in manufacturing Parle-G or Bourbon biscuits in India — all are ingredients as they are present in the final packaged product.

Turmeric powder, red chilli powder, and salt added during the preparation of packaged masala mix (like MDH or Everest) are ingredients since they are present in the finished product sold to consumers.

Monosodium glutamate (MSG) added to Maggi noodles during manufacture qualifies as an ingredient (and also a food additive) since it is present in the final noodle product, even if in a modified form after processing.
Milk, sugar, and cardamom used to manufacture Amul's gulab jamun mix are ingredients, as each substance is incorporated into and identifiable within the final food product.
Acetic acid used as a preservative in packaged pickle (achar) brands like Mother's Recipe is an ingredient because it is intentionally added and remains present in the final pickle product.
what_it_covers: Any raw material such as wheat flour, rice, or milk that is used in manufacturing a food product and remains present in the final form.
Food additives like preservatives (e.g., sodium benzoate), colours (e.g., tartrazine), and emulsifiers that are intentionally added during food preparation and persist in the final product.

Substances that undergo a chemical or physical transformation during processing but are still present in a modified form in the final product, such as yeast used in bread manufacturing which transforms but its by-products remain in the bread.
Water used in the manufacture or preparation of food when it is incorporated into and remains part of the final food product.
Compound ingredients (e.g., a spice blend) added during preparation that are present in the finished packaged food.
what_it_excludes: Processing aids that are used during manufacture but are removed or reduced to negligible levels in the final product and do not have a technological effect in the finished food (these are separately defined as 'processing aid').

Contaminants that are not intentionally added to food but are present as a result of production, environmental contamination, or packaging — these fall under the separately defined term 'contaminant'.
Substances that are used externally during food handling or transport but do not become part of the final food product, such as cleaning agents or fumigants.
Adulterants or extraneous matter that are unintentionally present in food, as these are governed by separate definitions under the Act.
Live animals or plants prior to harvesting, which are excluded from the definition of 'food' itself and therefore cannot qualify as ingredients in this context.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a substance as an 'ingredient' directly triggers mandatory labelling obligations under the Food Safety and Standards Act and regulations, requiring food business operators to declare all ingredients on the product label; failure to do so can result in the food being treated as 'misbranded' under Section 3, attracting penalties under the Act. It also determines compliance requirements around permissible substances, allergen declarations, and standards applicable to food composition.

definitions.definition: Though not formally defined in Section 3 of the Act, 'injurious to health' refers to any food or article of food that causes or is likely to cause physical harm, damage, or adverse health effects to the person consuming it, whether through its composition, contamination, adulteration, or otherwise; it is used in Section 48 in the context of offences relating to food that is dangerous or harmful to human health.
definitions.plain_english: Food that is 'injurious to health' is food that can harm or damage a person's physical wellbeing when eaten or consumed. This includes food that has been adulterated, contaminated, or prepared in an unsafe manner that makes it dangerous to the body. Even if the harm is not immediate, food that has a reasonable likelihood of causing health damage qualifies under this term.
real_world_examples: A street vendor in Mumbai selling pani puri made with contaminated water laced with harmful bacteria such as E. coli or cholera-causing organisms, causing gastroenteritis in consumers.
A dal mill operator in Punjab mixing industrial-grade yellow colour or lead chromate into turmeric powder to enhance its appearance, resulting in heavy metal poisoning among consumers.
A milk supplier in Uttar Pradesh adulterating milk with urea, detergent, or caustic soda to increase volume, rendering the product harmful to human kidneys and digestive systems.
A snack manufacturer in Gujarat using recycled or rancid oil containing harmful trans-fats and peroxides beyond permissible limits, leading to cardiovascular and liver damage in regular consumers.
A packaged water company in Delhi supplying bottled water with arsenic or fluoride levels exceeding prescribed safety standards under FSS regulations, causing chronic health conditions in consumers.
what_it_covers: Food adulterated with toxic substances such as lead chromate, pesticides, or industrial dyes that cause poisoning or organ damage upon consumption.
Food prepared or stored under unsanitary conditions leading to microbial contamination (e.g., Salmonella, Listeria) that causes foodborne illness.
Food containing additives, preservatives, or processing aids in quantities exceeding prescribed tolerance limits that cause cumulative or acute health damage.
Food items with pesticide residues or veterinary drug residues beyond permissible limits that harm the nervous system, liver, or kidneys of consumers.
Packaging materials leaching harmful chemicals (e.g., bisphenol A, phthalates) into food products, making them hazardous to health.
what_it_excludes: Food that is merely sub-standard or of inferior quality but does not pose any risk of physical harm or adverse health effects to the consumer.
Misbranded or mislabelled food that contains incorrect information on packaging but whose actual composition is safe for human consumption.
Food that causes minor aesthetic discomfort such as an unpleasant taste or smell but contains no ingredient or contaminant proven to be physically harmful.
Extraneous matter present in food (such as insect fragments or dust) that does not by itself render the food unsafe or cause a health injury.
Food that falls short of claimed nutritional values or functional benefits but is otherwise not chemically, biologically, or physically hazardous.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of 'injurious to health' under Section 48 directly determines the severity of criminal liability — a food business operator found selling food injurious to health faces imprisonment and heavy fines, as opposed to lighter penalties for mere sub-standard or misbranded food; it also triggers regulatory action such as recall, seizure, and cancellation of licence by the Food Safety Officer or Commissioner.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 48 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 'injury' includes any impairment, whether permanent or temporary, caused to the health of a person as a result of consuming food that is injurious to health.
definitions.plain_english: Injury means any harm or damage done to a person's health — whether it lasts forever or goes away after some time — due to consuming unsafe or adulterated food. It covers both serious, lasting conditions and minor, short-term health problems. The word 'injury' in this law is not limited to physical wounds; it broadly includes any negative impact on a person's wellbeing caused by food.
real_world_examples: A child in Mumbai develops acute gastroenteritis after consuming packaged juice contaminated with harmful bacteria — the temporary stomach illness constitutes an 'injury' under the Act.
A consumer in Delhi suffers permanent kidney damage after repeatedly consuming milk adulterated with melamine — the lasting organ impairment qualifies as a permanent injury under Section 48.

Several villagers in Rajasthan experience temporary vision loss after eating cooking oil adulterated with argemone oil — this temporary impairment is covered as an injury triggering liability under Section 59.

A schoolchild in Chennai falls ill with food poisoning after consuming mid-day meal prepared under unhygienic conditions, leading to a two-day hospitalisation — this short-term health impairment constitutes a non-grievous injury for purposes of sentencing under Section 59.

A diabetic consumer in Kolkata suffers a hypoglycaemic episode because a food label incorrectly stated sugar content, leading to a temporary but medically significant health crisis — the health impairment qualifies as an injury under the Act.
what_it_covers: Temporary impairments such as food poisoning, vomiting, or diarrhoea caused by consuming contaminated or adulterated food.
Permanent impairments such as organ failure, chronic illness, or disability resulting from long-term or acute exposure to unsafe food ingredients.
Cumulative health damage caused by repeated consumption of food with harmful additives or contaminants that individually may seem minor but collectively impair health.
Health sensitivities triggered in vulnerable consumer groups — such as infants, elderly persons, or those with pre-existing conditions — due to consuming food not suitable for them.
what_it_excludes: Death of a consumer, which is treated as a separate and more serious outcome under Sections 59 and 65 with distinct punishment and compensation provisions.
Economic or financial loss suffered by a consumer due to purchasing substandard food — only health impairment is captured within the definition of 'injury'.
Food that falls below specified standards solely due to natural causes beyond human control, which is explicitly excluded from being deemed unsafe or injurious under Section 48(2)(iii).

Acts of injury caused by a Food Safety Officer acting in good faith within the execution of duty, which are governed separately under Section 39 and not within the consumer-facing 'injury' definition of Section 48.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'injury' is critical because it determines the tier of criminal punishment under Section 59 — distinguishing between no injury, non-grievous injury, grievous injury, and death — and directly governs the quantum of compensation payable to the consumer or their legal representative under Section 65. Whether harm qualifies as an 'injury' (and whether it is permanent or temporary) thus decides both the length of imprisonment and the financial liability of the food business operator.

definitions.definition: Irradiated food means any article of food that has been subjected to ionising radiation for the purpose of preservation, decontamination, disinfestation, or extension of shelf life, using sources such as gamma rays, X-rays, or electron beams, and which is subject to regulation under Section 22 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, prohibiting its manufacture, distribution, sale, or import except in accordance with the Act and regulations made thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: Irradiated food refers to any food item that has been treated with a controlled dose of radiation energy (such as gamma rays or X-rays) to kill harmful bacteria, parasites, or insects, or to slow spoilage and increase shelf life. This process does not make the food radioactive, but it does require specific regulatory approval and labelling under India's food safety law. Such food cannot be sold or distributed in India without complying with the rules set by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based spice manufacturer irradiates packaged chilli powder and turmeric at a licensed facility using Cobalt-60 gamma rays to eliminate Salmonella contamination before export and domestic sale — this product qualifies as irradiated food requiring FSSAI approval.

An importer in Delhi brings in irradiated dried mango slices from the USA where irradiation is a standard preservation technique; under Section 22, such import is prohibited unless the product meets FSSAI regulations on irradiated food.

A poultry processing plant in Hyderabad seeks to irradiate chicken pieces to extend shelf life and reduce microbial load before supplying to supermarket chains across Telangana — the plant must obtain specific authorisation under FSSAI regulations as this constitutes manufacture of irradiated food.

An onion exporter in Nashik uses electron beam irradiation to inhibit sprouting in onions meant for Middle East markets; even though the treatment occurs before export, if the product re-enters Indian retail channels it would be governed as irradiated food under the Act.

A hospital dietary services company in Chennai wishes to serve irradiated ready-to-eat meals to immunocompromised patients to reduce infection risk — procurement and use of such food must comply with FSSAI's irradiated food regulations.

A wheat flour manufacturer in Punjab proposes to irradiate flour to control insect infestation instead of using fumigants — this requires regulatory clearance under Section 22 before the irradiated flour can be distributed or sold domestically.
what_it_covers: Spices, herbs, and dry food ingredients treated with gamma radiation for microbial reduction before domestic sale
Imported packaged food products that have undergone ionising radiation treatment abroad and are intended for sale in Indian markets
Fresh produce such as fruits, vegetables, or grains subjected to electron beam or X-ray irradiation to inhibit sprouting or extend shelf life
Meat and poultry products irradiated at licensed facilities to reduce pathogenic contamination before supply to retailers or food service operators in India
Any food article bearing the international Radura symbol or a declaration of irradiation treatment on its label, indicating it has undergone radiation processing
what_it_excludes: Food items that have been subjected to conventional heat pasteurisation, UV light surface treatment, or microwave treatment, as these do not involve ionising radiation
Genetically modified food and organic food, which are separately categorised and governed under distinct sub-definitions within Section 22 itself
Food packaging materials that may be irradiated solely for sterilisation purposes where the food contents themselves are not exposed to ionising radiation
Drugs and medicines (including Ayurvedic, Siddha, and Unani preparations) that may undergo radiation sterilisation, as these fall under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and not FSSAI jurisdiction
Naturally occurring background radiation exposure of food items during storage or transport, which does not constitute intentional irradiation under this provision
definitions.why_it_matters: Any person who manufactures, distributes, sells, or imports irradiated food without complying with FSSAI regulations under Section 22 commits an offence under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, attracting penalties including fines and possible imprisonment. The classification of a food product as 'irradiated food' triggers mandatory licensing, labelling obligations, and regulatory approval requirements, without which the food business operator cannot lawfully deal in such products in India.

definitions.definition: An itinerant vendor is a person who moves from place to place selling food articles, without a fixed premises or permanent establishment, and who is engaged in the business of selling food on a mobile or transient basis. Though not formally defined in the Act, the term is used in Sections 31 and 69 to denote a category of small, mobile food seller who is exempt from licensing but mandatorily required to register with the appropriate authority.
definitions.plain_english: An itinerant vendor is a person who sells food while moving around, such as a street food seller who pushes a cart through neighbourhoods or walks through markets calling out their wares. Unlike a shop owner, they do not operate from a fixed location. Under India's food safety law, they do not need a full licence but must register with the food safety authority.
real_world_examples: A person who pushes a wooden cart through residential colonies in Delhi selling chaat, golgappe, or bhel puri, stopping at different locations each day.
A vendor in Mumbai who walks through local trains or along marine drive selling roasted groundnuts, boiled eggs, or packaged snacks from a basket or bag.
A cycle-mounted ice cream or kulfi seller who travels between different streets and localities in Bengaluru, ringing a bell to attract customers.
A person who moves between weekly haats and bazaars in rural Rajasthan selling homemade pickles, papads, or fried snacks from a portable setup.
A street vendor in Kolkata who carries a portable stove and utensils on a handcart, selling freshly prepared jhalmuri or telebhaja at different spots throughout the day.
what_it_covers: A person selling cooked or prepared food from a mobile cart, basket, or cycle while moving through streets, markets, or residential areas without a fixed stall.
A vendor who participates in periodic markets, fairs, or public gatherings selling food while constantly shifting location and having no permanent premises.
A person who walks through trains, buses, or public transport hubs selling packaged or unpackaged food items on a transient basis.
A hawker carrying food items on their person or in a portable container, moving through neighbourhoods and selling directly to consumers at various spots.
what_it_excludes: A petty manufacturer who manufactures and sells food from a fixed home or small unit, as they fall under the distinct category of 'petty manufacturer' under Section 31.
A temporary stall holder who operates from a fixed, albeit temporary, location such as a stall at a fair or exhibition, as this is a separate defined category under the Act.
A licensed restaurant owner, dhaba operator, or food establishment with a fixed premises, even if small-scale, as they are required to hold a licence rather than mere registration.
A food business operator running a packaged food manufacturing unit, a distributor, or a wholesaler who engages in bulk trade rather than direct mobile retail selling to end consumers.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an itinerant vendor determines whether they need a full food business licence or only registration under Section 31, significantly lowering compliance burden; under Section 69, itinerant vendors are eligible for compounding of offences by paying a sum not exceeding one lakh rupees, thereby avoiding prosecution and custody, provided the offence does not carry imprisonment.

definitions.definition: "label" means any tag, brand, mark, pictorial or other descriptive matter, written, printed, stencilled, marked, embossed, graphic, perforated, stamped or impressed on or attached to container, cover, lid or crown of any food package and includes a product insert.
definitions.plain_english: A label is any writing, picture, symbol, or other information that appears on or is attached to a food package, including its container, lid, or cover. It also includes any separate information sheet placed inside the package. Essentially, it is everything that communicates information to the consumer about the food product through the packaging itself.
real_world_examples: The printed nutritional information, ingredient list, and manufacturing date on a Maggi noodles packet affixed directly to the outer wrapper constitutes a label under this Act.

A small folded instruction sheet placed inside a pack of Complan or a health supplement powder explaining usage directions qualifies as a label because it is a product insert included within the food package.
The embossed or stamped expiry date and batch number on the metal crown cap of a Pepsi or Thums Up glass bottle is a label as it is impressed on the lid of the food package.
A sticker bearing the brand name, MRP, FSSAI licence number, and 'Best Before' date pasted on a locally manufactured ghee tin by a Rajasthan-based dairy constitutes a label under the Act.
The pictorial allergen warning and vegetarian/non-vegetarian green or red dot symbol printed directly on the cardboard box of a Britannia biscuit pack forms part of the label.
A product insert inside a packaged Ayurvedic herbal tea box from Patanjali listing ingredients, health claims, and brewing instructions is considered a label under this definition.
what_it_covers: Any written, printed, or graphic matter directly printed on the outer wrapper or container of a food product, such as ingredient lists and nutritional facts on a biscuit packet.
A product insert — a separate sheet of paper or booklet enclosed within the food package providing additional information about the food product.
Embossed, stamped, or perforated marks on lids, crowns, or covers of food containers, such as batch numbers stamped on bottle caps.
Stickers or adhesive tags bearing food-related information attached to containers, covers, or lids of food packages.
Pictorial or graphic representations, logos, and brand marks that are printed or affixed to any part of the food packaging.
what_it_excludes: Standalone advertisements on hoardings, television commercials, or digital media, which fall under the separate definition of 'advertisement' rather than 'label'.
Verbal or oral descriptions made by a seller or vendor about a food product at the point of sale, which are not written or printed on the package.
General promotional pamphlets or leaflets distributed separately from the food package that are not enclosed within or attached to the food package as a product insert.
Information recorded only in internal business documents such as invoices, purchase orders, or warehouse stock records that do not appear on the food package itself.
Markings on the outer transport carton or secondary packaging not intended to reach the end consumer as part of the retail food package.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a piece of information qualifies as a 'label' is critical because obligations regarding mandatory declarations (ingredients, nutritional information, FSSAI licence number, best-before date) attach specifically to the label, and any false, misleading, or non-compliant label can render the food product 'misbranded' under Section 3, triggering penalties under Section 53 of the Act. Failure to comply with labelling regulations can result in fines, product recall, cancellation of licence, and prosecution of the food business operator.

definitions.definition: "Labelling" means any tag, brand, mark, pictorial or other descriptive matter written, printed, stencilled, marked, embossed or impressed on, or attached to, a container or package of food, and includes all information required to be displayed on a food article under this Act and the regulations made thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: Labelling refers to everything written, printed, or displayed on or attached to a food product's packaging — including the product name, ingredients, nutritional information, manufacturing details, and any health or marketing claims. It is the complete set of information a consumer sees on a food package before buying it. Good labelling helps consumers make informed choices and holds manufacturers accountable for what they sell.
real_world_examples: A packet of Maggi noodles displaying its ingredients list, nutritional facts per 100g, manufacturing date, best-before date, vegetarian green dot symbol, and FSSAI licence number on its wrapper — all of this collectively constitutes the labelling of the product.

Amul's butter pack carrying the brand name, net weight (500g), fat percentage, storage instructions ('Refrigerate below 8°C'), MRP, batch number, and the FSSAI logo printed on the outer carton is a standard example of compliant food labelling in India.

A juice brand selling 'Tropicana 100% Orange Juice' in a Tetra Pak carton where the front panel shows a health claim ('No added sugar') and the back panel carries the full nutritional declaration, allergen information, and country of origin — the entire carton surface including tags, stickers, and seals forms part of the labelling.

A small manufacturer in Pune selling packaged spices (turmeric powder) at a local kirana store must affix a label on each pouch mentioning the product name, net quantity, FSSAI licence number, manufacturer's address, date of manufacture, and best-before date — failure to do so is a violation of labelling requirements under Section 23.

An imported packaged food product such as a Korean instant noodle brand sold on Amazon India must carry a supplementary label in English or Hindi with mandatory declarations including importer's name and address, country of origin, and translated ingredient list — this supplementary sticker is part of the labelling obligation under FSSAI regulations.
what_it_covers: All text, graphics, symbols, and descriptive matter printed, embossed, or affixed directly on any container, wrapper, or package of a food article, including brand names, ingredient lists, nutritional tables, and allergen declarations.
Supplementary stickers or adhesive tags placed on imported food products to provide mandatory information in English or Hindi as required under Indian food safety regulations.

Health, nutrition, and dietary claims made on food packages, such as 'high in protein', 'no added sugar', or 'gluten-free', which fall within the scope of labelling standards prescribed by the Food Authority.
Batch numbers, lot numbers, date of manufacture, best-before or use-by dates, and FSSAI licence numbers that are required to be displayed on packaged food products sold in India.
Any hangtag, leaflet, or insert physically attached to or enclosed within a food package that carries product-related information intended for the consumer.
what_it_excludes: Verbal or oral representations made by a salesperson or vendor about a food product at the point of sale, which fall within the definition of 'advertisement' rather than labelling.
Information displayed on shelf-edge tickets, posters, or in-store display boards that are not physically attached to or part of the food product's packaging.

General promotional or advertising materials such as television commercials, newspaper ads, or digital banner advertisements for food products, which are governed separately as 'advertisement' under the Act.

Labelling of non-food products such as cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, or agricultural inputs even if sold in similar packaging, as the Act and its labelling provisions apply exclusively to 'food' as defined.
Bulk or loose food sold without any packaging or container (e.g., loose vegetables, open grains sold by weight at a mandi), where no label or package is attached.
definitions.why_it_matters: Non-compliance with labelling requirements under Section 23 can result in a food article being classified as 'misbranded' under the Act, triggering penalties, product recalls, and prosecution of the food business operator. Proper labelling is also a prerequisite for lawful manufacture, distribution, and sale of packaged food, and deficiencies can activate improvement notices, prohibition orders, and adjudication proceedings.

definitions.definition: A legal practitioner, as used in Section 71 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, means a person authorised to practise law and represent parties in legal proceedings, including advocates enrolled under the Advocates Act, 1961, who may be authorised by an appellant to represent his case before the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal.
definitions.plain_english: A legal practitioner is a trained and licensed lawyer — typically an advocate — who is allowed to argue a case on behalf of someone else in a court or tribunal. Under this law, if a food business operator or any other party appeals a decision before the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal, they can hire a lawyer to speak and act for them instead of appearing themselves. This gives parties professional legal help during tribunal proceedings.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based food manufacturer whose licence was cancelled by the Food Safety Authority hires a senior advocate from the Delhi High Court Bar to represent him before the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal instead of arguing the case personally.

A Mumbai snack company challenged an adjudicating officer's penalty order before the Tribunal; the company's board authorises its retained corporate lawyer — an enrolled advocate — to appear and file written submissions on its behalf.

A petty retailer in Chennai, penalised for selling misbranded food, cannot understand tribunal procedures and instructs a local advocate to represent him before the Tribunal, exercising the right conferred by Section 71.

A large food import company based in Bengaluru, facing an adverse Tribunal order, simultaneously authorises its in-house legal officer and an external senior advocate as legal practitioners to jointly represent the company's appeal before the Tribunal.

A food safety auditor whose certification was challenged before the Tribunal appoints an advocate specialising in food law to present legal arguments, cross-examine witnesses, and file affidavits on his behalf during the appellate proceedings.
what_it_covers: An advocate duly enrolled under the Advocates Act, 1961, authorised by the appellant to represent his case before the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal.
A senior counsel or specialist food law advocate engaged by a food business operator to argue on their behalf during tribunal hearings.
A panel of one or more advocates jointly authorised by the appellant company to collectively handle representation before the Tribunal.
An advocate appointed to file written submissions, examine witnesses on oath, and respond to ex parte proceedings on behalf of the appellant.
what_it_excludes: An officer of the appellant company who represents the company before the Tribunal under the same provision — such an officer is separately permitted but is not a 'legal practitioner' within the legal sense.
An unqualified person or paralegal who is not enrolled as an advocate under the Advocates Act, 1961, and therefore cannot act as a legal practitioner before the Tribunal.

A chartered accountant, company secretary, or other non-law professional who may advise the company internally but is not authorised to represent parties in judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings as a legal practitioner.
The appellant himself appearing in person, which is a separately permitted mode of appearance under Section 71 and is distinct from representation by a legal practitioner.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a legal practitioner determines who is validly authorised to represent an appellant before the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal; an invalid representative could render submissions legally infirm and jeopardise the appellant's case. It also defines the boundary of professional privilege and the accountability of the representative during proceedings deemed judicial under the Indian Penal Code.
