definitions.definition: "licence" means a licence granted under section 31 of this Act, authorising a food business operator to carry on any food business activity, subject to such conditions as may be specified.
definitions.plain_english: A licence is an official government permission that allows a person or business to carry out food-related activities such as manufacturing, processing, packaging, selling, or distributing food in India. Without this permission, operating a food business is illegal under the Food Safety and Standards Act. The licence is issued by a designated licensing authority and comes with specific conditions that the holder must follow.
real_world_examples: A biscuit manufacturing company in Pune must obtain a licence from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) before it can legally produce and sell its products in the market.

A restaurant chain operating across multiple states in India, such as a biryani franchise in Hyderabad, must hold a valid FSSAI licence for each of its outlets engaged in food preparation and service.

A packaged drinking water plant in Gujarat is required to secure a Central licence from FSSAI given its turnover exceeds the prescribed threshold, failing which it is liable to penalties under section 63.

A dairy processing unit in Anand, Gujarat, converting raw milk into pasteurised milk and butter must obtain and maintain a valid food business licence, and is subject to inspection under section 32 if an improvement notice is issued.

An online food aggregator platform operating in Bengaluru that sources and delivers food from cloud kitchens must ensure that each cloud kitchen partner holds a valid licence as a condition of listing on its platform.
A small-scale spice packer in Rajasthan with an annual turnover above Rs. 12 lakhs must upgrade from a mere registration to a State-level FSSAI licence and comply with all associated conditions.
what_it_covers: A licence granted to a manufacturer operating a food processing unit with an annual turnover exceeding Rs. 12 lakhs, permitting it to manufacture and sell food products.
A licence issued to an importer authorising the import of food articles into India through designated ports of entry.
A licence covering catering or food service establishments, hotels, and restaurants that prepare and serve food commercially.
A licence held by a food storage or cold chain operator engaged in the distribution and warehousing of perishable food items.
A licence issued to a packaged food company engaged in labelling, packaging and selling food products across state boundaries.
what_it_excludes: A registration certificate issued to petty food business operators or tiny food business operators whose annual turnover falls below the threshold prescribed under section 31, which is a registration and not a licence.
Home-based individuals preparing food solely for personal or family consumption without any commercial activity, who are not required to obtain a licence.
Farmers and primary producers engaged only in growing, harvesting or rearing food at the pre-processing stage, who are not subject to the licensing requirement under the Act.
Entities dealing exclusively in non-food items such as cosmetics, drugs, or animal feed, which fall outside the definition of food under the Act and hence outside the licensing regime.
Temporary hawkers or itinerant vendors who qualify only for registration under the simplified registration category and are not subject to full licensing requirements.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a food business operator holds a valid licence determines their legal authority to carry on food business activities — operating without one attracts imprisonment of up to six months and a fine up to five lakh rupees under section 63. Additionally, the licence is the nexus for regulatory powers under sections 32 and 64, enabling authorities to issue improvement notices, suspend or cancel the licence, and trigger prosecution for non-compliance with licence conditions.

definitions.definition: "local area" means any area, whether urban or rural, notified by the State Government or local authority as a defined territorial unit for the purposes of administration, regulation, or enforcement of food safety standards under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'local area' refers to a specific geographic region — such as a municipal ward, a town, a district, or a village panchayat zone — that has been officially designated by a state government or local authority. It sets the territorial boundary within which food safety rules and enforcement actions apply. Think of it as the 'jurisdiction map' that tells food safety officers where their authority begins and ends.
real_world_examples: The Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) area being designated as a 'local area' for the purposes of appointing a Designated Officer and Food Safety Officers to inspect restaurants and food stalls within Hyderabad city limits.

A gram panchayat area in rural Maharashtra being notified as a 'local area' under the Act, enabling local food safety enforcement against unlicensed village-level food processors and weekly market vendors.
The Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) jurisdiction being treated as a 'local area' for issuing improvement notices to food business operators operating cloud kitchens within Bengaluru city.

A district in Uttar Pradesh, such as Lucknow district, being identified as a 'local area' for the purposes of allocating jurisdiction to the Commissioner of Food Safety to oversee sampling and testing of food articles sold in that district.

A notified town area committee (NAC) in Odisha being considered a 'local area' enabling the State Food Safety Authority to deploy Food Safety Officers to inspect street food vendors and temporary stall holders operating within that town.
An industrial estate in Pune being demarcated as a specific 'local area' for the purposes of food safety audits and licensing of food manufacturing units located within that estate.
what_it_covers: Municipal corporation areas, municipal councils, and town area committees notified by State Governments, such as the Delhi Municipal Corporation area or Chennai Corporation limits.
Rural areas governed by gram panchayats or district panchayats that have been officially notified as a local area for food safety administration.
Special economic zones, industrial estates, or notified townships where a specific territorial boundary is recognised for deploying food safety officers and enforcing licensing requirements.
Cantonment board areas or notified urban agglomerations that fall under a defined local authority and are designated for food safety regulatory oversight.
Hill council areas or tribal autonomous district council areas in states like Meghalaya or Mizoram that are officially demarcated as distinct local areas for enforcement purposes.
what_it_excludes: Areas spanning multiple states or entire national territories — the term applies to sub-national, localised geographic units, not pan-India jurisdiction.
Private premises or individual food business establishments, which are not themselves 'local areas' but fall within a local area.
International waters or territory beyond Indian borders, even if food is imported through a port located within a local area.
Overlapping or un-notified geographic regions that have not been formally designated by the State Government or a local authority as a defined local area under the Act.
Purely virtual or online food delivery platforms with no fixed physical territorial presence, as these do not constitute a 'local area' in the geographic sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: The concept of 'local area' determines the territorial jurisdiction of Food Safety Officers, the Designated Officer, and the Commissioner of Food Safety, directly affecting which authority can license, inspect, sample, and prosecute food business operators. If a food business operates outside the notified local area of a given officer, enforcement actions, improvement notices, and prohibition orders issued by that officer may lack legal validity.

definitions.definition: A 'lot' refers to a definite quantity of a commodity produced essentially under the same conditions, used as a unit of grouping for food products; where any food which fails to comply with food safety requirements is part of a batch, lot or consignment of food of the same class or description, it shall be presumed until the contrary is proved, that all of the food in that lot fails to comply with those requirements.
definitions.plain_english: A 'lot' is a group or batch of food items that were made or packed under the same conditions and are treated as a single unit for inspection and safety purposes. If one item from a lot is found to be unsafe or non-compliant, the law assumes that all other items in that same lot are also unsafe unless proven otherwise. This helps food safety authorities act quickly to protect consumers without having to test every single item individually.
real_world_examples: A biscuit manufacturer in Pune produces 10,000 packets of cream biscuits in a single production run on a Tuesday afternoon — this entire production run constitutes a 'lot'; if one packet is found to contain a contaminant, all 10,000 packets are presumed non-compliant under Section 18(g).

A dairy cooperative in Amul dispatches 500 cartons of pasteurised milk packaged on the same date and shift — this constitutes a lot; if food safety officers test one carton and find it unsafe, the presumption extends to all 500 cartons in that lot.

A spice packing unit in Rajasthan fills 2,000 pouches of turmeric powder from the same grinding batch and assigns them a common lot number; when FSSAI inspectors detect excess lead content in a sampled pouch, the entire lot of 2,000 pouches is presumed adulterated.

An instant noodles manufacturer in Haryana produces a specific lot of 50,000 units bearing lot code 'L-2024-07-15'; following a consumer complaint, if one sample fails the pesticide residue standard, all units bearing that lot code are subject to recall under the presumption rule.

A cold-pressed oil unit in Kerala presses and bottles 300 litres of coconut oil in a single day's operation under identical conditions — constituting one lot; a food analyst finding rancidity in one sampled bottle triggers the presumption of non-compliance across the entire day's production lot.

definitions.definition: The term 'manager' is not formally defined in Section 3 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, but as used in Section 33, it refers to any person who manages, supervises, or is in charge of the day-to-day operations of a food business on behalf of the food business operator, and who may be held liable for contraventions of the Act, rules, or regulations committed in connection with such business.
definitions.plain_english: A 'manager' in the context of the Food Safety and Standards Act is the person who runs or oversees the daily operations of a food business — like a factory, restaurant, or food store — on behalf of the owner. This person is responsible for making sure the business follows food safety rules. If the business breaks the law, the manager can be held personally accountable along with the business owner.
real_world_examples: The operations manager of a biscuit manufacturing unit in Pune who oversees production, quality checks, and packaging on behalf of the company and ensures compliance with FSSAI regulations.
The restaurant manager of a popular dhaba chain in Delhi who supervises food preparation, storage hygiene, and staff practices, and is answerable to the Food Safety Officer during inspections.
The branch manager of a large grocery retail chain in Mumbai who is responsible for ensuring that food products on shelves are within expiry dates and stored at proper temperatures.

The factory in-charge of a dairy processing plant in Anand, Gujarat, who manages day-to-day pasteurisation and packaging operations and ensures adherence to FSSAI standards on behalf of the dairy cooperative.
The catering manager at a hospital in Chennai responsible for supervising meal preparation, hygiene protocols, and safe food handling for patients on behalf of the hospital administration.
semantic_tags: person in charge of food premises
what_it_covers: A salaried employee appointed by a food business operator to manage and supervise the food production or service operations at a specific premises.
A person who exercises day-to-day control and authority over the conduct of a food business, including staffing, hygiene, and compliance decisions.
An individual who acts on behalf of the food business operator in dealings with regulatory authorities such as the Food Safety Officer during inspections or enforcement actions.
A person designated as in-charge of a food establishment in the temporary or permanent absence of the owner or food business operator.
what_it_excludes: The food business operator themselves who owns and runs the business, as they have a distinct and separately defined role under the Act.
A Food Safety Officer or Designated Officer who is a government-appointed regulatory authority and not part of the food business management.
A contract labourer or daily-wage worker who performs manual tasks in a food unit but has no supervisory or managerial authority over the business operations.
A silent partner or investor in the food business who has no operational control or day-to-day involvement in managing the food premises.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 33, when a food business operator commits an offence under the Act, the manager of the business who was responsible for the day-to-day conduct can also be prosecuted and held criminally liable, unless they can prove the offence was committed without their knowledge or that they exercised due diligence to prevent it. This makes the definition critical for determining who bears personal legal responsibility during enforcement actions, inspections, and prosecutions under the Act.

definitions.definition: "manufacture" in relation to food means any processing or treatment carried out on raw materials or ingredients to produce an article of food, including all operations of production, preparation, mixing, formulating, filling, packaging, labelling, or any other process involved in bringing a food product to a state fit for sale or distribution.
definitions.plain_english: Manufacture means the process of making food products from raw materials or ingredients through steps like mixing, cooking, processing, packaging, and labelling. It covers everything done to turn basic inputs into a finished food item ready to be sold. In simple terms, if someone is involved in producing or making food at any stage before it reaches the consumer, they are engaged in manufacture.
real_world_examples: A biscuit factory in Pune that receives flour, sugar, and butter and processes them through mixing, baking, packaging, and labelling before dispatching biscuits to wholesalers is engaged in manufacture under the Act.

A spice grinding and blending unit in Rajasthan that purchases whole spices, grinds them, mixes them into masala blends, fills them into pouches, and seals them for retail sale is carrying out manufacture of food products.

A dairy plant in Anand, Gujarat that pasteurises raw milk, adds cultures to produce yoghurt or cheese, and then packs the finished product in labelled containers for distribution to retail outlets is engaged in manufacture.

A small-scale pickle-making unit in Andhra Pradesh that processes raw mangoes with salt, oil, and spices and then bottles and labels the finished pickle for sale in local markets constitutes manufacture under the Food Safety and Standards Act.

A packaged drinking water plant in Chennai that draws groundwater, subjects it to filtration, reverse osmosis, UV treatment, and ozonation, and then fills and seals it in labelled bottles is manufacturing food within the meaning of the Act.
what_it_covers: Large-scale industrial processing units that convert raw agricultural produce into packaged consumer food products.
Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and cottage industries engaged in processing food items such as pickles, papads, sweets, or namkeen for commercial sale.
Dairy processing plants that pasteurise, homogenise, or culture milk into finished dairy products like cheese, butter, ghee, or yoghurt.
Beverage production units, including those producing packaged drinking water, fruit juices, carbonated drinks, or energy drinks.
Bakery and confectionery units that bake, fill, frost, and package bread, cakes, biscuits, or chocolates for retail distribution.
Any operation involving mixing, formulating, or blending food ingredients to produce a distinct food article, even at a petty manufacturer scale.
what_it_excludes: Primary agricultural activities such as harvesting, threshing, or cleaning of crops in the field, which occur before any processing stage begins.
Retail sale or distribution of pre-manufactured food products where no further processing, treatment, or transformation of the food takes place.
Transportation and storage of finished food products where the food is merely moved or held without any processing, mixing, or treatment being applied.
Preparation of food by a consumer at home purely for personal or family consumption and not intended for sale or commercial distribution.
Live animals and plants prior to harvesting, which are explicitly excluded from the definition of food and therefore outside the scope of manufacture.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity is engaged in 'manufacture' determines its obligations under the Act, including the requirement to obtain a licence under Section 31, comply with food safety management systems, and adhere to standards set by the Food Authority; failure to comply exposes the manufacturer to penalties under Section 51 for manufacturing sub-standard or unsafe food, which can attract fines up to several lakhs of rupees or criminal prosecution depending on the severity of the violation.

definitions.definition: "manufacturer" means a person who is engaged in the manufacture of any article of food, and includes any person who through any form of activity causes any article of food to come into existence by transformation of ingredients or raw materials.
definitions.plain_english: A manufacturer is any person or business that makes or produces food products, whether by combining ingredients, processing raw materials, or transforming them into a finished food article. This includes large food companies as well as small-scale producers who create food items intended for sale or distribution. Essentially, if you are responsible for producing or creating a food product, you qualify as a manufacturer under this law.
real_world_examples: A biscuit company like Britannia Industries Ltd. that processes wheat flour, sugar, and fats in its factory to produce packaged biscuits sold across India.
A small-scale dal mill in Madhya Pradesh that cleans, sorts, and processes raw pulses into packaged branded dal for retail sale in local markets.
A Mumbai-based spice grinding unit that purchases raw whole spices and grinds, blends, and packages them as branded spice powders under its own label.
A dairy cooperative in Gujarat, such as Amul, that collects raw milk and converts it into pasteurised milk, butter, cheese, and yoghurt for nationwide distribution.
A home-based entrepreneur in Bengaluru who prepares and packages homemade pickles or murabbas for sale through online platforms or local grocery stores.
A namkeen (savoury snack) unit in Indore that fries and seasons chickpea flour mixtures to produce packaged ready-to-eat snacks sold through distributors.
what_it_covers: A large-scale industrial food processing unit that converts raw agricultural produce into packaged finished food products for commercial sale.
A petty manufacturer operating a small home-based or cottage-industry unit that produces food articles in limited quantities for local sale.
A contract manufacturer who processes food on behalf of another brand owner or licensor using specified ingredients and recipes.
A co-packer or third-party unit that receives semi-processed food material and carries out final processing, packaging, and labelling before the product reaches the market.
Any person who blends, mixes, fortifies, or otherwise transforms food ingredients to create a distinct new food product intended for human consumption.
what_it_excludes: A retailer or seller who merely stocks, displays, and sells pre-packaged food products without any transformation or processing of the food itself.
A transporter or logistics service provider who moves food articles from one location to another without altering the nature or composition of the food.
A farmer or primary producer who grows crops or rears animals but does not engage in any processing, packaging, or transformation of the harvested produce.
A distributor or wholesaler who only redistributes finished packaged food products originally manufactured by another registered entity.
A consumer who prepares food solely for personal or household consumption with no intent to sell or commercially distribute the prepared food.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'manufacturer' determines their obligation to obtain a mandatory licence under Section 27, comply with food safety standards and Good Manufacturing Practices, and bear primary legal liability for offences such as manufacturing sub-standard, misbranded, or unsafe food under Sections 27 and 78, including exposure to substantial monetary penalties and criminal prosecution.

definitions.definition: The term 'manufactures' as used in the Food Safety and Standards Act is not formally defined in a standalone provision, but is used in Section 63 to denote the act of producing, processing, preparing, or making any article of food by a person or food business operator, whether by himself or through another person acting on his behalf, intended for sale, distribution, or commercial use, without holding the requisite licence under Section 31.
definitions.plain_english: To 'manufacture' in the context of this law means to make, produce, or process any food product, whether on a small or large scale, for the purpose of selling or distributing it to consumers. This includes any steps taken to prepare food items from raw ingredients into a finished or semi-finished product. A person who does this without the required government licence is committing an offence under this Act.
real_world_examples: A biscuit-making unit in Rajkot producing packaged biscuits from flour, sugar, and oil on a commercial scale without obtaining a valid FSSAI licence from the Designated Officer.

A small jam and pickle producer in Pune preparing and bottling fruit preserves in her home kitchen and selling them directly to local grocery stores without registering or obtaining a licence under the FSS Act.
A dairy operator in Amul's supply chain region independently churning and packaging flavoured milk products in an unlicensed facility and distributing them to retailers across the district.

A roadside namkeen manufacturer in Indore operating a production unit that fries and packages snacks for wholesale supply to shops and eateries, without having applied for or obtained any food business licence.
A spice blending unit in Erode mixing and packing masala powders under a local brand name for inter-state sale, operating without a central or state-level FSSAI manufacturing licence.

A bakery chain in Hyderabad producing bread, cakes, and pastries on an industrial scale through hired workers on the proprietor's behalf, without maintaining a current and valid licence for the manufacturing premises.
what_it_covers: Any person or food business operator who produces or processes a food article for sale or commercial distribution, whether personally or through hired workers, without a valid licence under Section 31.
Large-scale industrial units engaged in processing raw food ingredients into packaged, branded, or labelled food products intended for retail or wholesale markets.
Small or medium food producers who prepare food articles on behalf of a principal manufacturer, acting as a contract manufacturer, without the requisite licence.
Home-based food preparers who produce food commercially (beyond the petty manufacturer threshold) and sell or distribute such products without registration or licence.
Any entity that assembles, blends, bottles, or packages food ingredients into a finished food article for the purpose of commercial sale.
what_it_excludes: Petty manufacturers who themselves manufacture or sell any article of food and are exempted under Section 31(2), provided they register with the appropriate authority as required by regulations.

Temporary stall holders, hawkers, itinerant vendors, and small-scale or cottage industry operators who fall within the exempted categories under Section 31(2) and comply with registration requirements.
Persons who prepare food solely for personal or household consumption with no commercial intent and no sale or distribution involved.
A food business operator who holds a valid and current licence issued by the Designated Officer and is therefore lawfully engaged in manufacturing activities.
Retailers or distributors who merely store or sell finished food articles manufactured by a third party, without themselves engaging in any production or processing activity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person's activity qualifies as 'manufactures' under Section 63 directly determines criminal liability — a person found to be manufacturing food without a licence is punishable with imprisonment up to six months and a fine up to five lakh rupees. This definition also triggers the licensing obligation under Section 31 and, where the food is sub-standard, misbranded, or contains extraneous matter, additional civil penalties under Sections 51, 52, and 54 may apply.

definitions.definition: The act of producing, preparing, or processing any article of food by oneself or through another person on one's behalf, with the intention or purpose of selling such article of food. Though not separately defined in the Act, 'manufactures for sale' is used throughout the Act to denote commercial production of food articles and is distinct from manufacture for personal consumption.
definitions.plain_english: This phrase refers to making or producing food products with the purpose of selling them to others, whether you do it yourself or hire someone to do it on your behalf. It covers any kind of commercial food production — from a large factory making packaged goods to a small unit preparing food for the market. The key element is that the production is intended for sale, not for personal or household use.
real_world_examples: A biscuit factory in Pune produces packets of biscuits using substandard ingredients and supplies them to retail stores across Maharashtra — the factory owner 'manufactures for sale' under Section 52.
A small ghee producer in Rajasthan hires workers to process and package ghee under a brand label for distribution to local grocery shops, making the owner liable as one who manufactures for sale.
A spice processing unit in Guntur grinds and packages chilli powder under a private label and sells it to wholesalers — the unit operator is considered to be manufacturing for sale.

A bakery in Mumbai outsources production of its branded bread loaves to a contract manufacturer who produces them on the bakery's behalf — both the bakery owner and the contract manufacturer may be treated as manufacturing for sale.
A dairy cooperative in Gujarat bottles and labels milk under its own brand for sale through retail outlets across the state, constituting manufacturing for sale of a food article.

A cottage industry unit in Himachal Pradesh prepares and packages fruit jams for sale at local fairs and through e-commerce platforms — this qualifies as manufacturing for sale regardless of the small scale.
what_it_covers: A large food processing company that produces packaged snacks in its own facility and sells them through distributors across India.
A person who engages a contract manufacturer or job worker to produce food articles under their brand or label for commercial sale.
A small-scale or cottage food unit that produces homemade pickles, sweets, or spices and sells them at local markets, fairs, or online platforms.
A food business operator who processes and repackages bulk food commodities into smaller retail units with their own label for sale.
A regional dairy that pasteurises, bottles, and distributes milk or milk products commercially under a registered brand name.
what_it_excludes: A household that prepares food solely for consumption by family members with no intent to sell, even if the quantities are large.
A charitable or religious institution that cooks and distributes food free of charge to the public without any commercial purpose.
A person who stores, transports, or distributes food articles made by someone else without being involved in the production or processing stage.
A retailer who merely sells pre-manufactured food articles produced by a third party without any involvement in the manufacturing process.
A food safety officer or analyst who handles or tests food samples in the course of official duties, with no manufacturing or commercial intent.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person 'manufactures for sale' is the threshold that determines liability under Sections 51, 52, 54, and 57 of the Act — if this element is established, the person can be penalised for producing misbranded, sub-standard, extraneous-matter-containing, or adulterant food, with penalties ranging from one lakh to ten lakh rupees. Without establishing this nexus between manufacturing and commercial sale, penal provisions targeting the production stage cannot be invoked against the accused.

definitions.definition: "Member" means a member of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India appointed under section 6 of this Act, and includes ex officio Members appointed by virtue of their office.
definitions.plain_english: A Member is a person who is officially appointed to serve on the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the central body that sets and enforces food safety rules in India. Some Members hold their position automatically because of another government role they occupy (ex officio), while others are appointed specifically for their expertise. Together, Members form the governing body that makes key decisions about food safety standards and regulations.
real_world_examples: A senior scientist from the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) is appointed as a Member of the Food Authority to contribute medical and nutritional expertise to the framing of food safety standards for packaged foods sold across India.

The Director General of Health Services, as an ex officio Member of the Food Authority under Section 6, participates in deliberations on setting permissible pesticide residue limits for vegetables exported from Maharashtra.

A representative from the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare is nominated as a Member of the Food Authority and votes on regulations governing the labelling requirements for genetically modified food products imported into India.

A food technology expert with over 20 years of industry experience from a leading institute such as the Central Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI) in Mysuru is appointed as a Member to advise on Good Manufacturing Practices for small-scale food processors in rural India.

A consumer advocacy representative appointed as a Member of the Food Authority raises concerns during a board meeting about misleading health claims made by popular nutraceutical brands sold on Indian e-commerce platforms.
what_it_covers: Persons specifically appointed to the Food Authority under Section 6 for their expertise in food science, technology, nutrition, public health, or consumer affairs.
Ex officio Members who are Members of the Food Authority by virtue of holding a specified government office, such as the Director General of Health Services or representatives of central ministries.
Independent experts or nominees from scientific institutions nominated to the Food Authority to provide technical input on food safety standards and regulations.
Representatives from relevant government departments (e.g., Ministry of Commerce, Ministry of Agriculture) who are appointed as Members to coordinate food policy across sectors.
what_it_excludes: The Chairperson of the Food Authority, who is separately defined and distinguished from Members under Section 3 of the Act.
The Chief Executive Officer of the Food Authority, who is a statutory functionary responsible for administration and execution rather than a Member of the governing body.
Food Safety Officers, Designated Officers, or Food Analysts appointed under other sections of the Act who perform operational or enforcement duties rather than governance roles.
Advisory or expert committee members, such as members of Scientific Panels or the Central Advisory Committee, who assist the Food Authority but are not Members of the Authority itself.
Employees or staff of the Food Authority engaged in day-to-day administrative or technical functions who are not constituted as part of the governing board.
definitions.why_it_matters: The legal status of 'Member' determines who has the authority to participate in decisions of the Food Authority, including the adoption of food safety standards, issuance of regulations, and exercise of statutory powers under the Act; only validly appointed Members can form a quorum and pass binding resolutions. Decisions made without a properly constituted membership may be legally challenged, affecting the validity of regulations, licences, or enforcement actions taken by the Food Authority.

definitions.definition: An article of food is deemed to be misbranded if it is not labelled in the manner required by the provisions of this Act or any rules or regulations made thereunder, or if its label contains any false or misleading statement, design or device, or if it is so coloured, coated, polished or powdered that the damage or inferiority is concealed, or if it is falsely stated to be the product of another country or place.
definitions.plain_english: A food product is 'misbranded' when its packaging, label, or advertising misleads the consumer about what the product actually is, where it comes from, what it contains, or its true quality. This includes false claims about ingredients, nutritional value, origin, or manufacture date. Essentially, if the label lies or hides important information, the food is misbranded.
real_world_examples: A packet of ghee sold in India labelled as '100% Pure Cow Ghee' but actually containing a blend of vegetable fat and animal fat is misbranded because the label falsely represents the product's composition.

A bottled fruit juice in Mumbai markets labelled 'Fresh Squeezed Orange Juice – No Preservatives' when it actually contains sodium benzoate as a preservative constitutes misbranding due to a false statement on the label.
A atta (wheat flour) brand sold in Delhi displaying 'Made in Switzerland' on its packaging when it is manufactured in Haryana is misbranded on account of a false declaration of country of origin.

A protein powder sold online in India claiming '50g of protein per serving' when laboratory analysis reveals only 20g per serving is misbranded because the nutritional label contains a false and misleading statement.

A turmeric powder product in Chennai whose label shows 'FSSAI Certified Organic' without possessing valid organic certification under FSSAI regulations is misbranded as the label creates a false impression regarding its nature and certification status.

A biscuit pack in Kolkata marked with an expiry date of December 2025 when the actual manufacturing date indicates it should have expired in June 2024 is misbranded due to false date labelling that conceals its inferior or degraded condition.
what_it_covers: Food products whose labels contain false or misleading statements about ingredients, nutritional content, weight, or composition.
Articles of food falsely represented as originating from a country or place other than where they were actually manufactured or produced.
Food items that are coloured, coated, polished, or treated in a manner that conceals damage, deterioration, or inferior quality from the consumer.
Packaged food sold without mandatory label information required under FSSAI regulations, such as missing batch number, manufacturing date, or list of ingredients.
Food products bearing forged or unauthorised certifications, marks, or seals (e.g., FSSAI logo, Agmark, organic certification) that the product does not legitimately hold.
what_it_excludes: Food that is unsafe or contains harmful substances beyond permissible limits, which is governed by the definition of 'unsafe food' rather than misbranding.
Food that is sub-standard due to failure to meet prescribed compositional standards, which falls under the separate category of 'sub-standard food' even if not accompanied by any labelling defect.
Adulterants present in food that render it harmful or of inferior quality, which are addressed under the definition of 'adulterant' and related provisions rather than misbranding.
Oral or verbal misrepresentations made by a seller at the point of sale without any connection to the physical label, packaging, or printed advertisement of the food product.
Minor typographical or printing errors on labels that do not mislead the consumer regarding the nature, quality, quantity, or origin of the food product.
definitions.why_it_matters: A finding that a food article is 'misbranded' triggers penal liability under Section 52 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, which prescribes a fine that may extend to three lakh rupees, and can also result in recall, seizure, and cancellation of the food business operator's licence under Sections 26 and 27. It determines whether a food business operator is in breach of their mandatory obligation to ensure accurate labelling, thus directly activating enforcement action by Food Safety Officers and Designated Officers.

definitions.definition: Food is misbranded if its label or packaging contains any false, misleading, or deceptive statement, design, or device; if it is sold under the name of another food; if it is an imitation of or is a substitute for another food and its label does not disclose this fact; if the container is so made, formed or filled as to be misleading; if it does not bear a label containing the required particulars; or if any word, statement, or other information required to appear on the label is not prominently or conspicuously displayed as prescribed by the Food Authority.
definitions.plain_english: Misbranded food refers to any food product whose label, packaging, or advertising contains false, misleading, or incomplete information — for example, claiming it is something it is not, hiding that it is a cheaper substitute, or using deceptive packaging that makes the quantity look larger than it is. The law requires that food labels be accurate, complete, and easy to read. If any of these requirements are violated, the food is considered 'misbranded' and the seller or manufacturer can face legal action.
real_world_examples: A manufacturer in Mumbai sells a dairy spread labelled as 'Pure Desi Ghee' when it is actually a blend of vegetable oil and animal fat, thereby misleading consumers about the product's true nature and composition.

A packaged fruit juice brand in Delhi labels its product as '100% Natural Orange Juice' on the front panel while the ingredients list reveals it contains synthetic flavours, artificial colours, and added sugar, constituting a false and misleading claim.

A Kolkata-based company sells a cheaper blended spice powder in packaging nearly identical in colour, font, and design to a well-known branded product, causing consumers to confuse the two products at the point of purchase.

A snack manufacturer in Hyderabad uses an oversized box with excessive empty space inside, making the net weight of 50 grams appear to be a much larger quantity, thereby deceiving consumers through misleading container fill levels.

A seller in Chennai markets a food supplement as 'clinically proven to cure diabetes' on the label without any regulatory approval for such a claim, constituting a false health claim that misbrands the product under the Act.
An e-commerce platform lists a packaged food item as 'Organic Certified' without any valid certification from a competent authority, misleading online consumers about the product's organic status.
what_it_covers: Food sold under a false name or brand that belongs to a different, established product, thereby deceiving the buyer about the product's identity.
Food whose packaging or container is deliberately designed or filled in a way that exaggerates the quantity or quality of the contents, such as slack-fill packaging.
Food labelled with unsubstantiated health, nutritional, or quality claims — such as 'fat-free,' 'sugar-free,' or 'clinically proven' — that are false or not permitted by the Food Authority.
Food that is an imitation or substitute for another food but whose label does not clearly and prominently disclose this fact to the consumer.
Food whose mandatory label particulars — such as net weight, date of manufacture, expiry date, or list of ingredients — are absent, obscured, or printed in a manner that is not easily readable.
what_it_excludes: Food that is genuinely sub-standard in quality or composition but whose label accurately reflects all required particulars — such food may be 'sub-standard' but not automatically 'misbranded.'
Food that contains a contaminant or adulterant but is otherwise correctly and truthfully labelled — adulteration and misbranding are distinct offences under the Act.
Food products whose labels contain minor typographical or formatting errors that do not mislead the consumer regarding the nature, quality, quantity, or origin of the product.
Verbal or oral representations made by a street vendor without any packaging or label, as misbranding primarily applies to labelled and packaged food articles.
Extraneous matter found in food that does not affect the accuracy of the label or the consumer's understanding of the product's identity or composition.
definitions.why_it_matters: A finding that food is 'misbranded' triggers penalties under Sections 25 and 80 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, including fines that may extend to three lakh rupees, and can result in prohibition orders, product recalls, and suspension or cancellation of the food business operator's licence. The classification directly determines whether regulatory action is taken against the manufacturer, packer, or seller and what level of penalty — civil or criminal — is applicable.

definitions.definition: The term 'mislead' is not formally defined in Section 3 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, but is used in Section 23 to mean any representation, claim, label, packaging, or promotional material relating to food that creates a false, deceptive, or erroneous impression in the mind of the consumer regarding the nature, quality, composition, origin, safety, nutritional value, or any other characteristic of the food article.
definitions.plain_english: To 'mislead' in the context of food law means to give consumers a false or deceptive impression about what they are buying or eating. This includes using fake claims on labels, exaggerated health benefits, false country-of-origin statements, or packaging that makes a product appear better or different than it actually is. Essentially, it covers any dishonest communication — written, visual, or otherwise — that tricks a consumer about the food they are purchasing.
real_world_examples: A branded packaged juice in India labelled '100% Natural' that actually contains artificial flavours and added preservatives, causing consumers to believe they are buying a purely natural product.

A ready-to-eat snack sold in Indian supermarkets claiming 'Zero Trans Fat' on its packaging when laboratory testing reveals the product contains partially hydrogenated vegetable oils with measurable trans fat content.

A honey brand sold across India advertising 'Pure Himalayan Honey' on its label when the product is actually blended with Chinese honey or sugar syrup, misleading consumers about geographic origin and purity.

A cooking oil brand in India using phrases like 'Clinically Proven to Reduce Cholesterol' without any valid scientific backing or regulatory approval, falsely implying a medically verified health benefit.

A baby food manufacturer in India depicting a plump, healthy infant on the packaging of a product that does not meet prescribed nutritional standards for infant food, creating a deceptive impression of suitability and quality.
A restaurant chain in India advertising menu items as 'Organic and Pesticide-Free' when the ingredients used are sourced from non-certified conventional farms, misleading health-conscious consumers.
what_it_covers: Labels or packaging that falsely claim a product is organic, natural, or free from certain substances when it is not.
Advertisements or promotional material that exaggerate or fabricate the nutritional, medicinal, or health benefits of a food product.
Country-of-origin or geographic source claims on food labels that are inaccurate or fabricated to suggest premium quality.
Visual imagery on food packaging (such as fresh fruits on a processed juice carton) that creates a false impression of ingredients or freshness.
Claims that a food product is allergen-free, gluten-free, or suitable for a specific dietary requirement when it is not, deceiving vulnerable consumer groups.
what_it_excludes: Accurate and substantiated health or nutritional claims that have been approved or permitted under FSSAI regulations and are truthful in all material respects.
Statements of general culinary description or serving suggestions that are clearly identified as such and do not constitute factual claims about composition or safety.
Unintentional or typographical errors on labels that are promptly corrected and do not create a systematic deceptive impression on consumers.
Scientific or technical information provided in educational or academic contexts that is not directed at influencing a consumer's purchase decision.
Internal quality or trade documentation not visible to or intended for the end consumer, such as business-to-business invoices or batch records.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a representation or label 'misleads' a consumer is a key trigger for liability under Section 23 of the FSSAI Act, which prohibits the manufacture, sale, or distribution of misbranded food and food with deceptive labelling; a finding that conduct was misleading can expose a food business operator to penalties, licence cancellation, product recall orders, and prosecution for misbranding or unfair trade practices under the Act.

definitions.definition: Misrepresentation, as used under Section 24 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, refers to any false or misleading statement, whether made orally, in writing, or by visible representation, concerning the standard, quality, quantity, grade, composition, need, usefulness, or efficacy of any article of food, made for the purpose of promoting its sale, supply, use, or consumption. It includes any unsubstantiated guarantee of efficacy not based on adequate or scientific justification.
definitions.plain_english: Misrepresentation means making false or misleading claims about food — for example, saying a product has certain health benefits it does not actually have, or claiming it meets quality standards when it does not. This can happen through spoken words, written labels, packaging, or images. It is essentially lying to consumers to get them to buy or use a food product.
real_world_examples: A packaged juice brand in India prints '100% natural' and 'no added sugar' on its label, but the product actually contains synthetic flavouring agents and added sweeteners — a false representation of composition and quality.

A health drink manufacturer advertises on television that its product 'guarantees immunity boost within 7 days' without any clinical or scientific evidence to back this claim, constituting misrepresentation through an unsubstantiated efficacy guarantee.

A seller of organic food products at a Delhi supermarket verbally assures customers that the vegetables are pesticide-free and organically certified, when in fact no such certification exists, amounting to oral misrepresentation.

A biscuit company displays 'high protein' and 'doctor recommended' on packaging in Maharashtra, when the protein content is negligible and no medical body has endorsed the product, misleading consumers about nutritional usefulness.

A spice brand in Gujarat labels its product as 'Grade A premium quality' complying with FSSAI standards, but the actual product is sub-standard and adulterated with fillers, constituting misrepresentation of standard and grade.
what_it_covers: False written statements on food packaging claiming a higher grade, standard, or quality than the product actually possesses.
Oral representations made by sellers or agents to customers falsely attributing health benefits, purity, or certifications to a food article.
Visible representations such as images, logos, or symbols on labels or in advertisements that create a false impression of the food's composition, usefulness, or efficacy.
Unsubstantiated guarantees of health or efficacy outcomes — such as 'clinically proven to cure' or 'guaranteed weight loss' — made without adequate scientific justification.
False or misleading claims about the need for a product, such as representing an ordinary food item as medically necessary for a particular condition without scientific basis.
what_it_excludes: Genuinely substantiated health or efficacy claims that are supported by adequate scientific evidence and comply with FSSAI regulations — these do not constitute misrepresentation.
Accurate, truthful descriptions of a food article's actual composition, quality, grade, or standard that are not misleading in any manner.

General promotional language that constitutes permissible 'puffery' (e.g., 'delicious taste' or 'loved by families') that no reasonable consumer would take as a factual representation of standard or efficacy.
Contamination or adulteration of food that does not involve any false claim or statement — such acts may be covered under separate provisions relating to unsafe or sub-standard food.
Mere errors in labelling due to typographical mistakes without intent to deceive, where the overall representation is not misleading to the consumer.
definitions.why_it_matters: A finding that a food business operator has engaged in misrepresentation triggers liability for engaging in unfair trade practices under Section 24, which can result in penalties, prohibition of the offending advertisement, and prosecution. It directly determines whether a person is guilty of an offence under the Act and whether regulatory actions such as improvement notices or prohibition orders may be issued.

definitions.definition: The term 'moral turpitude' is not formally defined in the Food Safety and Standards Act, but as used in Section 8, it refers to conduct underlying a criminal conviction that is inherently base, vile, depraved, or contrary to accepted moral standards and societal norms, as determined by the opinion of the Central Government. It encompasses offences that reflect dishonesty, fraud, or a serious disregard for the rights of others or for public welfare.
definitions.plain_english: Moral turpitude means behaviour that is considered deeply wrong or shameful by society's standards — like fraud, bribery, or serious violent crimes. If a Chairperson or Member of the Food Authority is convicted of such a crime, the Central Government can remove them from their position. It is not just about breaking the law, but about breaking the basic moral code expected of a public official.
real_world_examples: A Member of the Food Authority is convicted by a court in India for accepting bribes from a food manufacturer in exchange for overlooking safety violations — the Central Government determines this involves moral turpitude and removes the Member under Section 8.

The Chairperson of the Food Authority is found guilty of cheating under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code for fraudulently misrepresenting credentials to secure the appointment — the Central Government exercises its power under Section 8 to remove the Chairperson on grounds of moral turpitude.

A Member of the Food Authority is convicted of forgery under IPC Section 465 for fabricating laboratory test reports to clear an adulterated food batch — the Central Government concludes the offence involves moral turpitude and initiates removal proceedings.

A Member is convicted under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 for demanding illegal gratification from a food business operator seeking a licence — the Central Government, considering the corrupt nature of the offence, removes the Member citing moral turpitude under Section 8.

The Chairperson is convicted under the POCSO Act for an offence against a minor — the Central Government determines that such a conviction inherently involves moral turpitude and orders removal from office immediately.

A Member of the Food Authority is convicted of criminal conspiracy under IPC Section 120B for colluding with adulterers to suppress food safety audits — the Central Government treats this as moral turpitude warranting removal under Section 8.
what_it_covers: Conviction for offences involving fraud, cheating, or criminal breach of trust under the Indian Penal Code that reflect dishonest intent.
Conviction under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 for bribery or misuse of official position by a Member or Chairperson of the Food Authority.
Conviction for offences involving sexual misconduct, forgery, or criminal conspiracy that demonstrate a fundamental breach of societal moral standards.
Any offence where the Central Government, in its opinion, finds that the underlying conduct is inherently depraved or contrary to accepted standards of honesty and public duty.
Convictions in Indian courts for offences such as trafficking, money laundering, or criminal fraud that exhibit deliberate wrongdoing.
what_it_excludes: Technical or regulatory offences such as minor traffic violations or inadvertent procedural contraventions that do not involve dishonesty or moral depravity.
Civil liability or civil suits, including contractual disputes or tort claims, that do not result in a criminal conviction.
Offences for which the Member has been acquitted or where proceedings are merely pending without a final conviction by a competent court.
Physical or mental incapacity of a Member, which is a separate and distinct ground for removal under Section 8 and does not involve moral turpitude.
Financial interest conflicts or abuse of position as covered under Section 8(1)(d) and (e), which are separate removal grounds not premised on criminal conviction.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a conviction involves moral turpitude is determinative of the Central Government's power to remove the Chairperson or a Member of the Food Authority under Section 8(1)(b) — if the conviction is found to involve moral turpitude, mandatory removal may follow without the additional procedural safeguard of a prior hearing that applies to other removal grounds. This determination directly affects the tenure, accountability, and integrity of the Food Authority's governance structure.

definitions.definition: The term 'nature' is not formally defined in the Act but is used in Section 50 and elsewhere to refer to the intrinsic character, composition, or essential quality of a food article — encompassing its physical, chemical, and biological attributes that identify what the food fundamentally is, as distinct from its quality, substance, or commercial representation.
definitions.plain_english: The 'nature' of a food product refers to what the food essentially and inherently is — its basic identity, character, and composition. For example, whether a product is truly ghee, honey, or fruit juice is a matter of its 'nature'. If a food is sold or labelled in a way that misrepresents what it fundamentally is, that is a violation related to its nature.
real_world_examples: A trader in Maharashtra sells vanaspati (hydrogenated vegetable oil) by packaging and labelling it as pure desi ghee — misrepresenting the very nature of the food product being sold.

A juice manufacturer in Gujarat sells a synthetic, artificially flavoured drink as '100% natural mango juice', falsely representing the nature of the product, which is actually a reconstituted or imitation beverage.

A spice seller in Delhi mixes powdered brick dust or artificial colour into red chilli powder and sells it as pure chilli powder, fundamentally altering and misrepresenting the nature of the article of food.

A milk supplier in Punjab adulterates buffalo milk with synthetic milk made from detergent, urea, and refined oil — the resultant product is not milk in nature at all, deceiving consumers about the fundamental identity of the product.
A packaged food company in Tamil Nadu labels a product as 'whole wheat bread' when it is predominantly made from refined maida flour, thereby misrepresenting the intrinsic nature of the food article.
what_it_covers: The fundamental identity of a food product — what it inherently is based on its physical, chemical, and biological composition (e.g., whether a substance is genuinely ghee, honey, or milk).
Representations made on labels, advertisements, or invoices that describe or imply what a food article is, including claims about its origin, processing method, or intrinsic character.

Situations where a food article's essential constitution has been altered through adulteration or substitution, changing what the food fundamentally is (e.g., mixing chicory with coffee and selling it as pure coffee).
Assessments by Food Safety Officers and Food Analysts under Section 50 to determine whether a food article corresponds to its stated or implied nature when tested or inspected.
what_it_excludes: Mere degradation in quality of a food article that does not change its fundamental identity — for example, stale but unadulterated milk is sub-standard but its nature as milk is not misrepresented.
Extraneous matter present in food that does not alter the basic identity of the food article (e.g., insect fragments in grain that do not change the nature of the grain as a food product).
Nutritional value claims or health benefit representations which relate to quality or composition beyond identity, governed separately under 'claim' and 'misbranded food' provisions.
Packaging or labelling defects of a purely procedural or administrative nature (e.g., missing batch number or expiry date) that do not relate to what the food fundamentally is.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 50 of the Act, if a food article is found to be 'not of the nature, substance or quality demanded by the purchaser', the food business operator is liable for prosecution and penalty, including fines and licence cancellation. A determination that a food misrepresents its nature can trigger charges of selling misbranded or adulterated food, leading to imprisonment and significant monetary penalties under Sections 50, 51, and 59.

definitions.definition: Non-grievous injury refers to any bodily harm caused to a person as a result of consuming unsafe food, which does not amount to grievous injury as understood under Indian law. It denotes a lesser degree of physical harm — such as temporary illness, mild food poisoning, or recoverable bodily hurt — that falls short of the severe, permanent, or life-threatening harm classified as grievous injury under Section 320 of the Indian Penal Code.
definitions.plain_english: A non-grievous injury is a relatively minor physical harm that a person suffers after eating unsafe food — for example, a stomach upset, mild vomiting, or a temporary rash that heals without lasting damage. It is more serious than no harm at all, but less severe than injuries that are permanently disabling or life-threatening. Essentially, it covers harms from which the affected person can fully recover without major medical intervention.
real_world_examples: A customer in Mumbai buys adulterated milk from a local dairy and suffers a 24-hour bout of diarrhoea and vomiting that resolves with basic oral rehydration therapy, without requiring hospitalisation.

A group of school children in Delhi fall mildly ill after consuming mid-day meal rice contaminated with a low-level pesticide residue, experiencing nausea and stomach cramps that subside within two days under a doctor's observation.
A wedding guest in Hyderabad develops a moderate allergic skin rash after consuming sweets prepared with an undisclosed, substandard food additive, recovering fully within a week with antihistamines.

Consumers in Chennai who purchased packaged fruit juice with a higher-than-permitted microbial count suffer temporary gastroenteritis lasting 48 hours, with no hospitalisation or lasting health impact.

A worker in Pune's factory canteen contracts mild food poisoning from improperly stored cooked meat, experiencing fever and loose motions for three days before making a complete recovery without surgical or intensive medical intervention.
what_it_covers: Temporary gastrointestinal illness such as diarrhoea, vomiting, or stomach cramps caused by consuming unsafe food, from which the person fully recovers within a short period.
Mild allergic reactions — such as skin rashes or hives — resulting from consumption of food containing undisclosed or substandard ingredients that do not cause permanent damage.
Short-term fever, nausea, or food poisoning symptoms resulting from microbially contaminated packaged or prepared food, where the affected person does not require prolonged hospitalisation.

Temporary discomfort or recoverable bodily hurt suffered by a consumer due to the presence of contaminants, adulterants, or unsafe additives in food at levels that cause harm but fall below the threshold of grievous injury.
what_it_excludes: Grievous injury as defined under Section 320 of the Indian Penal Code — including permanent disability, loss of a limb or organ, serious disfigurement, fractures, or injuries endangering life — which attracts a higher punishment under Section 59.
Death resulting from consumption of unsafe food, which is governed by the most serious punishment tier under Section 59 (minimum seven years to life imprisonment).
Cases where unsafe food is consumed but causes absolutely no injury or harm to the consumer, which fall under the lowest punishment category under Section 59.

Psychological or economic harm suffered by a consumer (such as financial loss or mental distress) without any accompanying physical bodily harm, which does not constitute a non-grievous injury under this provision.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an offence under Section 59 results in a non-grievous injury directly determines the severity of criminal punishment: a conviction at this level carries imprisonment up to one year and a fine up to three lakh rupees, as opposed to the lower tier (no injury — six months and one lakh rupees) or the higher tier (grievous injury — six years and five lakh rupees). Establishing or disproving non-grievous injury is therefore pivotal in determining the charge framed, the sentence imposed, and the forum (summary trial or regular trial) in which the case is heard.

definitions.definition: "Notification" means a notification published in the Official Gazette, as used in this Act to denote a formal public announcement issued by the Central Government or other competent authority in the Official Gazette to give legal effect to declarations, appointments, rules, regulations, or other statutory actions under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
definitions.plain_english: A 'notification' is an official public announcement printed in the Government's Official Gazette — the government's formal publication used to make legal decisions, orders, or rules known to the public. Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, the Central Government uses notifications to do things like declare an article as food, bring the law into force, or appoint specific dates for different provisions. It is the government's legally recognised way of formally communicating its actions to citizens and authorities.
real_world_examples: The Central Government issues a notification in the Official Gazette to declare that a particular energy drink formula qualifies as 'food' under the FSSA 2006, thereby bringing it under the Act's regulatory framework.
The Ministry of Health publishes a notification specifying the date on which Section 92 of the Food Safety and Standards Act comes into force in a particular Union Territory.

definitions.definition: "Proprietary and novel food" means an article of food for which standards have not been specified but is not unsafe: Provided that such food does not contain any of the foods and ingredients prohibited under this Act and the regulations made thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: Novel food refers to any food product that does not yet have established safety or quality standards under Indian food law, but which is not considered harmful or unsafe to consume. It is a new or uncommon food item being introduced into the Indian market for which no specific regulatory benchmark exists. Such food must not contain any ingredient or substance that is banned or prohibited under the Food Safety and Standards Act or its regulations.
real_world_examples: A startup in Bengaluru launches an edible insect protein bar made from mealworms — this product has no defined standard under FSS regulations and would qualify as a novel food requiring special approval under Section 22.

A company imports and sells spirulina-based beverages blended with uncommon algae extracts not covered by existing FSSAI product standards, making it a novel food that cannot be freely sold without regulatory clearance.

A food manufacturer in Mumbai introduces a lab-grown or cultured meat product derived from animal cell cultures — since no standards exist for such products in India, it falls under the novel food category.

A Delhi-based firm markets a functional snack containing a newly identified plant-based bioactive compound (e.g., a rare Himalayan berry extract) for which FSSAI has not yet notified permissible limits or compositional standards, classifying it as novel food.

An e-commerce platform sells imported probiotic strains encapsulated in a novel food matrix not covered by existing FSSAI fermented food standards, triggering Section 22 compliance requirements before distribution.
what_it_covers: Food products newly introduced in the Indian market for which FSSAI has not yet notified compositional or safety standards.
Imported food items containing ingredients or formulations that have no corresponding standard under FSS Act regulations.
Domestically manufactured food articles using novel processing methods, novel sources, or novel ingredient combinations not previously consumed to a significant degree in India.
Lab-grown, insect-based, or other technologically derived food products that fall outside existing standard food categories.
Plant-based or algae-derived food products with no established regulatory benchmark under existing FSS regulations.
what_it_excludes: Food articles that are already classified as unsafe food under the FSS Act, as novel food must be 'not unsafe' to qualify.
Food products that contain ingredients prohibited under the FSS Act or regulations made thereunder, even if no standards exist for the overall product.
Genetically modified food, organic food, irradiated food, functional foods, nutraceuticals, and health supplements, which are separately governed under Section 22 and distinct regulatory categories.
Conventional food articles for which FSSAI has already notified standards, such as packaged milk, refined oils, or common spices.
Drugs, ayurvedic, siddha or unani medicines, and narcotic or psychotropic substances, which are regulated under separate legislation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Any person who manufactures, distributes, sells, or imports novel food without complying with Section 22 and applicable FSSAI regulations commits an offence under the FSS Act, exposing them to penalties, product seizure, and prohibition orders. The classification as novel food triggers the mandatory requirement of prior regulatory approval or notification before the product can legally enter the Indian food market.

definitions.definition: A nutraceutical means a food which is specially processed or formulated to satisfy particular dietary requirements, which may contain plants or botanicals, minerals, vitamins, proteins, metals or their compounds, amino acids, enzymes, or substances of animal origin, presented in the form of powders, granules, tablets, capsules, liquids, jelly or other dosage forms (but not parenterals) meant for oral administration, which does not claim to cure or mitigate any specific disease or disorder, and does not include a drug, narcotic drug, psychotropic substance, or ayurvedic, siddha or unani drug as defined under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.
definitions.plain_english: A nutraceutical is a food product that has been specially made or processed to provide health benefits or meet specific dietary needs, sold in forms like tablets, capsules, powders, or liquids rather than as ordinary food. It can contain plant extracts, vitamins, minerals, or animal-derived substances within permitted limits. Unlike medicines, it cannot claim to treat or cure any disease, and it is meant to be taken by mouth as a supplement to the regular diet.
real_world_examples: A brand like Himalaya or Dabur selling Ashwagandha root extract capsules marketed for general wellness and immunity support — regulated as a nutraceutical since it contains a botanical extract, is in capsule form, and makes no disease-cure claims.

Fish oil omega-3 softgel capsules sold by companies like Healthkart in India, containing animal-origin substances (fish-derived fatty acids) within permissible limits, labelled as dietary supplements for heart health but not claiming to treat cardiovascular disease.

A whey protein powder sold in sachets by brands like Muscleblaze, containing proteins and amino acids within Recommended Daily Allowance limits for Indians, marketed for muscle recovery but not as a drug or medicine.

A probiotic supplement in granule form sold by Mankind Pharma under a nutraceutical label, containing beneficial bacteria intended to supplement gut dietary intake, not claiming to cure irritable bowel syndrome or any specific disorder.

Vitamin D3 and calcium combination tablets sold over the counter by Pfizer India as a nutraceutical supplement for bone health, formulated to meet dietary gaps in the Indian population without claiming to treat osteoporosis.

A turmeric (curcumin) extract liquid tonic sold by an Ayurvedic FMCG brand positioned as a nutraceutical for general anti-inflammatory benefit, provided it does not claim to treat arthritis or any named disease and does not qualify as an Ayurvedic drug under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.

what_it_covers: Capsules, tablets, powders, granules, liquids or jelly forms containing plant or botanical extracts, vitamins, minerals, amino acids within Recommended Daily Allowance limits, or animal-origin substances, intended for oral administration.

Products labelled as 'nutraceutical' or 'food for special dietary uses' that are specially processed to meet particular physical or physiological dietary requirements, where the composition differs significantly from ordinary comparable food.
Dietary substances meant to supplement human diet by increasing total dietary intake, provided they do not represent themselves as conventional food and are not administered parenterally.
Products making permissible health benefit or health promotion claims as allowed by FSSAI regulations, without claiming to cure, treat or mitigate any specific disease or disorder.
Enzyme-containing food supplements within permissible limits and protein-based nutritional supplements formulated for special dietary requirements of specific physiological conditions.
what_it_excludes: Drugs as defined under clause (b) of Section 3 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, including allopathic medicines approved and licensed as drugs, even if in tablet or capsule form.
Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs as defined under clauses (a) and (h) of Section 3 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which are governed by a separate regulatory framework.

Narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances as defined in the Schedule of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, and substances listed in Schedules E and E1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.
Products administered parenterally (intravenously or by injection), as nutraceuticals are strictly limited to oral administration forms.
Conventional ordinary food products that are not specially processed or formulated for a particular dietary requirement and do not differ significantly in composition from comparable ordinary foods.
Products that claim to cure, treat or mitigate a specific disease, disorder or condition beyond the health benefit or promotion claims permitted under FSSAI regulations.
definitions.why_it_matters: Any person who manufactures, distributes, sells or imports a nutraceutical without complying with Section 22 of the Food Safety and Standards Act and the regulations made thereunder commits an offence under the Act, attracting penalties including fines and imprisonment. Classification as a nutraceutical rather than a drug or conventional food determines which regulatory authority (FSSAI versus CDSCO) governs the product, what labelling and licensing obligations apply, and whether health benefit claims on packaging are legally permissible.

definitions.definition: An 'offence' under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 means any act or omission that constitutes a violation of the provisions of this Act, the rules or regulations made thereunder, including but not limited to the manufacture, sale, storage, distribution or import of unsafe, sub-standard, misbranded or adulterated food, contravention of any prohibition order, improvement notice, or licensing condition, or any other act declared punishable under this Act. The term encompasses both acts punishable with imprisonment and those punishable with monetary penalty.
definitions.plain_english: An 'offence' is simply any act of breaking the rules set out in the Food Safety and Standards Act. This includes things like selling unsafe or dirty food, mislabelling products, running a food business without a licence, or ignoring orders from food safety authorities. If a person or business commits an offence, they can face fines or even imprisonment depending on how serious the violation is.
real_world_examples: A street food vendor in Mumbai is found selling chaat made with water contaminated with harmful bacteria, making customers ill — this constitutes an offence of selling unsafe food under the Act.

A packaged snacks manufacturer in Gujarat is caught adding a non-permitted food colourant to its product and mislabelling the ingredient list — this is an offence of manufacturing and selling misbranded and adulterated food.

A cold storage operator in Delhi continues to store and distribute frozen meat after receiving a prohibition order from the Food Safety Officer directing them to stop — knowingly violating the prohibition order is a separate offence punishable with a fine up to three lakh rupees.

A restaurant chain in Bengaluru is found to be operating food outlets without obtaining the mandatory food business licence from the FSSAI — running an unlicensed food business constitutes an offence under the Act.

An importer in Chennai introduces a consignment of imported edible oil into the market without getting it tested at an accredited laboratory as required, and the oil is later found to contain pesticide residues beyond permissible tolerance limits — this is an offence of importing and selling sub-standard food.

A manager of a dairy company in Punjab knowingly allows adulterated milk (mixed with detergent) to be bottled and sold to consumers — both the manager and the company are liable for an offence under the Act.
what_it_covers: Manufacture, storage, sale or distribution of unsafe, adulterated, sub-standard or misbranded food articles in violation of the Act.
Knowing contravention of a prohibition order issued by a court or food safety authority, such as continuing to operate after being ordered to stop.
Operating a food business without a valid licence or registration as required under the Act and regulations.
Importing food articles that do not conform to the standards specified by the Food Authority.
Failure to comply with an improvement notice issued by a Food Safety Officer within the stipulated time.
Any act involving moral turpitude by a Chairperson or Member of the Food Authority leading to their conviction under any law.
what_it_excludes: Civil or administrative infractions that attract only penalty proceedings before an Adjudicating Officer and are not specifically declared as criminal offences under the Act.
Acts or omissions by a food business operator that are covered by a valid defence of due diligence, where the operator can demonstrate all reasonable precautions were taken.

Technical or procedural irregularities in documentation or labelling that do not involve any element of fraud, misrepresentation or risk to public health and are addressed through improvement notices without criminal prosecution.
Actions of public servants or regulatory officers acting in good faith in the discharge of their duties under the Act, which are specifically protected from prosecution.
Matters relating to food quality disputes between private parties that are resolved through consumer forums and do not involve a breach of the specific standards prescribed under this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a particular act qualifies as an 'offence' under the Act determines whether criminal prosecution (including imprisonment) can be initiated by the Commissioner of Food Safety or a Special Court, as opposed to merely imposing a civil monetary penalty before an Adjudicating Officer. It also triggers consequential orders such as prohibition orders against the food business operator, disqualification from managing any food business, and affects the admissibility of compounding of offences under Section 64 and summary trial procedures under Section 66.
