definitions.definition: "organic food" means food products that have been produced in accordance with specified organic production standards.
definitions.plain_english: Organic food refers to food products that are grown or made following specific rules about organic farming and production — such as avoiding synthetic pesticides, chemical fertilisers, and genetically modified organisms. In India, these standards are set by the regulatory authority and manufacturers must comply with them before labelling or selling their products as 'organic'. Simply claiming a product is organic without meeting the prescribed standards is not permitted.
real_world_examples: A farmer in Sikkim growing rice without synthetic pesticides or chemical fertilisers and certifying the produce under India's National Programme for Organic Production (NPOP) before selling it as 'organic rice' in supermarkets.

A company in Pune selling 'organic cold-pressed coconut oil' labelled as organic, which must be produced using coconuts grown under certified organic agricultural practices and processed without chemical solvents.

An e-commerce platform like BigBasket listing 'organic turmeric powder' sourced from certified organic farms in Andhra Pradesh — the supplier must hold valid organic certification to sell it as such under FSSAI regulations.

A dairy brand in Gujarat marketing 'organic A2 milk', which requires the cows to be raised under organic livestock standards — fed organic feed, without routine antibiotic or synthetic hormone use — in compliance with prescribed organic production standards.

A tea estate in Darjeeling exporting 'organic Darjeeling tea' must obtain certification under recognised organic standards (such as NPOP or equivalent) and comply with FSSAI's organic food regulations before labelling the product as organic for domestic sale.

A small agri-entrepreneur in Kerala selling organic banana chips at a local market must ensure the bananas were grown under certified organic conditions and that the processing did not involve non-permitted additives, as required under specified organic production standards.
what_it_covers: Food products grown or processed strictly in accordance with prescribed organic production standards, such as certified organic fruits, vegetables, grains, pulses, and dairy products.

Processed food items (e.g., organic flour, organic oils, organic spices) where all constituent ingredients have been produced under certified organic agricultural practices and processed without prohibited substances.
Imported food products labelled as 'organic' that meet the specified organic production standards recognised or notified under Indian food safety regulations.

Any article of food — whether raw, minimally processed, or packaged — that bears an organic claim and has been produced, handled, and certified in accordance with the organic standards prescribed under FSSAI regulations.
what_it_excludes: Food products grown using synthetic chemical pesticides, artificial fertilisers, or prohibited substances, even if the seller informally claims they are 'natural' or 'chemical-free' without certification.
Genetically modified or engineered food products, which are separately governed under Section 22 as 'genetically modified food' and cannot qualify as organic food under the prescribed standards.

Conventional foods that merely use the word 'organic' in branding or marketing without having been produced in accordance with the specified organic production standards — such use would constitute misbranding.

Foods for special dietary uses, functional foods, nutraceuticals, and health supplements, which are separately defined and regulated under Section 22 and do not fall within the organic food category solely by virtue of being plant-based or natural.
definitions.why_it_matters: Any person who manufactures, distributes, sells, or imports food labelled as 'organic' without complying with the specified organic production standards violates Section 22 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, attracting penalties for sub-standard or misbranded food and potential prohibition of the product. The definition determines whether a food business operator must obtain organic certification and comply with the specific labelling and production requirements prescribed by FSSAI regulations before placing such products in the market.

definitions.definition: Packaged food means any food that is enclosed in a package, container, or wrapper in a manner that it is sold to the consumer in a pre-packed form, and which is required to be marked and labelled in the manner specified by regulations under the Food Safety and Standards Act. It includes all food products offered for manufacture, distribution, sale, despatch, or delivery to any agent or broker for the purpose of sale in a packaged condition.
definitions.plain_english: Packaged food refers to any food item that has been put into a sealed or wrapped container before being sold to the customer. Think of biscuits in a sealed packet, bottled water, or a box of breakfast cereal — these are all packaged foods. The key point is that the food is pre-packed and comes with a label before it reaches the buyer. Indian law requires that all such products carry accurate and truthful labels.
real_world_examples: A packet of Parle-G biscuits sold at a kirana store in Mumbai — sealed at the factory and bearing a printed label with manufacturer details, MRP, and expiry date — constitutes packaged food subject to mandatory labelling norms.
A 1-litre Tetra Pak of Amul milk distributed through a cold-chain network to retailers across Gujarat, bearing nutritional information and a batch number, qualifies as packaged food under Section 23.

A branded bag of Aashirvaad atta (wheat flour) sealed and labelled at an ITC manufacturing unit and shipped to distributors in Delhi for retail sale is a packaged food product requiring compliant labelling.

A 500 ml PET bottle of packaged drinking water sold under the brand 'Bisleri' at railway stations across India, bearing ISI mark, batch code, and expiry details, is regulated as packaged food under the FSS Act.

A foil-sealed cup of instant noodles (such as Maggi) dispatched to a food broker in Chennai for further distribution must carry labels as required by FSSAI regulations to qualify for lawful sale as packaged food.

A home-based entrepreneur in Bengaluru who vacuum-seals homemade mango pickle into labelled jars and sells them through an e-commerce platform is manufacturing and selling packaged food subject to Section 23 obligations.

Imported food products arriving in India in consumer-ready sealed packaging, which must comply with FSSAI labelling regulations before being offered for sale.
Food products sold through e-commerce platforms in sealed, labelled packaging, including home-made or artisanal food products sold in pre-packed condition.

Any food enclosed in a wrapper, tin, bottle, pouch, or other container bearing labelling information and distributed through any medium including modern trade, general trade, or direct-to-consumer channels.
what_it_excludes: Loose or unpackaged food sold in bulk by weight or measure at open markets, such as vegetables, grains, or spices sold without any enclosing package or wrapper.
Food prepared and served immediately at restaurants, dhabas, or street food stalls where the food is not pre-packed and is consumed on the premises or shortly after purchase without a sealed label.
Food items packed in the presence of the purchaser at the point of sale in response to a specific customer request, which are not pre-packed or labelled before being presented for sale.

definitions.definition: A packer is a person or entity engaged in the activity of packing an article of food into a package for the purpose of sale, distribution, or supply, and who is liable under this Act for ensuring that such packaged food meets all requirements of the Food Safety and Standards Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: A packer is any person or company that puts food items into packets, boxes, cans, pouches, or other containers and prepares them for sale to consumers or distributors. They are responsible for the safety and quality of the food they pack. If the packed food does not meet legal standards, the packer can be held legally responsible.
real_world_examples: A company in Pune that procures raw cashews from farmers, roasts them, and seals them into branded foil pouches for sale in supermarkets is acting as a packer and is liable if the product is found to be substandard or unsafe.
A Delhi-based firm that sources fresh paneer from a dairy co-operative and repackages it under its own brand name in vacuum-sealed packs for retail distribution is considered a packer under the Act.

A small enterprise in Gujarat that fills and seals glass bottles with homemade pickle and sells them through local grocery stores is functioning as a packer and bears liability for the food safety compliance of those products.

A contract packaging unit in Maharashtra that packs biscuits manufactured by a large FMCG brand into retail cartons bearing the brand's label is acting as a packer and is jointly liable with the manufacturer for ensuring the packed articles meet FSSAI standards.

A spice processing unit in Rajasthan that grinds, blends, and packs various masalas into retail-size sachets for nationwide distribution is a packer and must ensure the packaged product complies with all labelling and safety regulations under the FSSA.
what_it_covers: A company that procures bulk food commodities and packs them into branded retail units for sale in the market.
A contract packaging unit that packs food products on behalf of a manufacturer or brand owner and seals them for commercial distribution.
A small food business operator who prepares and packs homemade or locally produced food items into containers for sale to consumers or retailers.
An entity that repackages imported food articles into smaller retail-sized units under its own label for the Indian market.
A processing unit that packs processed or semi-processed food such as frozen vegetables, canned goods, or ready-to-eat meals for commercial sale.
what_it_excludes: A wholesaler or distributor who merely stores and forwards pre-packed food without opening, repacking, or altering the original packaging.
A retailer who sells food items in their original sealed packaging as received from the manufacturer or distributor without any repacking activity.
A consumer who purchases food in bulk and repacks it at home solely for personal consumption with no intent to sell or distribute.
A food safety officer or government inspector who handles packaged food samples solely for testing and inspection purposes.
A transporter or logistics provider who physically moves sealed packaged food goods from one location to another without engaging in any packing activity.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a person as a 'packer' under Section 27 directly triggers primary liability for any article of food that does not meet the requirements of the FSSA, including standards for safety, labelling, and quality, exposing them to penalties, prosecution, and product recalls. Establishing packer identity is essential in enforcement proceedings to determine the liable party when packaged food is found to be unsafe, substandard, or misbranded.

definitions.definition: A monetary sanction imposed on a person found to have contravened the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, or the rules and regulations made thereunder, the quantum of which is determined by an Adjudicating Officer or the Tribunal having regard to factors such as unfair advantage gained, loss caused, and repetitive nature of the contravention. Penalty is distinct from criminal punishment and operates as a civil liability enforceable under the adjudication mechanism established by this Act.
definitions.plain_english: A penalty under this law is a financial punishment imposed on a food business operator, manufacturer, seller, or officer who breaks the rules related to food safety. Unlike criminal prosecution, a penalty is determined by a designated official (Adjudicating Officer) or a Tribunal and results in the payment of a specified sum of money. The amount depends on how serious the violation was, how much profit was made from it, and whether it happened repeatedly.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based retailer sells adulterated turmeric powder that does not meet prescribed quality standards; the Adjudicating Officer imposes a penalty of up to five lakh rupees under Section 51 for selling sub-standard food.

A Food Safety Officer in Delhi vexatiously seizes stock from a street food vendor without reasonable grounds; the officer is found guilty and liable to a penalty extending to one lakh rupees under Section 39.

A packaged snack manufacturer in Bengaluru labels its product with misleading nutritional claims; the Tribunal, upon adjudication, imposes a monetary penalty after considering the unfair advantage gained and consumer loss caused.

A wholesale distributor in Kolkata is found repeatedly importing food articles that do not comply with FSSAI regulations; the Adjudicating Officer, noting the repetitive nature of the contravention, imposes an enhanced penalty under Section 51.

A petty retailer in a rural area of Maharashtra sells food not matching the nature or substance demanded by the purchaser; owing to their classification under Section 31(2), the penalty is capped at twenty-five thousand rupees under Section 50's proviso.

A complainant files a false complaint against a Food Safety Officer in Chennai, which is proved false in proceedings; the complainant is subjected to a fine (treated as penalty) of not less than fifty thousand rupees and up to one lakh rupees under the proviso to Section 39.
what_it_covers: Monetary sanctions imposed on manufacturers, sellers, distributors, or importers for selling sub-standard, misbranded, or non-compliant food articles.
Financial liability imposed on a Food Safety Officer who vexatiously seizes food articles or acts injuriously without lawful justification under Section 39.
Penalties determined by the Adjudicating Officer or Tribunal based on gain of unfair advantage, loss caused to consumers, and the repetitive or knowing nature of the contravention under Section 49.
Penalties on petty retailers and small food business operators covered under Section 31(2), subject to reduced caps such as twenty-five thousand rupees.
Financial sanction on a complainant who files a false complaint against a Food Safety Officer, proven to be false during proceedings.
what_it_excludes: Criminal punishment including imprisonment, which is governed separately under the offences and prosecution provisions of the Act and is not a 'penalty' in the civil adjudication sense.
Improvement notices or prohibition orders issued by authorities, which are regulatory directions and not monetary penalties.
Compensation payable to injured consumers through civil courts, which falls outside the adjudication penalty mechanism of this Act.
License suspension or cancellation actions taken by the Designated Officer or Commissioner of Food Safety, which are administrative remedies distinct from penalties.
Fines imposed by a Special Court upon criminal conviction, which are part of criminal sentencing and not the civil penalty regime under Chapter IX.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of 'penalty' determines whether a contravention is resolved through the civil adjudication route (before an Adjudicating Officer or Tribunal) or through criminal prosecution, directly affecting the procedural path, burden of proof, and consequences faced by a food business operator or officer. The nature and quantum of penalty also triggers or limits the enforcement powers of the Adjudicating Officer under Sections 49–68 and governs the appellate remedy available to aggrieved parties under Section 96.

definitions.definition: Pesticide residue means any specified substance in or on food, agricultural commodities, or animal feed resulting from the use of a pesticide, including any derivatives such as conversion products, metabolites, reaction products, and impurities considered to be of toxicological significance; no article of food shall contain pesticide residues in excess of such tolerance limit as may be specified by regulations under Section 21 of the Food Safety and Standards Act.
definitions.plain_english: A pesticide residue is the trace amount of a chemical pesticide (or its breakdown products) that remains in or on food after the crop has been treated during farming. Even though pesticides are used to protect crops, leftover amounts in the food we eat must be kept below safe limits set by food safety authorities. If these limits are crossed, the food is considered unsafe and cannot legally be sold.
real_world_examples: A consignment of basmati rice exported from Punjab is found to contain chlorpyrifos residues above the tolerance limit set by FSSAI regulations, leading to rejection at the port and seizure of the batch under Section 21.

Samples of fresh grapes grown in Nashik, Maharashtra are tested at an accredited laboratory and found to have organophosphate pesticide residues exceeding permissible limits, resulting in the food business operator being prosecuted for selling unsafe food.

A Delhi retailer selling imported apples from Himachal Pradesh is served an improvement notice after Food Safety Officers detect lambda-cyhalothrin residues beyond the prescribed maximum residue limit during routine market surveillance.

A packaged leafy vegetable brand in Bengaluru is recalled after FSSAI surveillance detects residues of a banned pesticide, endosulfan, in spinach packets, triggering emergency prohibition orders against the manufacturer.

Tea exported from Assam to the European Union is detained at the destination port because pesticide residue levels, though within Indian tolerance limits, exceed EU maximum residue limits, prompting FSSAI to review its domestic standards.
what_it_covers: Residues of organophosphate, organochlorine, pyrethroid and other classes of pesticides remaining in or on harvested food crops such as rice, wheat, fruits and vegetables.
Metabolites and breakdown products of pesticides that form after application and persist in the food at the time of sale or consumption.
Pesticide residues in processed food articles where the raw agricultural ingredient carried residues that survived manufacturing or processing steps.
Residues of fumigants used on stored grain or food commodities that remain detectable in the final food product above prescribed tolerance limits.

definitions.definition: A petty manufacturer is a person who himself manufactures and sells any article of food, and who, by virtue of the small scale of such activity, is exempt from the requirement to obtain a licence under Section 31(1) but is instead required to register with the appropriate authority; such a person is also eligible for compounding of offences under Section 69 in lieu of prosecution.
definitions.plain_english: A petty manufacturer is a small-scale food maker who personally makes and sells food items directly, rather than running a large or organised food business. Because their operations are small and personal, they do not need a formal licence but must register with the local food safety authority. If they break a rule, they may be allowed to pay a fine instead of facing a full court case.
real_world_examples: A woman in a Mumbai chawl who personally prepares and sells homemade pickles, papads, and chutneys to neighbours and at a local weekly bazaar, with no hired labour involved in manufacturing.
A village artisan in rural Rajasthan who hand-grinds and sells traditional spice blends (masalas) from his home, distributing them at the local haat market without any mechanised production setup.
A person in Kolkata who makes and sells homemade sweets like sandesh or moa from his residence, personally handling the entire production and sale process at a small scale.
A tribal woman in Chhattisgarh who personally collects, processes, and sells minor forest produce-based food items such as mahua-based snacks or tamarind paste directly at a local tribal market.
A small-town baker in Uttar Pradesh who bakes bread and snacks in a home kitchen and personally sells them door-to-door or at a small self-operated counter without any formal factory setup.
what_it_covers: An individual who personally and directly manufactures food articles and also personally sells them without employing a separate manufacturing unit or workforce at a commercial scale.
A home-based food producer such as a pickle maker, papad maker, or traditional sweet maker who handles the entire production-to-sale chain themselves at a tiny scale.
A person eligible to compound (settle by payment) any non-imprisonable offence under the Food Safety and Standards Act instead of facing full prosecution, as permitted under Section 69.
Any such small food maker who is required to register with the designated authority under regulations instead of obtaining a formal food business licence under Section 31.
what_it_excludes: A manufacturer who employs workers or operates a mechanised or semi-automated production facility, even if the output volume is small, as the personal manufacturing element would be absent.
A food business operator who manufactures food but sells through distributors, wholesalers, or retailers rather than personally selling the articles of food themselves.
A petty retailer, hawker, itinerant vendor, or temporary stall holder who only sells food manufactured by others and does not personally manufacture any article of food.
A medium or large-scale food manufacturer who must obtain a formal licence under Section 31(1) and does not qualify for the registration-only exemption applicable to petty manufacturers.
A company, firm, or any legal entity (as opposed to a natural person) engaged in food manufacturing, since the definition requires the person himself to manufacture and sell.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a petty manufacturer determines whether they must obtain a formal food business licence under Section 31(1) or merely register under the lighter regulatory regime, significantly reducing their compliance burden. Additionally, under Section 69, petty manufacturer status makes them eligible for compounding of non-imprisonable offences, allowing monetary settlement instead of criminal prosecution.

definitions.definition: A petty retailer is a small-scale seller of food articles who is exempt from the requirement of obtaining a licence under Section 31(1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, but is mandatorily required to register with the designated authority in the prescribed manner; the term refers to a retail food vendor operating at a minor or limited commercial scale, as distinguished from a licensed food business operator.
definitions.plain_english: A petty retailer is a small food seller who operates at a very small scale — like a local kirana shop owner or a small provisions store — and does not need a formal food business licence. However, they must still register with the food safety authority. They are allowed to sell food but must ensure what they sell is safe and wholesome for consumers.
real_world_examples: A small kirana (grocery) shop owner in a rural village in Uttar Pradesh who sells packaged biscuits, loose grains, and spices from a single-room shop without employing any staff.
A corner paan-bidi shop in Mumbai that also sells packaged namkeen, toffees, and cold drinks to neighbourhood customers on a retail basis.
A small provisions store in a Chennai residential colony run by a single person selling everyday food items like rice, dal, oil, and packaged snacks to local households.
A tiny neighbourhood dairy booth in Jaipur operated by one person selling milk pouches, curd, and butter to regular local customers each morning.
A small general store in a Bihar town that retails biscuits, noodles, bottled water, and other packaged food products without any manufacturing or processing activity on-site.
what_it_covers: A small kirana or general provisions store owner who retails packaged or loose food items at a neighbourhood level without large-scale operations.
An individual operating a tiny retail food outlet from a fixed premises with minimal turnover and no manufacturing activity, who sells directly to end consumers.
A small retail seller of food articles who does not employ staff at scale and operates within a limited local area, meeting the threshold criteria for petty status as prescribed by regulations.

Any retail food vendor whose scale of operations qualifies as petty under the Food Safety and Standards (Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations, such as those with annual turnover below the prescribed limit.
what_it_excludes: A licensed food business operator who manufactures, processes, or packages food articles for retail sale, as such entities require a full licence under Section 31(1).

A hawker, itinerant vendor, or temporary stall holder, who are separately categorised under Section 31(2) and are distinct from a petty retailer even though they share the registration (not licensing) requirement.
A petty manufacturer who manufactures food articles himself for sale, as such a person falls under the separate category of 'petty manufacturer' under Section 31(2).
A wholesaler or distributor of food articles, who operates at a scale and in a capacity that is beyond mere retail selling to end consumers and would typically require a licence.
Any food business operator whose annual turnover or scale of operation exceeds the threshold prescribed by regulations for classification as a petty retailer.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a petty retailer determines whether they need a formal food business licence or merely a registration — failure to obtain the required licence by a non-petty operator is an offence under the Act, whereas a petty retailer only commits a violation if they fail to register. This distinction also affects the scope of inspections, penalties, and improvement notices applicable to the operator.

definitions.definition: "premises" includes any shop, stall, food vehicle, vessel, aircraft, or place where any food business is carried on, and any place where any article of food is manufactured, stored, exposed or offered for sale, or used in the manufacture of any article of food intended for sale.
definitions.plain_english: Premises refers to any physical location or structure where food is made, stored, sold, or served as part of a food business. This can be a shop, factory, warehouse, vehicle, stall, vessel, or even an aircraft. Essentially, any place connected to food-related commercial activity falls under this term.
real_world_examples: A dal mill in Kanpur where pulses are cleaned, processed and packaged for sale to wholesalers — the mill building and its storage area together constitute 'premises' under the Act.
A dhaba on a National Highway in Haryana where food is cooked and served to travellers is considered 'premises', making it subject to licensing, inspection and hygiene standards under the Act.
A cold storage facility in Pune that stores frozen meat and dairy products on behalf of multiple food businesses qualifies as 'premises', liable to inspection by Food Safety Officers.

A mobile food van operating in Bengaluru selling street food such as dosas and chaat from a converted vehicle is treated as 'premises', requiring registration or licensing and compliance with food safety norms.
A wholesale warehouse in Mumbai's APMC market that stores packaged food products pending distribution to retailers is covered under 'premises', subject to storage hygiene and labelling compliance.

An airline catering unit at Indira Gandhi International Airport, Delhi that prepares in-flight meals constitutes 'premises' under the Act and must comply with Food Safety Management System requirements.
what_it_covers: A licensed food factory or manufacturing plant where packaged food products are produced.
A retail shop, supermarket, or grocery store where food articles are displayed and sold to consumers.
A food storage warehouse or cold storage unit used to hold food products before distribution.
A roadside stall or temporary market kiosk selling cooked or raw food items.
A vehicle such as a food van, refrigerated truck, or vessel used to sell or transport food for commercial purposes.
An airline or railway catering kitchen preparing food for service on board.
what_it_excludes: A private household kitchen where food is prepared solely for personal or family consumption and not for any commercial purpose.
Agricultural land or crop fields where food is grown but not yet harvested, as primary food prior to harvesting is excluded from the Act's definition of food.
A pharmaceutical manufacturing facility that produces drugs or medicinal products, even if such products may contain food-like substances, since drugs are expressly excluded from the Act.
A cosmetics production unit manufacturing items that may contain food-grade ingredients but are not intended for human consumption as food.
A veterinary feed production facility producing animal feed not intended for human consumption.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a location as 'premises' directly triggers the obligations of licensing or registration under Section 31, the power of Food Safety Officers to enter, inspect, search, and seize under Sections 37 and 38, and the issuance of improvement notices or prohibition orders under Sections 32 and 33. Failure to maintain compliant premises can result in penalties, cancellation of licence, and prosecution of the food business operator.

definitions.definition: The Presiding Officer of the Tribunal means the sole member constituting the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal, appointed by notification by the Central Government or the State Government, as the case may be, who must be or have been a District Judge, and who is vested with the jurisdiction and powers to hear and decide appeals from decisions of the Adjudicating Officer under section 68.
definitions.plain_english: The Presiding Officer is the single judicial authority who heads the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal. This person must be a current or former District Judge appointed by the government. Their job is to hear and decide appeals filed by food business operators or others who are unhappy with the punishment or order given by the Adjudicating Officer.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based food manufacturer penalised by the Adjudicating Officer for selling sub-standard packaged spices files an appeal before the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal; the Presiding Officer, a retired District Judge appointed by the Central Government, hears the case and decides whether to uphold or overturn the penalty.

A Mumbai street food vendor whose licence was cancelled by the Adjudicating Officer challenges the order before the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal in Maharashtra; the Presiding Officer appointed by the State Government conducts proceedings and passes a fresh order.

A large dairy company in Punjab disputes a heavy monetary penalty imposed for use of adulterants; the company files an appeal before the Tribunal, where the Presiding Officer examines evidence, hears arguments, and either modifies or confirms the Adjudicating Officer's decision.

A Tamil Nadu-based restaurant chain contests an emergency prohibition order that effectively shut down its operations; the Presiding Officer of the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal constituted by the State Government adjudicates the appeal and has the power to stay the original order pending final decision.

A small-scale food processor in Rajasthan who was fined for misbranding of organic food products approaches the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal; the Presiding Officer, exercising jurisdiction prescribed by the State Government, reviews procedural compliance and the merits of the original order before ruling.
what_it_covers: A sitting or retired District Judge appointed by notification by the Central Government or State Government to head the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal.
The sole person constituting the Tribunal who is authorised to hear appeals against decisions of the Adjudicating Officer under section 68 of the Act.
A Presiding Officer whose qualifications, salary, allowances, term of office, resignation, and removal are governed by rules prescribed by the Central Government.
A Presiding Officer who exercises jurisdiction over matters and areas as prescribed by the Central Government or State Government in the relevant notification establishing the Tribunal.
what_it_excludes: The Adjudicating Officer appointed under section 68, who is a separate authority responsible for conducting original proceedings and imposing penalties at the first instance.
Members of the Food Authority, including the Chairperson or ex officio Members, who perform regulatory and policy functions and are not empowered to hear appellate matters under section 70.
Any judicial officer below the rank of District Judge, or an officer who has never held the position of District Judge, who is statutorily disqualified from appointment as Presiding Officer.
A Food Safety Officer or Commissioner of Food Safety, who are enforcement and regulatory officials without appellate adjudicatory powers under the Tribunal framework.
Any person appointed to a multi-member appellate body, since the Tribunal under section 70 consists of one person only, making a multi-member bench configuration expressly outside this definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity and valid appointment of the Presiding Officer is a jurisdictional prerequisite for the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal to exercise appellate powers; any appeal decided by a person not duly appointed or not qualifying as a District Judge would be void and without legal effect. The Presiding Officer's decisions determine whether penalties, licence cancellations, or prohibition orders imposed by the Adjudicating Officer are upheld, modified, or set aside, directly affecting the rights and liabilities of food business operators.

definitions.definition: 'primary food' means any fresh food product which has not been processed in any manner except being cleaned, chilled, trimmed, sorted or graded, and includes fresh fruits and vegetables, fresh fish, fresh poultry, fresh meat and fresh eggs, but does not include any processed, partially processed or manufactured food product.
definitions.plain_english: Primary food refers to natural, raw food items that have not been cooked, chemically treated, or significantly altered from their original state. Basic handling steps like washing, chilling, cutting, or sorting are allowed without disqualifying a food from being 'primary food'. Examples include fresh tomatoes from a farm, raw chicken at a butcher, or freshly caught fish at a market.
real_world_examples: A farmer selling freshly harvested spinach and tomatoes at a local mandi in Pune — these vegetables are washed and sorted but not cooked or chemically treated, so they qualify as primary food.
A fisherman landing freshly caught pomfret at the Sassoon Docks in Mumbai and selling them directly to retailers — the fish are iced and sorted but otherwise unprocessed, making them primary food.
A poultry farm in Namakkal, Tamil Nadu supplying freshly slaughtered broiler chickens that are cleaned and chilled but not frozen or marinated — these qualify as primary food.

A dairy farmer in Anand, Gujarat selling raw, unprocessed milk directly collected from cows, which has only been chilled and filtered — this constitutes primary food before it enters any pasteurisation process.
A fruit vendor at Azadpur Mandi in Delhi selling freshly graded and sorted alphonso mangoes that have undergone no chemical ripening or processing — these are considered primary food under the Act.
what_it_covers: Fresh fruits and vegetables that have only been washed, sorted, graded, or chilled before sale, such as freshly harvested onions at a wholesale market.
Raw meat, poultry, and fish products that have been cleaned and chilled but not marinated, smoked, or otherwise processed.
Freshly laid eggs sold in their natural state, subject only to basic sorting and cleaning.
Raw, unprocessed milk freshly collected from cattle or buffaloes before pasteurisation or homogenisation.
Freshly harvested grains or pulses that have been cleaned and sorted but not milled, ground, or otherwise transformed.
what_it_excludes: Frozen or preserved food products, such as frozen peas or canned tomatoes, which have undergone processing beyond basic cleaning or chilling.
Pasteurised or homogenised milk, since these involve heat treatment that goes beyond the permitted minimal handling for primary food.
Marinated, smoked, pickled, or cured meat and fish products, as these involve added substances or chemical/physical transformation.
Packaged cut fruits or vegetables treated with preservatives or modified atmosphere packaging for extended shelf life.
Flour, refined oil, or any other food product derived from milling, grinding, or extraction of primary raw materials.

definitions.definition: A 'processing aid' means any substance not consumed as a food ingredient by itself, intentionally used in the processing of raw materials, foods or their ingredients to fulfil a certain technological purpose during treatment or processing, and which may result in the unintentional but technically unavoidable presence of residues of the substance or its derivatives in the final product, provided such residues do not present any health risk and do not have any technological effect on the finished food.
definitions.plain_english: A processing aid is a substance used during the manufacturing or processing of food to help the process work correctly, but it is not meant to remain in the final product as an ingredient. It serves a technical function during production — like helping filter, clarify, or stabilise the food — and may leave only tiny, harmless traces in the end product. It is different from a food additive because it is not intentionally added to the final food for any lasting effect.
real_world_examples: Hexane used as a solvent to extract edible oil from oilseeds such as groundnut or soybean in Indian oil mills — the hexane is removed after extraction but trace residues may remain in the final cooking oil.
Bentonite clay or activated charcoal used to clarify and filter fruit juices or wine during processing in Indian beverage factories, which is subsequently removed before bottling.
Enzyme preparations such as papain derived from papaya used in Indian meat processing plants to tenderise meat during production, which become inactive and do not function in the final product.

Carbon dioxide or nitrogen gas used during the processing and packaging of packaged snacks and namkeen products in Indian food plants to flush out oxygen and prevent oxidation, serving only a processing function.

Fuller's earth or activated bleaching earth used to decolourise and refine crude edible oils such as palm oil or vanaspati in Indian refineries, which is filtered out before the finished oil reaches consumers.

Dilute food-grade hydrochloric acid used to adjust pH during the manufacture of glucose syrup or corn starch in Indian starch factories, subsequently neutralised and not present as an active substance in the final product.
what_it_covers: Solvents such as hexane used in the extraction of edible oils from oilseeds where traces may remain in the final oil product.

Filtering and clarifying agents such as bentonite, diatomaceous earth, or activated carbon used during juice, wine, or edible oil processing that are physically removed before the final product is sold.
Enzyme preparations used during food manufacturing to perform a specific function such as hydrolysis, tenderisation, or starch conversion, which are inactivated or removed in the final product.
Acids or alkalis used for pH adjustment during processing of starch, glucose syrup, or other food ingredients, subsequently neutralised so they have no technological effect in the final food.
Anti-foaming agents used in frying oil processing or sugar refining operations in Indian food factories where the agent itself does not become part of the finished food.
what_it_excludes: Food additives that are intentionally present and functional in the final food product, such as preservatives, colours, or emulsifiers that perform a technological function in the finished food.

Food ingredients or components that are deliberately incorporated into the final food formulation and are consumed as part of the food, such as spices, flavourings added for taste, or nutritional supplements.

Pesticide residues, veterinary drug residues, or environmental contaminants that enter the food supply unintentionally through agricultural or environmental pathways and are not used for any processing function.
Packaging materials or substances in contact with food that may migrate into the food but serve a containment or preservation function rather than a direct processing function.

Any substance that, even if used during processing, remains present in the final food at levels sufficient to perform a detectable technological function in the finished product, as such a substance would be classified as a food additive rather than a processing aid.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a 'processing aid' under the Food Safety and Standards Act determines whether it is subject to the permissible limits and labelling requirements applicable to food additives under Section 16 regulations, or whether it falls under the separate and distinct regulatory limits for processing aids; misclassification can expose a food business operator to liability for using an unauthorised additive, sub-standard food offences, or violations of the limits prescribed by the Food Authority under Section 16(2)(b), potentially resulting in penalties, product recall, or licence cancellation under the Act.

definitions.definition: A 'prohibition order' means an order issued under section 33 of this Act by a court, upon conviction of a food business operator for a food safety offence, prohibiting the use of a food business, any process or treatment, or any equipment used in the food business, where the court is satisfied that there is a risk of injury to health if the business, process, treatment, or equipment is used.
definitions.plain_english: A prohibition order is a formal court order that stops a food business or specific activities within it from continuing to operate, because they pose a danger to public health. It is issued after a food business operator has been found guilty of a food safety violation. The order can ban the use of a particular premises, equipment, process, or the entire food business until the health risk is addressed and the ban is officially lifted.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based packaged snacks manufacturer is convicted for repeatedly using unsafe artificial colouring agents banned under FSSAI regulations; the court issues a prohibition order barring the use of the factory's mixing and packaging equipment until safety compliance is established.

A Delhi restaurant is found guilty of causing a food poisoning outbreak due to severely unhygienic kitchen conditions; the magistrate issues a prohibition order shutting down the kitchen premises entirely to prevent further injury to consumers.

A Chennai cold storage facility operator is convicted for storing dairy products at temperatures that render them unsafe; a prohibition order is issued prohibiting use of the defective refrigeration equipment in the food storage business.

A Kolkata street food processing unit is convicted for using adulterated edible oil in large-scale production; the court issues a prohibition order against the specific cooking process and frying equipment identified as the source of the health risk.

A licensed water bottling plant in Hyderabad is convicted following detection of harmful contaminants in its packaged drinking water; a prohibition order is issued against the entire bottling and filtration process until the plant meets prescribed safety standards.
what_it_covers: An order prohibiting the use of the entire premises of a food business where health risk conditions are found after conviction of the operator.
An order prohibiting the use of specific equipment, machinery, or tools used in the manufacture or processing of food that pose a risk of injury to health.
An order prohibiting the continuation of a particular food processing, preparation, or treatment method that has been identified as causing or capable of causing injury to consumers.
Situations where a food business operator has been convicted of an offence under the Act and the court is satisfied that ongoing operations would cause a health risk to the public.
what_it_excludes: An improvement notice issued under section 32, which is an administrative pre-conviction directive to rectify conditions rather than a court-ordered prohibition.
An emergency prohibition notice or emergency prohibition order issued by the Commissioner of Food Safety or a designated officer acting on urgent public health grounds without a prior conviction.
Voluntary suspension or closure of a food business by the food business operator without any court proceedings or conviction.
Licence cancellation or suspension by the food authority as an administrative action independent of a court conviction under the penal provisions of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The issuance of a prohibition order under section 33 directly prevents a convicted food business operator from legally continuing the prohibited activity, process, or use of equipment, and any violation of such an order constitutes a further criminal offence attracting additional penalties under the Act. It determines whether a food business can continue operations and triggers obligations on the operator to demonstrate rectification of health risks before the order can be lifted.

definitions.definition: "Proprietary and novel food" means an article of food for which standards have not been specified but is not unsafe: Provided that such food does not contain any of the foods and ingredients prohibited under this Act and the regulations made thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: Proprietary food refers to a food product that does not yet have officially prescribed standards under Indian food law, but is safe to consume and does not contain any banned ingredients or substances. These are typically unique or innovative food products created by a manufacturer that fall outside existing standard food categories. They are permitted to be manufactured and sold, but only if they meet safety requirements and avoid prohibited contents.
real_world_examples: A Bengaluru-based startup launches a novel protein bar combining moringa, quinoa, and ashwagandha in a unique formulation for which no FSSAI standard currently exists — this product qualifies as a proprietary food and must comply with Section 22 regulations.

A Mumbai dairy company introduces a flavoured probiotic drink blended with regional spices that does not match any existing standardised dairy product category under FSSAI regulations, requiring it to be registered and sold as a proprietary food.

A Delhi food company markets a ready-to-eat fusion meal combining traditional Indian dal with imported grains in proportions and formulations not covered by any existing FSSAI product standard, making it a proprietary food subject to special approval.

A Pune-based nutraceutical company creates a chewable tablet-like food product containing tulsi extract and vitamin C at novel concentrations not covered under existing standards — it is categorised as a proprietary food under Section 22.

A Kerala coconut oil brand launches a cold-pressed, blended edible oil combining coconut oil with MCT fractions in ratios for which no compositional standard exists under FSSAI, thereby classifying it as proprietary food requiring prior FSSAI product approval.
what_it_covers: Unique food products manufactured in India for which FSSAI has not yet prescribed compositional or quality standards, provided they are safe and free from prohibited ingredients.
Imported food articles that do not correspond to any existing standardised food category under Indian food regulations but are otherwise safe for consumption.
Newly developed food formulations by food business operators that combine ingredients in novel ways not recognised under any current FSSAI product standard.
Fusion or hybrid food products blending traditional and modern ingredients in proportions or combinations not specified under existing regulations.
what_it_excludes: Food products for which FSSAI has already prescribed specific compositional, quality, or safety standards — those are governed by the applicable standard and not treated as proprietary food.
Food articles that are 'unsafe' as defined under the Act, i.e., those injurious to health, even if no standard exists for them — such products cannot qualify as proprietary food.
Any food or ingredient that is explicitly prohibited under the FSS Act or regulations made thereunder, regardless of whether a standard exists for the overall product.
Drugs, ayurvedic, siddha, or unani medicines, narcotic drugs, or psychotropic substances, which are excluded from the food category altogether under the Act.
Genetically modified food, organic food, irradiated food, and functional foods/nutraceuticals, which are separately defined and regulated under the same Section 22.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a product qualifies as proprietary food determines whether a food business operator must seek specific prior approval or product registration under Section 22 before manufacturing, distributing, selling, or importing it; failure to obtain such approval constitutes a contravention of the Act, attracting penalties and possible prosecution. It also defines the boundary between lawful innovation in food products and regulated or prohibited food categories.

definitions.definition: The term 'public interest' is not formally defined in the Act but is used to denote the collective welfare and safety of the general public that the Union seeks to protect through regulation of the food industry. In the context of Section 8, it refers to the standard against which the conduct of a Member of the Food Authority is measured, such that continuance in office of a Member who has abused their position to the detriment of that collective welfare renders their removal justified.
definitions.plain_english: Public interest means the overall well-being and safety of ordinary people in India, particularly consumers of food products. When a senior official like a Member of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) misuses their position in a way that harms this collective good, the government can remove them from office. Essentially, it is a standard to ensure that those in power act for the benefit of everyone, not for personal or private gain.
real_world_examples: A Member of FSSAI who secretly accepts bribes from a large food manufacturer to overlook safety violations in that company's products is found to have abused their position prejudicial to public interest, enabling the Central Government to remove them under Section 8.

An FSSAI Member who leaks confidential regulatory inspection schedules to a food business operator, allowing them to hide adulterants before inspections, thereby endangering consumers across multiple states, would be acting against public interest and subject to removal.

The Central Government invokes public interest under Section 2 to justify Union-level control over food standards, preventing a patchwork of conflicting state-level food regulations that could compromise consumer safety across India.

A State Government, finding that a cluster of food poisoning deaths is linked to a particular food manufacturer, invokes public interest under Section 74 to constitute a Special Court to expeditiously try the offences involving grievous injury and death of consumers.

An FSSAI Chairperson who systematically delays enforcement actions against pesticide-contaminated food products due to undisclosed financial interests in the agro-chemical sector is deemed to be acting in a manner prejudicial to public interest, triggering removal proceedings.
what_it_covers: Conduct of an FSSAI Member that undermines consumer food safety through abuse of their regulatory position, justifying removal from office.
The constitutional and legislative rationale for Union control over the food industry to ensure uniform safety standards benefiting all citizens.
Situations where expedient constitution of Special Courts is warranted to protect consumers from grievous injury or death caused by food offences.
what_it_excludes: Private or personal interests of individual food business operators, even if their business is lawful and economically significant.
The commercial interest of a specific industry lobby or trade association in avoiding regulatory oversight, which does not constitute public interest.

Minor procedural irregularities or administrative inefficiencies by a Member that do not materially harm consumer welfare or regulatory integrity, and thus do not rise to the level of being prejudicial to public interest.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a Member's conduct is found to be prejudicial to public interest directly determines whether the Central Government has the legal authority to remove them from the Food Authority under Section 8(1)(e); without this finding, the removal would be legally invalid and challengeable. It also underpins the Union's jurisdiction to regulate the entire food industry under Section 2 and enables constitution of Special Courts under Section 74 for expeditious consumer protection.

definitions.definition: A Public Prosecutor, for the purposes of this Act, is a person appointed by the Central Government or the State Government for every Special Court constituted under Section 74, to conduct prosecution of offences relating to grievous injury or death of a consumer, and must have been in practice as an Advocate for not less than seven years or have held a post requiring special knowledge of law for a period of not less than seven years under the Union or a State.
definitions.plain_english: A Public Prosecutor is a legally qualified government-appointed lawyer who represents the state in criminal cases before a Special Court set up under the Food Safety and Standards Act. They handle prosecutions for serious food safety offences that have caused severe harm or death to consumers. To be eligible, the person must have at least seven years of experience as a lawyer or in a government role requiring legal expertise.
real_world_examples: In Mumbai, after a mass food poisoning incident at a mid-day meal scheme kills three children, the Maharashtra Government appoints a senior advocate with over ten years of practice as the Public Prosecutor to present the case before the Special Court constituted under Section 74 of the FSSA.

The Central Government appoints a Public Prosecutor for a Special Court in Delhi to prosecute a large food manufacturer whose adulterated baby food caused the grievous injury of multiple infants, resulting in long-term neurological damage.

Following deaths linked to contaminated packaged drinking water sold across several states, the State Government of Uttar Pradesh designates a Public Prosecutor to conduct trials in the Special Court formed to handle the inter-district food safety offence cases.

A Special Court in Chennai, on an application made by the appointed Public Prosecutor, shifts its sitting location from its ordinary court premises to a venue closer to the affected district to facilitate witnesses in a case involving mass hospitalisation due to toxic street food.

The Central Government appoints a Special Public Prosecutor specifically for a high-profile case involving a multinational food company accused of selling pesticide-laced spices that caused deaths, as the complexity of the case demands a prosecutor with specialised food law knowledge.
what_it_covers: A person appointed by the Central or State Government with at least seven years of practice as an Advocate to prosecute food safety offences before a Special Court.
A person who has held a government post for not less than seven years requiring special knowledge of law, appointed to conduct prosecution under Section 74.
Additional Public Prosecutors appointed alongside the primary Public Prosecutor to assist in prosecutions before a Special Court.
A Special Public Prosecutor appointed for a specific case or class of cases involving grievous injury or death of a consumer under the FSSA.

definitions.definition: The Members, officers of the Food Authority and the Commissioners of Food Safety and their officers shall be deemed, when acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of this Act, to be public servants within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860).
definitions.plain_english: Certain officials under the Food Safety and Standards Act — including members and officers of the Food Authority and Commissioners of Food Safety along with their staff — are treated as government public servants under the Indian Penal Code. This means they get the legal protections given to public servants, and anyone who obstructs, bribes, or acts against them faces serious criminal consequences. This status applies only when they are carrying out duties under this Act.
real_world_examples: A Food Safety Officer (FSO) conducting a surprise inspection at a Mumbai bakery is deemed a public servant; if the bakery owner physically obstructs or threatens the FSO, the owner can be prosecuted under IPC Section 353 for assault on a public servant.

A member of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) sitting on a regulatory panel in New Delhi is offered a bribe by a food manufacturer to approve a substandard product; the briber can be charged under the Prevention of Corruption Act as the FSSAI member is a public servant.

A Commissioner of Food Safety in Tamil Nadu issues an emergency prohibition order against a chilli powder unit found using artificial colouring; if a company director tries to intimidate or coerce the Commissioner, it amounts to criminal intimidation of a public servant under the IPC.

An officer of the Food Authority deputed to collect samples from a spice market in Khari Baoli, Delhi is falsely accused of misconduct; because such an officer is deemed a public servant, the false complaint itself could attract liability under IPC Section 182 for giving false information to a public servant.

A Designated Officer in Karnataka seizes a consignment of adulterated ghee; if the transporter destroys evidence to mislead the officer, he can be prosecuted for causing disappearance of evidence with intent to screen an offender from justice, as the officer is protected under public servant provisions.
what_it_covers: Members of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) acting in pursuance of the Act
Officers of the Food Authority, including the Chief Executive Officer and Food Safety Officers, while discharging official duties under the Act
Commissioners of Food Safety and their subordinate officers in every State and Union Territory when acting under provisions of the Act
Any person purporting to act under the Act's provisions in an official capacity within the Food Authority or Commissioner's office
what_it_excludes: Private food safety auditors and accredited laboratory personnel who are not officers of the Food Authority or Commissioner of Food Safety
Food business operators, manufacturers, or importers even if they hold government licences, as they are regulated parties, not enforcement officers
Members of the Scientific Committee or Scientific Panels when acting outside the specific enforcement or regulatory functions governed by this Act
Employees of State food testing laboratories who are not officers of the Commissioner of Food Safety or the Food Authority
Legal practitioners or Presiding Officers of Tribunals adjudicating food safety disputes, as they derive their public servant status from other laws
definitions.why_it_matters: This deeming provision ensures that any offence committed against FSSAI members and food safety officials — including bribery, obstruction, assault, or intimidation — attracts the full criminal penalties applicable to offences against public servants under the Indian Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act. Conversely, these officials also bear the duties and accountability of public servants, making them liable for misconduct, abuse of power, or dereliction of duty under those same laws.

definitions.definition: "Purchaser" is not formally defined in the Act, but as used in Section 50, it refers to any person who buys or obtains an article of food from a food business operator, seller, or any person engaged in the sale of food, for the purpose of having it analysed or tested, or in the ordinary course of trade or personal consumption.
definitions.plain_english: A purchaser is simply someone who buys food — whether to eat it, to get it tested for safety, or as part of a business transaction. Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, this includes people who buy food from shops, vendors, or manufacturers. The term is especially relevant when a Food Safety Officer or authorised person buys a food sample to check if it meets legal standards.
real_world_examples: A Food Safety Officer in Mumbai purchases a packet of spices from a local grocery store to send for testing at an accredited laboratory to check for adulteration.
A housewife in Delhi buys packaged paneer from a supermarket and later reports it to the food safety authority after finding it to be sub-standard — she is considered a purchaser.
A restaurant owner in Chennai purchases bulk edible oil from a wholesaler for use in cooking; as a purchaser in a commercial transaction, they can be subject to scrutiny under the Act.
An authorised officer in Kolkata buys a sample of street food from an itinerant vendor under Section 50 to test it for unsafe ingredients, acting in the capacity of a purchaser for official purposes.

A consumer in Bengaluru purchases a bottled fruit drink from a retail outlet, and upon finding foreign matter inside, lodges a complaint with the Commissioner of Food Safety, exercising rights as a purchaser.
what_it_covers: A Food Safety Officer who buys a food article from a seller or food business operator for the purpose of obtaining a sample for analysis under Section 50.
An ordinary consumer who purchases packaged or unpackaged food from a retail outlet, vendor, or manufacturer for personal consumption.
A food business operator who purchases raw materials or food ingredients from another operator or supplier in the course of trade.
An authorised officer or third-party individual buying food on behalf of a regulatory body to verify compliance with food safety standards.
A person who obtains food through a commercial transaction, whether in a market, supermarket, hawker stall, or online platform.
what_it_excludes: A person who receives food as a gift or donation without any commercial transaction — such individuals are not purchasers in the legal sense under this Act.
A food business operator's employee who handles food internally within the manufacturing or processing unit without buying it.
A Food Safety Officer who seizes food under an official order without conducting a purchase transaction — seizure is distinct from purchase.
A person who merely inspects or examines food without completing a buying transaction.
Animals or non-human entities that consume food, as the Act is confined to human transactions and consumption.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity of a 'purchaser' is critical under Section 50 because it determines the legitimacy of a food sample collected for analysis — only a lawful purchase by an authorised person or officer gives evidentiary standing to the sample in proceedings for offences such as selling adulterated, sub-standard, or unsafe food. If the purchaser is an authorised Food Safety Officer, the sample can be used as evidence to initiate prosecution or penalty proceedings against the food business operator.

definitions.definition: Though not expressly defined in Section 3 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, 'quality' as used in Section 50 refers to the compositional, physical, chemical, microbiological, and organoleptic characteristics of a food article that determine its grade, purity, and conformity to prescribed standards, distinguishing it from safety-related attributes; it encompasses attributes such as nutritional content, texture, appearance, taste, and other specifications laid down by the Food Authority.
definitions.plain_english: Quality refers to the overall standard of a food product — including its ingredients, taste, texture, nutritional value, and composition — as measured against official benchmarks set by food regulators. It is distinct from food safety, which is about whether food can harm you. Quality is about whether a food product is as good as it is supposed to be — whether it meets the promised or prescribed specifications. For example, a juice labelled '100% fruit content' must actually have that level of fruit content to meet quality standards.
real_world_examples: A packet of Amul butter sold in Mumbai is tested and found to contain less fat content than the minimum percentage prescribed under FSSAI regulations — this is a quality violation as the product does not meet compositional standards.

A bag of basmati rice sold in Delhi is found to contain a significant proportion of non-basmati rice grains mixed in — the product fails to meet the quality standard for basmati rice specified by the Food Authority.

A manufacturer in Pune produces bottled fruit juice labelled as containing 85% fruit pulp, but laboratory analysis reveals only 40% pulp content — this constitutes a quality deficiency under Section 50 as the product is sub-standard.

A dal (lentil) packet sold in Chennai is found to have excessive moisture content beyond the permitted limit, causing faster spoilage and fungal growth — even if not immediately harmful, this represents a failure to meet prescribed quality parameters.

A honey brand sold across India is found to contain added sugar syrups reducing its natural purity below the prescribed threshold — a quality non-compliance triggering regulatory action under Section 50.

Packaged cow's milk sold in Kolkata is tested and found to have a lower fat percentage than the FSSAI-mandated minimum for full-cream milk — the product is sub-standard in quality though not necessarily unsafe.
what_it_covers: Compositional attributes of food such as fat content, moisture content, protein percentage, and purity that must meet FSSAI-prescribed standards.
Organoleptic properties like taste, smell, colour, and texture that are benchmarked against notified quality specifications for each food category.
Microbiological parameters such as permitted bacterial counts and absence of specified pathogens that define the quality grade of a food product.
Nutritional characteristics including vitamin, mineral, and caloric content that must align with declared or regulated values on food labels.
Physical attributes such as the proportion of genuine ingredients (e.g., fruit pulp in juice, cocoa in chocolate) as specified under applicable food standards.
what_it_excludes: Safety-related attributes that cause acute harm to consumers — these fall under 'unsafe food' and 'food safety' provisions rather than quality provisions.
Packaging or labelling deficiencies that misrepresent the product — these are governed separately under 'misbranded food' provisions of the Act.
Extraneous matter present in food that does not affect the compositional quality but is carried from raw materials or processing — addressed separately under the definition of 'extraneous matter'.
Adulterants deliberately added to food to make it unsafe — these are covered under 'adulterant' and 'unsafe food' definitions rather than quality standards.
Cosmetic products and medicinal/drug substances that are excluded from the definition of 'food' entirely and hence from food quality regulation under this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a food article meets the prescribed 'quality' standard determines if it constitutes 'sub-standard food' under the Act, which attracts a penalty of up to five lakh rupees under Section 51; a food business operator found repeatedly selling sub-standard food may also face suspension or cancellation of licence, and the term directly governs the scope of inspections, sampling, and enforcement actions under Section 50.

definitions.definition: A referral food laboratory is a laboratory established or recognised by the Food Authority by notification, to which appeals against the report of a Food Analyst may be referred for opinion by the Designated Officer, and which carries out such other functions as are entrusted to it under the Food Safety and Standards Act or any rules and regulations made thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: A referral food laboratory is a specially designated, high-authority testing lab that the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) officially sets up or recognises to act as a second-level checker. When someone disagrees with the result of a food test done by a Food Analyst, the case can be sent to this lab for a final, more authoritative opinion. It serves as a superior laboratory for settling disputes about food safety test results.
real_world_examples: A spice manufacturer in Rajasthan whose turmeric sample is declared adulterated by the local Food Analyst challenges the report before the Designated Officer, who then refers the second part of the sample to the notified referral food laboratory in Delhi for an independent opinion.

A milk processing dairy in Punjab disputes the Food Analyst's finding that their packaged milk contains excess adulterants; the Designated Officer sends the retained sample to the referral food laboratory at National Dairy Research Institute, Karnal, as notified by FSSAI.

A food business operator in Mumbai whose imported olive oil fails a food analyst's test for purity appeals the result, leading the Designated Officer to forward the matter to the referral food laboratory for a binding re-analysis before any enforcement action is finalised.

A small snack manufacturer in Hyderabad contests a Food Analyst's report claiming excessive artificial colouring in their product; the designated referral food laboratory conducts fresh analysis, and its findings are used to determine whether prosecution should proceed.

FSSAI notifies the Central Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI), Mysuru, as a referral food laboratory for certain categories of processed food, enabling it to receive and analyse disputed samples sent by Designated Officers across southern states.
what_it_covers: Laboratories established directly by the Food Authority through a gazette notification to serve as referral bodies for disputed food sample analysis.
Existing accredited laboratories or research institutions officially recognised by the Food Authority by notification to perform referral functions under the Act.
The function of receiving disputed samples referred by the Designated Officer when a food business operator or other party appeals against a Food Analyst's report.
Carrying out additional functions assigned to it by the Food Authority through rules and regulations framed under the Act, including standard-setting analysis and specialised food testing.
Issuing an authoritative scientific opinion on the composition, quality, or safety of a food sample that supersedes or supplements the original Food Analyst's report.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary food laboratories or private testing labs that are accredited by NABL but not specifically notified by the Food Authority as referral food laboratories.
Food Analysts working in State or local government laboratories who perform routine first-instance sample analysis under Section 46 — they do not constitute a referral food laboratory.
Research institutions or universities that conduct food-related research but have not been formally notified by the Food Authority to carry out referral functions under the Act.
Laboratories outside India or international testing bodies, which have no standing as referral food laboratories under the Food Safety and Standards Act.
Any laboratory that analyses food samples at the request of a consumer or food business operator directly, without a referral from the Designated Officer under the appeal process.
definitions.why_it_matters: The referral food laboratory is the decisive authority in food safety disputes: its opinion on an appealed Food Analyst report directly influences whether the Designated Officer proceeds with prosecution, issues a prohibition order, or exonerates a food business operator, making its findings critical to enforcement outcomes. Failure to refer a contested matter to the notified referral food laboratory, or reliance on a non-notified laboratory, can render enforcement proceedings legally infirm and liable to be set aside.

definitions.definition: A referral laboratory is a laboratory designated under the Food Safety and Standards Act to provide a final and binding analysis in cases where the test reports of the Food Analyst and the accredited laboratory are found to be at variance; the decision of the referral laboratory on such analysis shall be final.
definitions.plain_english: A referral laboratory is a specially designated government-approved testing lab that steps in to give the final verdict when two earlier food test results disagree with each other. Its decision is binding and cannot be overridden. Think of it as the 'supreme court' of food testing under this law.
real_world_examples: A Food Safety Officer in Mumbai collects a sample of branded ghee; the Food Analyst's lab declares it adulterated, but the food business operator's accredited private lab clears it — the Designated Officer then sends the third sample portion to the referral laboratory (e.g., CFTRI, Mysuru) whose finding settles the dispute permanently.

In Delhi, a spice manufacturer's chilli powder sample tests positive for Sudan Red dye at the government Food Analyst's lab but negative at the NABL-accredited lab chosen by the operator; the Designated Officer forwards the sealed sample to the referral laboratory to resolve the conflict, and its result is used to decide prosecution.

A dairy cooperative in Punjab disputes a sub-standard finding on its pasteurised milk after variance arises between the two lab reports; the referral laboratory's analysis determines whether penalty proceedings and licence suspension are initiated against the cooperative.

An importer of processed cheese in Chennai receives conflicting reports on permissible preservative levels; upon variance, the Designated Officer dispatches the retained sample to the referral laboratory, and its conclusive report governs whether the consignment is cleared or confiscated.

A street food vendor in Kolkata whose oil sample shows conflicting trans-fat readings between the Food Analyst and the accredited lab has the dispute resolved by the referral laboratory, whose decision determines whether a fine or prosecution under the FSS Act is pursued.
what_it_covers: Government-designated laboratories authorised to conduct final binding analysis when results of the Food Analyst and accredited laboratory are at variance.
The analysis of a retained sealed sample portion held in the custody of the Designated Officer, sent specifically due to a conflict in earlier test reports.
Any category of food article or adulterant for which conflicting test reports have been received, including adulterated, sub-standard, or misbranded food products.
Laboratories listed or notified under the Food Safety and Standards framework as referral food laboratories, such as CFTRI Mysuru or other FSSAI-notified institutions.
what_it_excludes: The Food Analyst's laboratory conducting the initial first-instance analysis of food samples — that role belongs to a food laboratory, not the referral laboratory.
Accredited laboratories chosen by the food business operator for independent parallel testing under Section 47(iii) — these are distinct from referral laboratories.
Private or NABL-accredited commercial laboratories that are not specifically notified or designated as referral laboratories by the competent authority under the FSS Act.
Notified laboratories used for analysis of imported articles of food under Section 47(5), which operate in a separate procedural track.
Laboratories conducting routine food safety audits or food safety management system assessments, which serve a compliance-monitoring rather than dispute-resolution function.
definitions.why_it_matters: The referral laboratory's finding is legally final and determinative — it directly decides whether prosecution, penalty, licence cancellation, or product seizure proceedings are initiated or dropped against a food business operator. Without the referral laboratory mechanism, conflicting test reports would create an irresolvable evidentiary deadlock, making enforcement of food safety standards impossible in contested cases.
