definitions.definition: The phrase 'specified by regulations' refers to any requirement, practice, standard, procedure, or matter that is to be prescribed, detailed, or determined through regulations framed by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India under this Act, as opposed to being enumerated in the Act itself. It operates as a legislative delegation mechanism enabling the Food Authority to specify technical or operational details through subordinate legislation.
definitions.plain_english: When the law says something is 'specified by regulations,' it means the exact details or rules on that particular matter will be written out separately by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) in official regulations, not in the main law itself. This allows the FSSAI to update technical requirements without having to change the entire Act. Think of it as the Act saying: 'the specifics will be filled in by the regulator.'
real_world_examples: FSSAI specifying through regulations the exact Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) that a biscuit manufacturer in Pune must follow as part of the Food Safety Management System, such as temperature controls, hygiene protocols, and equipment sanitation schedules.

FSSAI issuing the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations to specify permissible limits of preservatives in packaged namkeen snacks sold across India, a detail 'specified by regulations' rather than in the parent Act.

A dairy cooperative in Amul, Gujarat being required to implement Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) practices as specified by FSSAI regulations under the Food Safety Management System definition in Section 3.

A catering service provider for railway pantry cars being required to follow specific hygiene and food handling practices 'specified by regulations' under FSSAI's Food Safety and Standards (Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations.

A nutraceutical manufacturer in Hyderabad needing to comply with labelling requirements 'specified by regulations' by FSSAI detailing mandatory declarations, font sizes, and nutritional information formats on product packaging.
what_it_covers: Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), Good Hygienic Practices (GHP), HACCP, and other food safety practices that the Food Authority specifies through regulations as part of the Food Safety Management System.

Any technical, procedural, or operational requirement that the FSSAI deems necessary to prescribe for food businesses through formal regulations under the Act, such as permissible additive limits or packaging standards.

Standards, methods of testing, labelling requirements, and licensing conditions that are too technical or subject to frequent update to be included in the body of the Act itself, and are therefore left to be specified via FSSAI regulations.
Practices related to food safety audits, food safety programmes, and food safety management systems whose precise content and scope are delegated to be determined by FSSAI through regulations.
what_it_excludes: Requirements, definitions, or obligations that are directly and explicitly stated within the text of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 itself, without any reference to regulations for further specification.

Rules, orders, or notifications issued by the Central Government or State Governments under other provisions of the Act, which are not 'regulations' framed by the Food Authority under its regulation-making power.
Informal industry guidelines, voluntary codes of practice, or international standards (such as Codex Alimentarius) that have not been formally adopted or incorporated into FSSAI regulations.
Administrative circulars or advisories issued by FSSAI that do not carry the force of formal regulations published in the Official Gazette as required by the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a practice or standard has been 'specified by regulations' determines whether a food business operator is legally bound to follow it and can be held liable for non-compliance, attracting penalties, licence cancellation, or prosecution under the Act. If a requirement has not been formally specified by regulations, enforcement action for its breach may be legally untenable, making this mechanism central to the entire compliance and penalty framework of the Act.

definitions.definition: "Standard" in the context of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 refers to the specific requirements, limits, parameters, and specifications prescribed by the Food Authority through regulations with respect to food articles, including requirements as to the nature, substance, quality, purity, labelling, packaging, contaminant levels, pesticide residues, food additives, and microbiological limits that a food article must conform to for it to be deemed safe and not sub-standard.
definitions.plain_english: A 'standard' is the official benchmark or set of rules that defines what a food product must be like — including what it can contain, how much of it, and how it must be labelled or packaged. If a food product does not meet these benchmarks, it is considered sub-standard or unsafe. Think of it as the government's official recipe or specification that every food manufacturer and seller must follow.
real_world_examples: FSSAI prescribes that packaged drinking water must not contain arsenic beyond 0.01 mg/litre — this maximum limit is the 'standard' that every bottled water brand like Bisleri or Kinley must comply with.

The Food Authority sets a standard for milk that specifies minimum fat content (e.g., 3.5% for full cream milk) and SNF levels; a dairy in Punjab selling milk below these levels would be selling sub-standard food.

Maida (refined wheat flour) sold by a flour mill in Rajasthan must conform to FSSAI standards for moisture content, ash content, and gluten — if the product deviates, it violates the prescribed standard.

A spice manufacturer in Kerala exporting chilli powder must ensure the pesticide residue levels do not exceed FSSAI-prescribed limits, which constitute the applicable 'standard' for that food article.

Baby food manufacturers such as Nestlé or Heinz must ensure their infant formula meets the compositional standards set under FSSAI regulations, including minimum protein levels and prohibited additives.
A street food operator in Mumbai selling packaged snacks must ensure the trans-fat content in the oil used does not exceed the FSSAI-notified standard of 2% per 100g of total fat.
what_it_covers: Maximum permissible levels of contaminants, pesticide residues, and heavy metals in food articles as prescribed by the Food Authority.
Compositional requirements such as minimum fat, protein, or moisture content for specific food categories like dairy, cereals, and oils.
Microbiological standards specifying limits for pathogens such as E. coli or Salmonella in processed foods.
Labelling and packaging specifications that a food article must display to comply with regulatory requirements.
Standards for food additives, including permitted types and maximum usage levels in particular food categories.
Quality parameters for primary foods such as grains, pulses, and fresh produce under FSSAI regulations.
what_it_excludes: Standards applicable to animal feed or live animals not intended for direct human consumption, which fall outside the scope of the Act.
Pharmacopoeial standards for drugs and medicinal products, which are governed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and not under FSSAI.
Cosmetic product specifications or quality benchmarks, which are excluded from the definition of 'food' and hence from food standards.
Voluntary or industry-adopted quality certifications (such as ISO 22000) that have not been formally notified under FSSAI regulations.
Standards for narcotic or psychotropic substances, which are regulated under separate legislation and excluded from the Act's ambit.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a food article meets the prescribed 'standard' determines whether it is classified as 'sub-standard food' under the Act, triggering penalties under Section 51 and liability for the food business operator. Failure to conform to standards can also lead to product recall, cancellation of licence, and prosecution, while compliance protects operators from regulatory action.

definitions.definition: State Authority, as used in the Food Safety and Standards Act, refers to the State Food Safety Authority established under the Act, being the body constituted at the state level responsible for implementation and enforcement of food safety standards within a State, before which representations or appearances may be made in the context of food safety matters.
definitions.plain_english: The State Authority is the food safety regulatory body set up at the level of each Indian state. It is responsible for overseeing and enforcing food safety rules within that state's jurisdiction. When someone like a former Chairperson or Member of the central Food Authority leaves their post, they are prohibited from appearing or lobbying before this body on behalf of any person.
real_world_examples: A former Member of the central Food Authority who retired from service attempts to represent a large dairy company in a licensing dispute before the Maharashtra State Food Safety Authority — this is prohibited under Section 7.

In Tamil Nadu, the State Authority conducts inspections of local food processing units and issues improvement notices to non-compliant manufacturers, acting as the state-level enforcement arm of food safety law.
A food business operator in Punjab appeals against a penalty imposed by a Designated Officer; the matter is heard before the Punjab State Food Safety Authority functioning as the State Authority.

The Uttar Pradesh State Authority coordinates with Food Safety Officers to investigate a reported outbreak of food poisoning traced to a local packaged snack manufacturer and takes regulatory action accordingly.

A former Chairperson of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), after retirement, is approached by a multinational food company to represent them in a standards dispute before the Karnataka State Authority — such representation is expressly barred by Section 7(5).
what_it_covers: The State Food Safety Authority constituted under the Act at the level of each Indian state.
Bodies before which former Chairpersons or Members of the central Food Authority are prohibited from appearing or representing any person post-tenure.
State-level adjudicatory or regulatory forums dealing with food safety enforcement, licensing, and compliance matters within their respective state jurisdictions.
what_it_excludes: The central Food Authority (FSSAI) itself, which is the national-level body distinct from the State Authority.
District-level or local body food safety enforcement officers such as Designated Officers or Food Safety Officers, who are not themselves the State Authority.
Central Government ministries or departments involved in food regulation, which operate at a different tier of governance and are not covered by the term State Authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: The legal consequence directly triggered by this term in Section 7 is the post-tenure prohibition: a former Chairperson or Member of the Food Authority is permanently barred from representing any person before the State Authority, preventing conflicts of interest and misuse of insider knowledge. Violation of this restriction could attract legal consequences and undermines the integrity of state-level food safety adjudication.

definitions.definition: The State Commissioner of Food Safety is the officer appointed by the State Government under Section 30 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, who is responsible for carrying out the functions and duties assigned to the State Government under the Act, including overseeing food safety administration, enforcement, and regulatory compliance within the State. The State Commissioner of Food Safety acts as the apex food safety authority at the State level, coordinating with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and directing Designated Officers and Food Safety Officers within the State.
definitions.plain_english: The State Commissioner of Food Safety is the top food safety official appointed by each State Government. Think of this person as the chief food safety officer for the entire state, responsible for making sure food laws are followed, overseeing inspections, and enforcing food safety rules across the state. They work under the broader national framework set by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India but have their own authority and duties within their state.
real_world_examples: The State Commissioner of Food Safety in Maharashtra issues directives to all Designated Officers across districts to conduct surprise inspections of street food vendors ahead of a major festival season in Mumbai.

Following a reported food poisoning outbreak at a school in Bengaluru, the State Commissioner of Food Safety of Karnataka initiates an inquiry, orders sampling of the mid-day meal supply, and directs suspension of the food supplier's licence pending investigation.

The State Commissioner of Food Safety in Uttar Pradesh approves and publishes rules under Section 94 regarding the manner in which rewards shall be paid to whistleblowers who assist in detecting adulteration offences in the state's dairy supply chain.

In Tamil Nadu, the State Commissioner of Food Safety exercises powers under Section 30(2)(f) to perform other functions prescribed by state rules, such as setting up a rapid response food safety team for monitoring packaged food quality in retail markets across Chennai.

The State Commissioner of Food Safety in Rajasthan oversees the earmarking of a state fund for rewarding individuals who report illegal sale of adulterated edible oils, as authorised by rules framed under Section 94.

During a crackdown on sub-standard spices in West Bengal, the State Commissioner of Food Safety coordinates with the Food Authority and directs all Designated Officers to submit monthly compliance reports on seizures and prosecutions.
what_it_covers: The officer appointed by the State Government under Section 30 who heads food safety enforcement within the State.
Exercise of functions and duties assigned to the State Government under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, at the state level.
Supervision and coordination of Designated Officers and Food Safety Officers within the State.
Implementation of state-specific food safety rules made under Section 94 with prior approval of the Food Authority.
Actions related to rewarding informants, initiating prosecutions, and overseeing food safety audits within the State.
what_it_excludes: The Chairperson or CEO of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), who operates at the central level.
Designated Officers or Food Safety Officers who operate at district or local levels subordinate to the State Commissioner.
Officers of the Central Government exercising powers under the Act at the national level, such as those enforcing import-related food safety provisions.
State-level officers of other departments (e.g., health, agriculture) who may incidentally deal with food but are not appointed as State Commissioner of Food Safety.
Private food safety auditors or accredited laboratory personnel who perform technical assessments but hold no statutory enforcement authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity and authority of the State Commissioner of Food Safety is critical because state-level enforcement actions — including directions to Designated Officers, initiation of prosecutions, suspension of licences, and framing of state food safety rules — are legally valid only when taken by or under the authority of this specific office. Rules made under Section 94 that govern the functions of this role and state-level reward mechanisms are binding on all state food safety personnel, and any action taken without proper delegation from or appointment as the State Commissioner of Food Safety could be challenged as ultra vires.

definitions.definition: The State Food Safety Authority means the authority constituted or designated at the State level that, together with the Food Authority, is jointly responsible for the enforcement of the Food Safety and Standards Act, including monitoring and verifying compliance by food business operators at all stages of food business, and maintaining a system of control and public communication on food safety within the State.
definitions.plain_english: The State Food Safety Authority is the official government body in each State or Union Territory responsible for making sure food safety laws are followed within that State. It works alongside the central Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to inspect, monitor, and regulate food businesses at all levels. It oversees food safety officers and designated officers who carry out enforcement actions on the ground.
real_world_examples: The Maharashtra State Food Safety Authority directing its Designated Officers and Food Safety Officers to conduct surprise inspections of restaurants and street food stalls in Mumbai during a festive season to check for adulteration and hygiene violations.

The Tamil Nadu State Food Safety Authority launching a State-wide surveillance programme to test samples of packaged milk and dairy products sold across Chennai, Coimbatore, and Madurai for pesticide residues and adulterants.

The Delhi State Food Safety Authority issuing improvement notices to a large chain of sweet shops during Diwali after Food Safety Officers collected samples that were found to be sub-standard and misbranded.

The Uttar Pradesh State Food Safety Authority coordinating with local municipal bodies to shut down unlicensed food processing units in Kanpur that were manufacturing adulterated edible oils and storing them in unsanitary conditions.

The Karnataka State Food Safety Authority conducting a public awareness campaign in Bengaluru advising consumers about safe food practices and communicating identified food safety risks following an outbreak of food poisoning linked to a catering company.

The West Bengal State Food Safety Authority empowering its Commissioner of Food Safety to invoke emergency prohibition orders against a fish processing plant in Kolkata found to be using prohibited preservatives.
what_it_covers: The State or Union Territory level governmental authority constituted or designated under the FSS Act to enforce food safety law within its territorial jurisdiction.
Oversight and supervision of Food Safety Officers, Designated Officers, and the Commissioner of Food Safety operating within the State.

Monitoring and verification of compliance by all categories of food business operators — manufacturers, distributors, retailers, importers — across all stages of the food supply chain within the State.
Maintenance of State-level food safety surveillance systems, including food sampling programmes, laboratory testing coordination, and public communication about food safety risks.
Coordinated enforcement actions with the central Food Authority, including sharing of information, data, and enforcement outcomes as required under regulations.
what_it_excludes: The central Food Authority (FSSAI) itself, which is a separate and distinct national-level body with overarching regulatory and standard-setting powers under the Act.

Individual Food Safety Officers, Designated Officers, or the Commissioner of Food Safety acting in personal capacity — these are officers operating under the State Food Safety Authority, not the Authority itself.

definitions.definition: The term 'stores' is not formally defined in the Food Safety and Standards Act, but is used consistently to denote the act of keeping, stocking, or holding any article of food or adulterant in any premises, godown, cold storage, warehouse, or other place for the purpose of sale, distribution, or further processing. It encompasses any form of physical retention or custody of food articles or adulterants at a location prior to their eventual sale, distribution, or use.
definitions.plain_english: Storing means physically keeping or holding food products or adulterants at any location — such as a warehouse, shop, cold storage, or godown — before they are sold or distributed. If someone keeps food that is below standard, mislabelled, contaminated, or unsafe in such a place, they can be held legally responsible. You don't have to be the one selling the food to be penalised — simply keeping it in your custody is enough.
real_world_examples: A wholesale trader in Mumbai keeps thousands of packets of adulterated spices in a godown before dispatching them to retail shops — the act of keeping those packets in the godown constitutes 'storing' under the Act.
A cold storage facility in Punjab retains a consignment of dairy products beyond their expiry date, making them sub-standard — the facility operator is liable for 'storing' sub-standard food.

A street food vendor in Delhi stacks bags of maida (refined flour) containing extraneous matter in the back room of their stall — this back-room retention amounts to 'storing' food containing extraneous matter.
A supermarket chain in Bengaluru keeps misbranded packaged drinks in its stockroom before placing them on shelves — the stockroom retention itself qualifies as 'storing' misbranded food.

A rice mill owner in West Bengal holds stocks of artificially coloured rice in a warehouse pending sale to wholesalers — this holding constitutes storing an unsafe article of food and attracts penal liability.
A restaurant in Hyderabad keeps containers of chemical adulterants (not injurious to health) in its kitchen store for use in food preparation — this amounts to storing an adulterant under Section 57.
what_it_covers: Keeping sub-standard, misbranded, or unsafe food articles in a warehouse, godown, cold storage, or any other premises prior to sale or distribution.
Retention of any adulterant (whether injurious or non-injurious to health) at a business premises, storage facility, or manufacturing unit.
Holding food containing extraneous matter in a stockroom, back-office, or on-site storage area of a food business establishment.
Temporary stocking of food articles at distribution hubs or transit warehouses even without direct involvement in the final sale transaction.
Keeping packaged or unpackaged food in premises under one's control or management, even if held on behalf of another person.
what_it_excludes: Casual, domestic storage of food for personal household consumption not intended for sale or commercial distribution.
Transit or transport of food articles through a location without deliberate retention or holding at that point — mere movement does not constitute storing.
Keeping food in sealed, unbroken, original manufacturer packaging at a licensed premises where the operator has no knowledge or means of knowing the non-compliance of the food.
Storage by a government-authorised officer who has seized food articles pursuant to an official inspection or court order, as such custody is not commercial storing.
Food held temporarily at a consumer's premises after purchase and solely for personal consumption, with no intent of resale or distribution.
definitions.why_it_matters: The act of 'storing' independently triggers penal liability under Sections 51, 52, 54, and 57 of the Act — meaning a person can be penalised even without having manufactured or sold the offending food or adulterant, solely on the basis of keeping it in their custody. This makes warehouse operators, cold storage owners, distributors, and stockroom managers directly liable for non-compliant food or adulterants found on their premises, closing any loophole that would otherwise require proof of an actual sale.

definitions.definition: An article of food shall be deemed to be sub-standard if it does not meet the standards specified by the Food Authority under this Act or the rules and regulations made thereunder, including standards relating to composition, quality, and nutritional value, without necessarily rendering it unsafe for consumption.
definitions.plain_english: A food product is called 'sub-standard' when it does not meet the quality or composition requirements set by food safety rules, even if it may not directly harm your health. For example, if a packet of milk has less fat content than the prescribed standard, it is sub-standard. It is different from 'unsafe' food, which poses a direct health risk — sub-standard food falls short of quality benchmarks but may still be edible.
real_world_examples: A dairy company in Punjab sells toned milk with only 1.2% fat content, whereas the prescribed standard under FSS Regulations requires a minimum of 3% fat — the milk is declared sub-standard even though it is not harmful to consume.

A spice manufacturer in Gujarat produces turmeric powder with a curcumin content below the minimum standard prescribed by FSSAI, causing the entire batch to be classified as sub-standard during routine Food Safety Officer inspection.

A packaged fruit juice brand in Maharashtra is found to contain less than the declared percentage of fruit pulp as specified on the label and as required by FSS regulations, making it sub-standard due to compositional deficiency.

A rice miller in Andhra Pradesh sells rice with broken grain percentage exceeding the permissible limit set under FSS standards, resulting in the consignment being marked sub-standard following Food Analyst testing.

A Bengaluru-based bakery is found using flour with lower protein content than the standard specified for the particular grade claimed on packaging, leading to a sub-standard classification by the Designated Officer after sampling.

A packaged drinking water brand in Delhi is found to have total dissolved solids marginally exceeding the permissible limit under FSS (Water) Regulations, classifying the product as sub-standard at the accredited laboratory.
what_it_covers: Food products whose composition, nutritional value, or physical properties fall below the minimum standards prescribed under FSS Regulations, such as milk with insufficient fat content.
Packaged or processed foods that contain less of a declared or mandated ingredient than the prescribed standard, such as fruit juices with insufficient fruit pulp percentage.
Food articles that have been diluted, blended, or processed in a manner that reduces their quality below the regulatory threshold without making them directly harmful or unsafe.
Spices, cereals, or staple foods where moisture content, grain quality, or purity levels do not conform to the specified standards set by the Food Authority.
Beverages where key quality parameters such as pH, sugar content, or dissolved solids deviate from prescribed standards even if they pose no immediate health hazard.
what_it_excludes: Food that is 'unsafe' — i.e., food that is injurious to health or unfit for human consumption — which is governed by a separate and more serious legal classification under the Act.
Food that is 'misbranded' — where the product may meet quality standards but is incorrectly labelled, described, or advertised in a misleading manner.
Food containing adulterants that render it unsafe or injurious to health, which falls under the definition of 'adulterated' or 'unsafe food' rather than merely sub-standard.
Food with extraneous matter that does not affect safety — such articles may be separately classified under relevant provisions without necessarily being sub-standard.
Naturally occurring variation in food products that falls within the prescribed tolerance limits set by the Food Authority under FSS Regulations.
definitions.why_it_matters: A finding that food is 'sub-standard' triggers liability under Section 51 of the FSSAI Act, which prescribes a penalty of up to five lakh rupees on the food business operator, without requiring proof of harm to any consumer. It is a distinct and lesser classification than 'unsafe food' but still attracts mandatory regulatory action, including improvement notices under Section 32, prohibition orders, and potential cancellation of licences under Section 26, making it a critical compliance threshold for all food business operators.

definitions.definition: Sub-standard food means any article of food which does not meet the standards specified by the Food Authority under the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the rules and regulations made thereunder, but is not unsafe food. It is food that falls below the prescribed quality or compositional requirements without necessarily posing an immediate risk to health.
definitions.plain_english: Sub-standard food is food that does not meet the official quality or composition rules set by the government's food regulator (FSSAI), even though it may not directly harm your health. Think of it as food that is 'below par' — it may have less of an ingredient than required, or fail a quality test, but is not necessarily dangerous to eat. Selling, manufacturing, distributing, or importing such food is a punishable offence in India.
real_world_examples: A dairy company in Rajasthan sells packaged milk with a fat content of 2.5% instead of the FSSAI-mandated minimum of 3.5% for full-cream milk — the milk is sub-standard because it fails the compositional standard even though it is not unsafe.

A spice manufacturer in Gujarat packages turmeric powder with a curcumin content below the prescribed FSSAI limit, making it sub-standard food that can attract a penalty of up to five lakh rupees under Section 51.

An importer in Mumbai attempts to bring in a consignment of honey from China where the moisture content exceeds the maximum limit set by the Food Authority, making the imported honey sub-standard and subject to prohibition under Section 25.

A cold drink manufacturer in Delhi bottles a fruit juice with less than the prescribed percentage of fruit pulp, failing the quality standard set under FSSAI regulations and rendering the product sub-standard.

A wheat flour (atta) producer in Punjab sells flour with ash content exceeding the prescribed FSSAI limit, which does not make it unsafe but causes it to be classified as sub-standard, exposing the business operator to regulatory penalties.

A street food vendor in Chennai uses edible oil that has an acid value above the permissible FSSAI limit due to repeated heating, making the food sub-standard even though a single consumption may not cause immediate harm.
what_it_covers: Any article of food that fails to meet the compositional, quality or purity standards prescribed by the Food Authority under FSSAI regulations, such as milk with insufficient fat content.
Imported food articles that do not conform to the standards laid down by the Food Authority, prohibited from entry into India under Section 25.
Food manufactured, stored, sold or distributed domestically that falls below the specified standards but does not qualify as unsafe food, attracting penalty under Section 51.
Packaged or processed food products where a specific ingredient is present in a quantity below the minimum prescribed limit, such as fruit juice with insufficient pulp content.
Batches, lots or consignments of food where one sample is found sub-standard, which raises a presumption that the entire batch is sub-standard unless proven otherwise.
what_it_excludes: Unsafe food, which poses an actual risk to human health and is governed by a separate and more stringent set of provisions and penalties under the Act.
Misbranded food, which relates to incorrect, false or misleading labelling or packaging rather than the intrinsic quality or composition of the food itself.
Food containing extraneous matter, which is separately categorised and treated as a distinct violation under Section 25 and related provisions.
Food produced by farmers at the farm level or fishermen in their operations, which is explicitly excluded from the application of the Act under Section 18(3).
Food that meets all prescribed FSSAI standards but is merely of inferior commercial grade or consumer preference — non-compliance with standards is the threshold, not subjective quality.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a food article qualifies as 'sub-standard' directly determines liability under Section 51, which imposes a monetary penalty of up to five lakh rupees on any person who manufactures, stores, sells, distributes or imports such food; it also triggers prohibition on import under Section 25. The classification as sub-standard (rather than unsafe or misbranded) affects the severity of the regulatory action and the type of penalty or enforcement measure applicable.

definitions.definition: "Substance" is not separately defined in the Act but is used as a foundational constituent element within the definitions of "food", "ingredient", "contaminant", "food additive", and related terms, referring to any matter — whether solid, liquid, gas, chemical compound, biological agent, or mixture thereof — that is present in, added to, or used in the manufacture, preparation, treatment, or composition of an article of food.
definitions.plain_english: A 'substance' under this law simply means any kind of matter — solid, liquid, or gas — that can be part of food or used in making food. This includes natural ingredients, chemicals, additives, water, or any other material that goes into or comes into contact with food during its production or preparation. The term is used broadly to cover anything that could affect what food is made of or how safe it is.
real_world_examples: A food manufacturer in Gujarat adds a chemical preservative (sodium benzoate) to packaged mango pickles — this chemical preservative is a 'substance' used as a food additive in the manufacture of food.

A Mumbai street vendor's chaat is found to contain water from an unclean source used during preparation — this water is a 'substance' incorporated into the food during its preparation, making it subject to FSSAI safety standards.

A Delhi-based dairy plant uses hydrogen peroxide for treating milk to extend shelf life — hydrogen peroxide is a 'substance' used in food processing and falls under scrutiny as a processing aid or additive under the Act.

Pesticide residue from agricultural spraying is found in spinach sold at a Bengaluru market — the pesticide residue is a 'substance' that qualifies as a contaminant present in food as a result of crop husbandry operations.
A Kolkata confectionery unit uses artificial food colouring (tartrazine) in sweets — tartrazine is a 'substance' constituting a food additive intentionally added for organoleptic (colour) purposes.

A food safety officer in Chennai samples packaged drinking water from a branded bottle and tests it for dissolved substances — the dissolved minerals and any harmful chemical compounds in the water are 'substances' within the meaning of the Act.
what_it_covers: Chemical compounds intentionally added to food, such as preservatives, colorants, or flavour enhancers used during manufacture.
Water incorporated into food during its preparation, treatment, or manufacture, including water used for washing, cooking, or mixing.
Naturally occurring or incidentally present materials in food, such as pesticide residues, veterinary drug residues, or environmental contaminants that enter food through production processes.
Biological agents such as enzymes or microbial cultures added during fermentation or food processing.
Gases such as carbon dioxide used in carbonated beverages or nitrogen used in modified atmosphere packaging of food products.
what_it_excludes: Live animals in their entirety before slaughter and processing, which are explicitly excluded from the definition of 'food' and thus outside the scope of 'substance' in this context.
Plants prior to harvesting, which are excluded from the scope of 'food' and therefore their constituent matter before harvest does not qualify as a regulated 'substance' under the Act.

Drugs and medicinal products as defined under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, which are excluded from the definition of 'food' even if consumed orally, and thus their chemical components are not regulated as 'substances' under this Act.

Cosmetics and narcotic or psychotropic substances, which are explicitly carved out of the definition of 'food', meaning their constituent matter falls outside the regulatory ambit of 'substance' under this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a material qualifies as a 'substance' under this Act determines whether it falls within the regulatory reach of FSSAI standards for food safety, labelling, and permissible limits — triggering obligations on food business operators to comply with standards for additives, contaminants, and ingredients, and potentially exposing them to penalties under Sections 50 and related provisions for use of unsafe or sub-standard substances in food.

definitions.definition: A summary trial, under Section 73 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, is a expedited mode of trial conducted by a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or a Metropolitan Magistrate for all food safety offences not triable by a Special Court, in accordance with sections 262 to 265 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, wherein the Magistrate may impose a sentence of imprisonment not exceeding one year; provided that if the nature of the case warrants a sentence exceeding one year or summary trial is otherwise undesirable, the Magistrate shall convert the proceeding to a regular trial after hearing the parties.
definitions.plain_english: A summary trial is a faster, simplified court process used for less serious food safety offences, handled directly by a lower-level magistrate without the full length of a regular criminal trial. In such a trial, the magistrate can sentence a person to jail for up to one year if convicted. If the magistrate feels the case is more serious and might require a longer sentence, the case is converted into a full regular trial instead.
real_world_examples: A small street food vendor in Mumbai is found selling adulterated spices with synthetic colour additives. The Food Safety Officer files a complaint, and the Metropolitan Magistrate tries the case summarily under Section 73, completing the proceedings quickly and imposing a fine and a short imprisonment term of six months.

A petty retailer in Delhi is caught storing packaged milk beyond its expiry date and selling it to consumers. The Judicial Magistrate of the first class initiates summary trial proceedings, records evidence swiftly, and convicts the retailer within a few hearings.

A food stall operator at a railway station in Chennai is found selling misbranded food items without proper labelling. The case is taken up as a summary trial before the Metropolitan Magistrate, who disposes of the matter expeditiously with a conviction and sentence within the one-year cap.

A local bakery owner in Kolkata is prosecuted for using a prohibited food additive in bread. During the summary trial, the Magistrate determines that the offence may warrant a sentence exceeding one year and accordingly converts the matter to a regular trial after hearing both parties and recalling earlier witnesses.

A hawker in Bengaluru is found selling sub-standard packaged drinking water. The complaint is filed before a Judicial Magistrate of the first class who tries the case summarily, records the evidence concisely under CrPC sections 262-265, and delivers a verdict within weeks rather than years.
what_it_covers: All food safety offences under the Act that are not triable by a Special Court, tried summarily by a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or a Metropolitan Magistrate.
Convictions resulting in imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, lawfully passed by the Magistrate in a summary proceeding.

Application of procedural provisions of sections 262 to 265 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 to the conduct of such trials.
Offences by petty manufacturers, hawkers, itinerant vendors, temporary stall holders, and retailers involving sub-standard or misbranded food tried before a magistrate.
what_it_excludes: Offences triable exclusively by a Special Court under the Food Safety and Standards Act, which are outside the scope of summary trial under Section 73.
Cases where the Magistrate determines mid-trial that the sentence required exceeds one year — such cases are converted to regular trial and no longer proceed as summary trials.
Sessions Court or High Court level proceedings, as summary trial jurisdiction under this section is limited to Judicial Magistrates of the first class and Metropolitan Magistrates.
Civil or administrative adjudication proceedings before the Adjudicating Officer or the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal, which are not criminal summary trials.
Offences that require elaborate evidence, expert witnesses, or complex procedural safeguards incompatible with the simplified summary procedure under CrPC sections 262-265.

This distinction affects whether an accused faces a quick disposal of their case or a prolonged regular criminal proceeding with its attendant costs and procedural rights.

definitions.definition: A temporary stall holder is a person who operates a food business from a temporary or makeshift stall, as distinguished from a permanent establishment, and is exempted from the requirement of obtaining a licence under Section 31, being instead required only to register with the appropriate authority in such manner as may be specified by regulations.
definitions.plain_english: A temporary stall holder is someone who sells food from a temporary setup — like a stall at a fair, festival, market, or roadside event — rather than from a fixed, permanent shop or business premises. They do not need a full food licence like a regular restaurant or factory would, but they must register with the food safety authority. They are still legally obligated to sell safe and wholesome food.
real_world_examples: A vendor setting up a chaat and snacks stall during the annual Diwali mela in Lucknow, operating for the duration of the festival before dismantling the stall.
A person selling fresh sugarcane juice and fruit chaat from a temporary bamboo-and-tarpaulin stall erected near a temple during a major pilgrimage season in Varanasi.
A food seller operating a temporary biryani and kebab counter at a trade exhibition or agricultural mela organised by the state government in Pune.
A local sweet-maker setting up a makeshift stall outside a school or college campus during annual cultural fests or sports events, selling homemade laddoos and barfis.
A vendor operating a temporary south Indian breakfast counter — serving idli, dosa, and sambar — at a weekly Sunday bazaar in Chennai's T. Nagar area.
A person selling fried snacks and beverages from a temporary stall erected alongside a religious procession route during Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations in Mumbai.
what_it_covers: A person selling food from a temporary stall erected at a festival, fair, mela, or religious event for a limited duration.
A vendor operating a makeshift food counter at a seasonal market, trade exhibition, or public gathering without a permanent shop structure.
A food seller who sets up a stall periodically (such as at weekly bazaars or annual events) and does not maintain a fixed permanent food establishment.
An individual operating a temporary food counter at sports events, cultural programmes, or government-organised exhibitions.
what_it_excludes: A person running a permanent, fixed food shop, restaurant, dhaba, or eatery with a stable physical structure, who requires a full licence under Section 31(1).
A licensed manufacturer or processor operating from a permanent factory or food processing unit, regardless of the scale of operation.

A food business operator who qualifies as a petty manufacturer, petty retailer, hawker, or itinerant vendor — these are separately categorised entities under the Act, though they share a similar registration-only regime.
Large-scale or corporate food businesses operating temporary counters as part of an organised chain, where the parent entity holds a licence and does not fall under the exempted category.
A tiny food business operator, who is a distinct category also requiring registration but defined separately under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: A temporary stall holder is exempt from mandatory licensing under Section 31(1) and instead must only register with the food authority, reducing the compliance burden; however, they remain fully subject to food safety standards and consumer protection obligations, and under Section 69, the Commissioner of Food Safety may empower the Designated Officer to compound offences committed by such a person for a sum not exceeding one lakh rupees, provided the offence is not one carrying imprisonment.

definitions.definition: A tiny food business operator is a person or entity engaged in a food business at a very small or minimal scale, who is exempt from obtaining a licence under Section 31(1) but is required to register with the designated authority in the manner specified by regulations, without prejudice to the availability of safe and wholesome food for human consumption or affecting the interests of consumers.
definitions.plain_english: A tiny food business operator is someone who runs a very small food-related business — smaller even than a cottage or small-scale food industry. Instead of getting a full food safety licence, they only need to register with the local food authority. They must still ensure the food they make or sell is safe to eat.
real_world_examples: A woman in a rural village in Rajasthan who makes and sells homemade pickles and papad from her home kitchen to a handful of neighbours on a very small scale.
A small roadside stall owner in a tier-3 town in Uttar Pradesh who prepares and sells freshly made snacks like chaat or poha only during morning hours with minimal daily turnover.
An individual in a slum locality in Mumbai who makes and supplies small quantities of home-cooked tiffin meals to five or six nearby factory workers each day.
A tribal artisan in Chhattisgarh who collects and sells small quantities of forest produce-based food items like honey or dried fruits directly to local consumers without any formal commercial setup.
A self-help group member in Tamil Nadu who occasionally prepares and sells traditional sweets or snacks at local festivals or weekly markets on a very limited basis.
what_it_covers: An individual operating a micro-level food production or sale activity from home or a makeshift setup with negligible annual turnover.
A person who is smaller in scale than a petty manufacturer or cottage industry food operator and does not have a fixed commercial establishment.
Self-help group members or home-based food preparers who sell directly to consumers in very limited quantities without organised commercial distribution.
Informal food preparers in semi-urban or rural areas who supply food to a very small and local consumer base with no mechanised production.
what_it_excludes: A petty manufacturer who manufactures or sells food on a slightly larger scale and is separately classified under Section 31(2).
A licensed food business operator running a restaurant, hotel, packaged food factory, or organised retail outlet, regardless of size.
A hawker, itinerant vendor, petty retailer, or temporary stall holder, who are separately identified categories under the same exemption provision.
A food business operator with commercial turnover or scale of operations that meets the threshold for a small-scale or cottage industry.
Any food business operating across multiple states or with organised supply chains, even if individual units appear small.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a tiny food business operator determines whether they need a licence or only a registration under Section 31, significantly reducing their compliance burden. However, they remain bound by food safety and wholesomeness standards, and failure to register or to supply safe food can still attract regulatory action under the Act.

definitions.definition: Tolerance limit means the maximum permissible level of insecticides or pesticide residues, veterinary drug residues, antibiotic residues, solvent residues, pharmacologically active substances, and microbiological counts that may be present in an article of food, as specified by regulations made under the Food Safety and Standards Act.
definitions.plain_english: A tolerance limit is the highest amount of a harmful substance — such as pesticide residues, antibiotic residues, or harmful microorganisms — that is legally allowed to remain in food without making it unsafe for consumption. Think of it as a safety ceiling: any food found to contain these substances above this set level is considered non-compliant and unsafe. These limits are decided by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) through regulations.
real_world_examples: A batch of mangoes from Maharashtra is tested and found to contain chlorpyrifos (a pesticide) at 0.8 mg/kg, which exceeds the FSSAI-prescribed tolerance limit of 0.5 mg/kg for that pesticide — the consignment is rejected and the seller is liable under the Act.

A poultry processing unit in Punjab is found to be selling chicken with oxytetracycline (an antibiotic) residues at 300 ppb, exceeding the prescribed veterinary drug residue tolerance limit — the food business operator faces prosecution and the batch is recalled.

A milk sample from a dairy cooperative in Rajasthan tests positive for aflatoxin M1 levels beyond the tolerance limit set by FSSAI regulations — the batch is seized and the manufacturer is served an improvement notice.

Packaged drinking water from a Delhi-based manufacturer is found to have total coliform counts exceeding the microbiological tolerance limit specified under FSSAI regulations, triggering enforcement action by the Food Safety Officer.

Wheat flour imported into India is found to contain fumigant solvent residues above the prescribed tolerance limit, leading to the consignment being stopped at customs and returned to the exporting country under food safety norms.
what_it_covers: Maximum permissible levels of insecticide and pesticide residues in food articles such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and processed foods.
Upper limits for veterinary drug residues and antibiotic residues in animal-derived food products such as meat, poultry, fish, eggs, and dairy.
Permissible microbiological counts (such as coliforms, Salmonella, E. coli) in food products including packaged water, milk, and ready-to-eat foods.
Limits on solvent residues and pharmacologically active substances that may remain in food as a result of processing or agricultural practices.
Pesticide residues entering food from environmental contamination, even if not directly applied to the food item.
what_it_excludes: Food additives intentionally added to food, which are governed separately under Section 19 and their own specific limits.
Contaminants, toxic substances, and heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, or cadmium, which have separate permissible limits under Section 20.

Direct application of insecticides on food articles, which is categorically prohibited under Section 21 except for fumigants registered under the Insecticides Act, 1968 — the tolerance limit concept does not legitimise such direct use.
Extraneous matter or adulterants in food, which are addressed under separate provisions of the Act and do not fall under the tolerance limit framework.
Substances that are completely prohibited in food with zero permissible presence — such substances are not subject to a tolerance limit but are governed by absolute prohibition rules.
definitions.why_it_matters: If residues, drug remnants, or microbiological counts in a food article exceed the prescribed tolerance limit, the food is deemed non-compliant and potentially 'unsafe food' under the Act, exposing the food business operator to penalties, product seizure, licence cancellation, and criminal prosecution under Sections 49, 50, and related provisions. Conversely, if levels are within the tolerance limit, the food is considered legally compliant and cannot be penalised solely on the basis of those residues being present.

definitions.definition: "Tribunal" means the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal established under section 70 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, being the designated adjudicatory body to hear and decide appeals against orders passed by the Adjudicating Officer and other authorities under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Tribunal is a special legal body set up under the Food Safety and Standards Act to hear appeals from businesses or individuals who are unhappy with penalty orders or decisions made by food safety officials. It functions like a court but is specifically dedicated to food safety disputes. People can challenge fines or adverse orders before this body instead of going directly to a regular civil court.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based food manufacturer penalised Rs. 5 lakh by the Adjudicating Officer for selling sub-standard packaged snacks files an appeal before the Tribunal challenging the quantum of penalty imposed.
A Delhi restaurant chain whose food licence was cancelled by the Commissioner of Food Safety for repeated hygiene violations approaches the Tribunal to contest the cancellation order.

A Hyderabad spice exporter found guilty of adulteration by an Adjudicating Officer under Section 49 appeals to the Tribunal arguing that the laboratory test results were not conducted in an accredited laboratory and should be set aside.
A Pune dairy company penalised for misbranding its milk products files an appeal before the Tribunal under Section 72, seeking a stay on the penalty order while the matter is heard.

A street food aggregator in Chennai challenges before the Tribunal an order passed against it under the Act, claiming it does not qualify as a food business operator and the penalty is therefore without jurisdiction.
what_it_covers: Appeals filed by food business operators against penalty orders passed by the Adjudicating Officer under Section 49 of the Act.
Appeals against orders relating to cancellation or suspension of food licences passed by competent food safety authorities.
Proceedings under Sections 71 and 72 involving appeals on questions of fact or law arising from decisions of food safety adjudicating authorities.
Cases where a party aggrieved by an order seeks stay, modification, or reversal of an adverse food safety decision.
Matters where the Tribunal exercises original or appellate jurisdiction specifically conferred by the Food Safety and Standards Act.
what_it_excludes: Criminal prosecutions for food safety offences, which are tried before a Special Court designated under the Act and not before the Tribunal.
Matters falling under the original jurisdiction of civil courts or consumer forums not connected to appellate proceedings under this Act.
Disputes between private parties regarding commercial food contracts that do not involve a penalty or order by a food safety authority.
Appeals or proceedings governed by other statutes such as the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (now repealed) that were not subsumed under FSSAI jurisdiction.
Administrative or policy decisions of the Food Authority (FSSAI) that are not in the nature of adjudicatory orders subject to appeal under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a forum qualifies as the 'Tribunal' under the Act determines which body has jurisdiction to hear an appeal under Sections 71 and 72, and an appeal filed before a wrong forum will be dismissed as not maintainable, leaving the penalty or adverse order intact. The existence and functioning of the Tribunal is also the procedural gateway that bars parties from approaching civil courts directly, making it the mandatory first appellate authority in food safety enforcement disputes.

It functions like a court but is specifically dedicated to food safety disputes. People can challenge fines or adverse orders before this body instead of going directly to a regular civil court.

Legal text: "Tribunal" means the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal established under section 70 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, being the designated adjudicatory body to hear and decide appeals against orders passed by the Adjudicating Officer and other authorities under this Act.

Examples: A Mumbai-based food manufacturer penalised Rs. 5 lakh by the Adjudicating Officer for selling sub-standard packaged snacks files an appeal before the Tribunal challenging the quantum of penalty imposed. | A Delhi restaurant chain whose food licence was cancelled by the Commissioner of Food Safety for repeated hygiene violations approaches the Tribunal to contest the cancellation order. | A Hyderabad spice exporter found guilty of adulteration by an Adjudicating Officer under Section 49 appeals to the Tribunal arguing that the laboratory test results were not conducted in an accredited laboratory and should be set aside. | A Pune dairy company penalised for misbranding its milk products files an appeal before the Tribunal under Section 72, seeking a stay on the penalty order while the matter is heard. | A street food aggregator in Chennai challenges before the Tribunal an order passed against it under the Act, claiming it does not qualify as a food business operator and the penalty is therefore without jurisdiction.

Tags: appellate adjudicatory body, food safety dispute resolution, statutory tribunal food law, appeal against penalty order, food law quasi-judicial forum, review of Adjudicating Officer orders, food business operator remedy, independent appellate authority, Food Safety Act enforcement review, judicial oversight food regulation

Covers: Appeals filed by food business operators against penalty orders passed by the Adjudicating Officer under Section 49 of the Act.; Appeals against orders relating to cancellation or suspension of food licences passed by competent food safety authorities.; Proceedings under Sections 71 and 72 involving appeals on questions of fact or law arising from decisions of food safety adjudicating authorities.; Cases where a party aggrieved by an order seeks stay, modification, or reversal of an adverse food safety decision.; Matters where the Tribunal exercises original or appellate jurisdiction specifically conferred by the Food Safety and Standards Act.

Excludes: Criminal prosecutions for food safety offences, which are tried before a Special Court designated under the Act and not before the Tribunal.; Matters falling under the original jurisdiction of civil courts or consumer forums not connected to appellate proceedings under this Act.; Disputes between private parties regarding commercial food contracts that do not involve a penalty or order by a food safety authority.; Appeals or proceedings governed by other statutes such as the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (now repealed) that were not subsumed under FSSAI jurisdiction.; Administrative or policy decisions of the Food Authority (FSSAI) that are not in the nature of adjudicatory orders subject to appeal under the Act.

Why it matters: Whether a forum qualifies as the 'Tribunal' under the Act determines which body has jurisdiction to hear an appeal under Sections 71 and 72, and an appeal filed before a wrong forum will be dismissed as not maintainable, leaving the penalty or adverse order intact. The existence and functioning of the Tribunal is also the procedural gateway that bars parties from approaching civil courts directly, making it the mandatory first appellate authority in food safety enforcement disputes.

definitions.definition: An unfair trade practice, for the purposes of this Act, means any unfair or deceptive practice adopted by a person for the purpose of promoting the sale, supply, use and consumption of articles of food, including the practice of making any statement, whether orally or in writing or by visible representation, which falsely represents that the foods are of a particular standard, quality, quantity or grade-composition; makes a false or misleading representation concerning the need for, or the usefulness of, the food; or gives to the public any guarantee of efficacy that is not based on adequate or scientific justification.
definitions.plain_english: An unfair trade practice means any dishonest or deceptive method used by a food business to sell or promote food products. This includes making false claims about the quality, quantity, grade, or health benefits of a food item — whether spoken, written, or shown visually — that mislead consumers into buying something based on incorrect information. For example, labelling a product as 'scientifically proven to cure diabetes' without any scientific backing would be an unfair trade practice.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based packaged snack company prints '100% Natural, No Preservatives' on its chips packaging when the product actually contains artificial preservatives, misleading consumers about the product's composition.

A health drink brand in Delhi runs a television advertisement claiming its product 'guarantees a 20% increase in children's height within 3 months' without any clinical or scientific evidence to support the claim.

A wholesale food distributor in Chennai sells rice bags labelled as 'Grade A Basmati' when the product is actually a lower-grade non-basmati variety blended to resemble premium rice, falsely misrepresenting quality and grade.

An online food retailer on a popular Indian e-commerce platform falsely advertises its protein powder as 'FSSAI certified for treating nutritional deficiencies' when no such certification or therapeutic approval exists, exploiting consumer trust in regulatory labels.

A street-facing dairy outlet in Kolkata orally assures customers that its packaged ghee is 'pure cow ghee from organic farms' when the product is adulterated with vegetable fat, constituting a verbal unfair trade practice.
what_it_covers: Making written, oral, or visual statements that falsely represent the standard, quality, quantity, or grade-composition of a food article during its promotion or sale.
Publishing advertisements or making representations that give consumers a false or misleading impression about the need for or usefulness of a particular food product.
Offering guarantees of health efficacy or therapeutic benefits of a food product to the public without adequate scientific or clinical justification to back such claims.
Any deceptive trade method — including misleading packaging, labelling, or promotional campaigns — intended to induce consumers to purchase food based on false information.
what_it_excludes: Genuine and scientifically substantiated health or nutritional claims about a food product that are supported by adequate scientific evidence and do not mislead consumers.
Accurate and truthful advertising of food products that correctly represents their ingredients, grade, quality, and composition in compliance with FSSAI regulations.
Farming operations, agricultural practices, or activities of a farmer or fisherman at the farm level, which are expressly excluded from the purview of this Act under Section 18.
Regulatory or government-issued public advisories and information campaigns about food safety risks, which are communications in the public interest and not promotional trade activities.
Honest statements of opinion or puffery that a reasonable consumer would not interpret as factual claims about efficacy, standard, or composition of a food product.
definitions.why_it_matters: Engaging in an unfair trade practice under Section 24 constitutes a contravention of the Food Safety and Standards Act, exposing the person or food business operator to penalties, prosecution, and regulatory action by the Food Authority or the Commissioner of Food Safety. A finding that a practice qualifies as an 'unfair trade practice' triggers prohibition, potential cancellation of licences, and liability under the Act's penal provisions, while the burden of proving any defence of scientific justification rests on the person making the efficacy claim.

definitions.definition: Though not expressly defined in Section 3 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, 'unhygienic' as used in Section 56 refers to conditions, practices, or situations relating to the manufacture, preparation, storage, sale, or distribution of food that do not conform to prescribed standards of cleanliness and sanitation, thereby rendering the food likely to be contaminated or unsafe for human consumption.
definitions.plain_english: Unhygienic refers to any dirty, unclean, or unsanitary condition in which food is made, stored, handled, or sold that could make it harmful or unfit to eat. This includes things like using dirty utensils, preparing food in pest-infested areas, or storing food near waste or sewage. Essentially, it means any condition that falls below the basic cleanliness standards required for safe food handling.
real_world_examples: A street food vendor in Mumbai preparing pav bhaji using unwashed hands and dirty utensils near an open drain, exposing the food to bacterial contamination.
A dairy unit in Punjab storing milk in rusted, uncleaned containers kept in a room shared with cattle waste and without any ventilation or refrigeration.
A mid-day meal kitchen in a government school in Uttar Pradesh where cooked food is left uncovered and exposed to flies, rodents, and dust before being served to children.
A small sweet shop in Kolkata where mithai is manufactured in a room with peeling walls, standing water on the floor, and rodent droppings visible on the premises.
A slaughterhouse in Hyderabad where meat is processed without proper drainage, waste disposal, or regular cleaning of equipment, leading to cross-contamination of the product.
A packaged water unit in Delhi operating without adequate sanitation facilities for workers and without regular cleaning of storage tanks, resulting in microbial contamination of the final product.
what_it_covers: Food prepared or stored in premises infested with rodents, insects, or pests without adequate pest control measures.
Use of unclean, rusted, or contaminated equipment, utensils, or containers in the manufacture or serving of food.
Handling of food by persons who have not followed basic personal hygiene practices such as handwashing, or who are suffering from communicable diseases.
Storage of food in proximity to waste material, sewage, chemicals, or other substances likely to contaminate it.
Food business premises lacking adequate drainage, ventilation, potable water supply, or proper waste disposal systems as prescribed under food safety regulations.
what_it_excludes: Food that is sub-standard in terms of nutritional composition or quality parameters but manufactured under clean and sanitary conditions.
Food that contains a permitted food additive or processing aid that may affect taste or appearance but does not involve any unsanitary practice.
Conditions or premises that meet the prescribed Good Hygienic Practices and Food Safety Management System standards even if the final food product is otherwise deficient.
Extraneous matter present in food as a result of raw material sourcing that does not arise from unhygienic practices at the manufacturing or handling stage.

Naturally occurring contaminants in primary food (such as pesticide residues within tolerance limits from agricultural practices) that are not the result of unhygienic handling by the food business operator.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 56 of the Act, manufacturing, storing, selling, or distributing any article of food in unhygienic conditions is a punishable offence attracting imprisonment of up to six months and/or a fine of up to one lakh rupees; a finding that conditions are 'unhygienic' can also trigger improvement notices, prohibition orders, and licence cancellation, making it a critical threshold for regulatory action by the Food Safety Officer or Designated Officer.

definitions.definition: Food is 'unsafe' for the purposes of this Act if it is injurious to health or unfit for human consumption, having regard to the normal conditions of use of the food by the consumer, the information provided to the consumer including information on the label and any other information generally available, the immediate and/or cumulative effect on the health of the consumer, particular health sensitivities of a specific category of consumers, and the presence of any contaminant or adulterant rendering the food harmful.
definitions.plain_english: A food item is called 'unsafe' when it is likely to harm the health of a person who eats it or when it is simply not fit to be eaten at all. This includes food that is contaminated, adulterated, spoiled, or contains harmful substances. Even if just one part of a batch or consignment is unsafe, the whole lot may be treated as unsafe under the law.
real_world_examples: A batch of packaged milk in Maharashtra found to contain melamine or formalin, making it hazardous for consumption, would be classified as unsafe food.
Street food in Delhi prepared using recycled cooking oil that has exceeded safe peroxide levels and poses a risk of liver damage to consumers qualifies as unsafe.
Spices sold in Kerala adulterated with artificial colour containing Sudan Red, a carcinogenic substance banned in India, constitute unsafe food.
Packaged drinking water sold in Tamil Nadu found to exceed permissible limits of arsenic or lead contamination is treated as unsafe under FSSAI regulations.
Sweets prepared and sold during festivals in Uttar Pradesh using synthetic khoya containing urea or starch that causes gastrointestinal injury are classified as unsafe food.
Ready-to-eat packaged snacks in Mumbai found to contain Salmonella or E. coli beyond permissible limits during laboratory testing are deemed unsafe.
what_it_covers: Food containing biological, chemical, or physical hazards such as pathogens, pesticide residues beyond tolerance limits, or heavy metals that can cause adverse health effects.
Adulterated food where the adulterant renders the food injurious to health, such as milk diluted with detergent or oil mixed with non-edible substances.
Food that has decomposed, is putrid, rotten, or otherwise unfit for human consumption even if it does not contain any added harmful substance.
Food in which contaminants are present at levels exceeding the safe limits specified by FSSAI regulations, posing a health risk to consumers.
Packaged or processed food that has been tampered with or stored under conditions (such as broken cold chains) that render it harmful to eat.
what_it_excludes: Food containing extraneous matter that does not render the article unsafe, such as minor packaging residues that do not cause harm to health.
Food that is sub-standard or misbranded but does not pose any direct health risk to the consumer, as sub-standard status alone does not make food unsafe.
Food that is not intended for human consumption at the point of examination, such as animal feed or live animals not yet processed for the market.
Food additives or processing aids that are present within permissible limits set by FSSAI regulations and do not cause any adverse health effect.
Extraneous matter such as insect fragments or rodent hairs that fall within the definition of extraneous matter and do not independently render the food unsafe.
definitions.why_it_matters: Classification of food as 'unsafe' directly triggers penal liability under Sections 59 and 27 of the FSSA, including imprisonment up to six months to life and fines up to ten lakh rupees or more depending on the severity of injury caused; it also empowers Food Safety Officers under Section 26 to seize, recall, or destroy such food and enables adjudication of compensation to affected consumers under Section 48.

definitions.definition: "Unsafe food" means an article of food whose nature, substance or quality is so affected as to render it injurious to health, or which fails to comply with the provisions of this Act or the rules and regulations made thereunder, including food that contains any contaminant, adulterant, or extraneous matter in excess of the limits prescribed, or is prepared, packed, or stored under unhygienic or unsanitary conditions, or is the product of a diseased animal or decomposed substance, or is adulterated within the meaning of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: Unsafe food is any food that is harmful or likely to be harmful to your health, or food that has been made, stored, or sold in conditions that are dirty or unhygienic. It includes food containing dangerous levels of chemicals, germs, pesticides, or other harmful substances. Essentially, it is food that no reasonable person should eat because it poses a risk to health or does not meet the safety standards set by the law.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai street vendor selling pani puri prepared with contaminated water containing harmful bacteria like E. coli, causing food poisoning among consumers.
A Delhi dairy company selling milk adulterated with urea, detergent, or synthetic milk, making it injurious to health when consumed.
A packaged snack brand in Chennai found to contain pesticide residues above the permissible limits set by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).
A Kolkata sweet shop using non-permitted synthetic food colours or artificial sweeteners in mithai at concentrations that exceed safe limits.
A cold storage facility in Punjab storing meat products at incorrect temperatures, resulting in microbial growth and decomposition, rendering the meat unfit and unsafe for human consumption.
A baby food manufacturer in Pune found to have products contaminated with Salmonella bacteria during FSSAI inspection, posing serious health risk to infants.
what_it_covers: Food containing contaminants, adulterants, or pesticide residues exceeding the prescribed tolerance limits under FSSAI regulations.
Food prepared, processed, or stored under unhygienic or unsanitary conditions that are likely to render it harmful to human health.
Food derived from diseased animals or decomposed, putrid, or rotten substances that pose a health risk to consumers.
Food containing non-permitted additives, colourants, or preservatives, or permitted additives in excess of allowable concentrations.
Food that has been tampered with or mishandled in a manner that compromises its safety during transportation or distribution.
what_it_excludes: Extraneous matter that does not render the article of food unsafe, such as minor packaging residues that fall within permissible limits.
Food that is merely sub-standard or misbranded but does not pose an actual or potential injurious health effect on the consumer.
Animal feed and live animals not prepared for human consumption, as these fall outside the definition of 'food' under the Act.
Drugs, medicinal products, cosmetics, and narcotic or psychotropic substances, which are excluded from the definition of 'food' and thus cannot be classified as 'unsafe food' under this Act.
Food that does not meet labelling or packaging requirements but whose actual substance or nature is not injurious to health.
definitions.why_it_matters: A finding that food is 'unsafe' triggers serious criminal liability under Sections 25 and 80 of the Act, including penalties, prosecution, and imprisonment of the food business operator; it also empowers authorities to issue prohibition orders, seize and destroy the food, and cancel licences, whereas food that is merely sub-standard or misbranded attracts lesser penalties without the possibility of imprisonment for grievous or non-grievous injury.

definitions.definition: Conditions under which food is manufactured or processed that are unhealthy, unclean, or fail to meet basic standards of hygiene and sanitation, including the use of contaminated water, exposure to filth, vermin, or waste, or the absence of adequate sanitary facilities in a food manufacturing or processing environment.
definitions.plain_english: Unsanitary refers to conditions in a food factory or processing unit that are dirty, unhygienic, or harmful to health — for example, having open drains, pest infestations, or contaminated surfaces where food is being made. These are conditions that a reasonable person would recognize as unfit for safely preparing food meant for human consumption. Simply put, if the place where food is made would make a health inspector cringe, it likely qualifies as unsanitary.
real_world_examples: A small snack manufacturer in Uttar Pradesh found to be processing namkeen in a room shared with open sewage drainage, exposing the product to fecal contamination and foul odours.
A dairy unit in Punjab bottling milk in a facility where rats and cockroaches are visibly present, floors are covered in animal waste, and walls are coated in mould.
A street-level bakery in Mumbai producing bread in a basement where stagnant water pools near the kneading area and workers handle dough without any handwashing facilities.
A mid-sized spice processing plant in Rajasthan found during FSSAI inspection to be storing raw spices directly on the floor next to open garbage bins with no pest control measures in place.
A fish processing unit in Kerala operating with workers who lack access to toilets, leading to open defecation near the processing area, directly compromising food safety.
what_it_covers: Food processing units with visible pest infestations such as rats, cockroaches, or flies contaminating food contact surfaces.
Manufacturing premises where wastewater, sewage, or garbage is present in or adjacent to food preparation areas.
Facilities lacking adequate handwashing stations, toilet facilities, or clean water supply for workers involved in food handling.
Food factories where walls, floors, equipment, or utensils are visibly covered in mould, filth, or residues from previous batches without proper cleaning.
Processing environments where raw food ingredients are stored or handled in conditions that expose them to chemical, biological, or physical contaminants.
what_it_excludes: Minor cosmetic issues in a facility, such as peeling paint in non-food-contact areas, that do not directly pose a contamination risk to food.
Temporary and isolated lapses in cleanliness that are immediately corrected before any food processing takes place, with no risk of actual contamination.
Conditions that relate solely to the quality or composition of the food itself rather than the physical environment or premises in which it is manufactured.
Food business operators who process food in full compliance with FSSAI-prescribed sanitation and hygiene standards, even if premises appear modest or small-scale.
Purely administrative or documentation failures, such as missing sanitation records, where actual physical conditions of the premises meet hygiene standards.
